articles.title: Rains welcome Bar Examinees on first day
articles.summary: Undeterred by heavy rain, bar examinees made their way to their respective testing centers, backed by steadfast supporters who braved the weather with them.

blocks.text: September 6, 2026 | 10:35am
Rain showers at the University of Santo Tomas on Sept. 6, 2026, during the first day of the 2026 Bar Examinations.
Philstar.com / Ian Laqui
MANILA, Philippines — The first day of the 2026 Bar Examinations has been welcomed by rainshowers on Sunday, September 6.
Undeterred by heavy rain, bar examinees made their way to their respective testing centers, backed by steadfast supporters who braved the weather with them.
The Supreme Court has designated 15 local testing centers across the country for this year’s examination for admission to the practice of law.
Seven of the 15 testing centers are located in Metro Manila, with San Beda College Alabang in Muntinlupa as the headquarters.
On the first day, bar aspirants will take political and public international law in the morning and commercial and taxation laws in the afternoon.
For the second day of the Bar Exams on September 9, bar aspirants will take Civil Law and Land Titles and Deeds and Labor Law and Social Legislation.
On the last day of the exams, examinees will take Criminal Law and Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics, with Practical Exercises.
In a message to Philstar.com, Manila Police District Spokesperson Major Philip Ines said that there are 900 personnel from the Philippine National Police who are deployed for the Bar Examinations.
It takes a village to raise a lawyer
For the Bar Operations support for the bar examinees, the journey toward the Bar is never a solo march.
For University of Santo Tomas law student Claire Pascual, raising a lawyer requires a supportive community, emphasizing that to build that network, one must first step up and be a part of it.
“It takes a village to raise a lawyer and to have a village, you must first be a villager,” Pascual told Philstar.com.
Lester Rodil, also a law student from the Polytechnic University of the Philippines, went out as early as 4 a.m. at the New Era University in Quezon City.
Despite getting drenched in the rain, he said that supporting the bar examinees was "worth it" because it showed the "true spirit of the law school community."
“Every law student shares the same conundrum and hardship. If there is any moment a bar taker needs unwavering support, it is during the bar exam week,” Rodil told Philstar.com.
His message to the Bar Examinees: “Your years of hard work have led to this moment. It’s time to harvest the fruits of your labor.”
In this year’s Bar Exams, the Supreme Court cleared 13,441 applicants to take the 2026 Bar Examinations out of 14,291 total registered candidates.
Last year, there were 5,594 examinees who passed the exams, yielding a passing rate of 48.98%.

articles.title: Light traffic at NLEx on Sunday morning
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Light traffic was reported at the North Luzon Expressway (NLEx) Sunday morning despite flooded areas in San Simon, Pampanga, according to the NLEx Corporation. In its latest…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Light traffic was reported at the North Luzon Expressway (NLEx) Sunday morning despite flooded areas in San Simon, Pampanga, according to the NLEx Corporation.

In its latest traffic update as of 9:15 a.m. on Sunday, the NLEx Corporation said water buildup was still present in Lane 3 southbound of Tulaoc in San Simon and San Simon Interchange, and Lanes 2 and 3 of the northbound of Tulaoc.
Meanwhile, the water buildup has subsided in the northbound portion of San Simon.
The northbound segment of Balintawak, Valenzuela, Meycauayan, and San Simon are passable to all types of vehicles.
Only lanes 2 and 3 of the Tulaoc area are passable to all types of vehicles while lane 3 remains impassable.
Meanwhile, the Libtong Exit is temporarily closed to motorists.
On the other hand, the southbound portions of Mindanao Exit, Valenzuela, Candaba Viaduct, Tulaoc, and San Simon Interchange are passable to all types of vehicles.

Last Monday, the Metro Pacific Tollways Corporation, the operator of NLEx, apologized to inconvenienced motorists for the flooding situation last weekend and vowed to install concrete barriers in affected areas along the expressway.
NLEx Corporation was also directed by the Toll Regulatory Board (TRB) to explain the flooding situation in the area.

The TRB also expected it to alert motorists three hours before the expected rainfall through Variable Message Signs (VMS), portable VMS, and other messaging platforms that the San Simon-Pulillan Segment of NLEx will be closed to traffic if the water level reaches critical level due to heavy rainfall. /gsg

articles.title: US envoys set for Ukraine talks after meeting Putin in Moscow
articles.summary: Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner leave Moscow talks with hopes for "equally productive meetings" in Ukraine.

blocks.text: As Witkoff and Kushner were negotiating at the Kremlin, Zelensky said he was ready for "a substantive conversation".
Saturday's talks in Moscow lasted three hours and were held behind closed doors in Putin's official residence in the heart of the Russian capital, according to Russian state media.
Details are still emerging, but both sides have given broadly positive remarks without going into specifics.
Putin adviser Yuri Ushakov described the talks as "constructive, extremely frank".

"The talks were not limited to an exchange of views on resolving the Ukrainian crisis - economic issues and potential major, mutually beneficial Russian-American projects were discussed in considerable detail," he said.
Ushakov also said "note was made of the Russian army's tangible advances in the combat zone" and that there was acknowledgement that talks needed to address "the root causes of the conflict".

Despite an escalation of Russian missile and drone strikes on Ukrainian cities including Kyiv, Russian ground forces have made very slow advances for most of the conflict, incurring enormous casualties. Russia still controls about one-fifth of Ukrainian territory - areas that it seized back in 2022.

Kushner and Witkoff have visited Russia several times but given Ukraine's airspace has been closed since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, it is not clear how they will be travelling to Kyiv from Moscow.
The talks come after Russia and Ukraine have intensified aerial attacks in recent months.

Ukraine says it has struggled to repel ballistic missile attacks due to a lack of interceptor missiles, while Kyiv has focused its strikes on Russian economic infrastructure targets, notably oil installations.

articles.title: Senate extends aid to families of 3 Tacloban school shooting victims
articles.summary: TACLOBAN CITY, LEYTE, Philippines — The families of the three students killed in the June 22 shooting at San Jose National High School received financial assistance from the Senate on Friday,…

blocks.text: TACLOBAN CITY, LEYTE, Philippines — The families of the three students killed in the June 22 shooting at San Jose National High School received financial assistance from the Senate on Friday, September 4, as the chamber pushes legislation aimed at strengthening school safety nationwide.

Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian’s staff personally delivered P50,000 each to the bereaved families of Chris Lorenz Fabian, Joyancee Separa, and Ayessa Nicole Dazo, who were killed when two fellow students opened fire inside the school campus.
The assistance was received by the victims’ families, including Christopher and Erbea Fabian, parents of Chris Lorenz; Jenelyn Badoria, mother of Joyancee; and Nico and Ariet Dazo, parents of Ayessa.
The Senate had earlier adopted a resolution expressing sympathy and condolences to the families of the three learners and providing P50,000 in assistance to each bereaved family.

The June 22 shooting claimed the lives of Fabian, Separa and Dazo and injured 20 others. Fabian, 15, a Grade 10 student and Boy Scout, was hailed for attempting to protect his classmates during the attack. Separa was also 15, while Dazo was 14.

The tragedy has since prompted calls for stronger security measures in schools and greater government attention to bullying, mental health, access to firearms and possible harmful online influences affecting young people.
Gatchalian said the Senate would continue pursuing measures designed to prevent similar incidents and strengthen the capacity of schools to respond to threats.
“We will focus on proposed laws that will promote the safety of schools. We will not allow violence that results in tragedy to happen again,” he said in a press statement.

Among the measures being considered by the Senate is Senate Bill No. 2426, or the Comprehensive School Safety Act, which seeks to establish a National School Safety Framework that would set standards for preventing, responding to and recovering from threats and incidents affecting school safety.

The proposed framework seeks a more comprehensive approach to school security rather than relying solely on physical measures, covering prevention, emergency response and recovery following incidents.

Government agencies have also provided continuing assistance to the victims’ families. The Department of Social Welfare and Development has extended financial and psychosocial support, while the National Housing Authority later provided housing units to the families of the three slain students.
The shooting also triggered broader discussions on juvenile accountability.

During a Senate hearing in July, Joyancee’s mother, Jenelyn Badoria, called for stronger accountability measures, including a review of the minimum age of criminal responsibility. The family of Ayessa also sought charges against the younger suspect.
The families have repeatedly called for justice and urged authorities to strengthen school security and prevent a similar tragedy from happening again.
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. also honored Fabian, Separa and Dazo during his 2026 State of the Nation Address, describing their courage and selflessness as an inspiration to the nation. /cb /gsg

articles.title: Japan Prince Hisahito, 2nd in line to throne, turns 20
articles.summary: Prince Hisahito, the nephew of Emperor Naruhito and second in line to the Chrysanthemum Throne, turned 20 on Sunday, a year after a series of traditional ceremonies commemorated his coming of age. As…

blocks.text: Prince Hisahito, the nephew of Emperor Naruhito and second in line to the Chrysanthemum Throne, turned 20 on Sunday, a year after a series of traditional ceremonies commemorated his coming of age.

As an adult member of the imperial family, the prince has taken part in royal events and performed official duties, often alongside his parents, Crown Prince Fumihito and Crown Princess Kiko, and his elder sister Princess Kako, while prioritizing his studies at the University of Tsukuba, northeast of Tokyo.
The prince feels grateful for the various support he has received from people, according to the Imperial Household Agency.

In April, he began his second year at university. He takes English classes to read biology papers and has also enrolled in specialized courses for lectures and laboratory work in the field of biology.
The prince participated in fieldwork in the summer and is active in club activities with friends.

He has a place to live in Tsukuba, Ibaraki Prefecture that is close to his university. When he returns to Akasaka Estate in Tokyo, where his family resides, he cultivates vegetables and rice and continues to observe the habitats of creatures such as dragonflies.

After completing the coming-of-age rites in September last year, the prince renewed his commitment to fulfilling his responsibilities as an adult member of the imperial family, according to the agency.

He attended imperial ceremonies such as the New Year’s Greeting and the New Year’s Poetry Reading for the first time and debuted at a state banquet hosted by Emperor Naruhito and Empress Masako in May to welcome Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his wife Louise Araneta-Marcos.
At the dinner, the prince exchanged words in English with the Philippine guest seated next to him, the agency said.
Over the past year, he has visited six prefectures, including Mie and Kyoto, for trips related to the coming-of-age ritual and other purposes.
During a solo visit to Hiroshima Prefecture in August, he laid flowers at the Cenotaph for the A-bomb Victims, commemorating the victims of the U.S. atomic bombing in 1945.
Visiting an exhibition about an elementary school where many children lost their lives, the prince was once again struck by the tragedy of the atomic bombing, according to the agency.
He also attended a boy scout camp gathering in Jinsekikogen in Hiroshima Prefecture and delivered a speech for the first time at an official ceremony.
In November last year, his entire family attended the opening ceremony of the Tokyo Deaflympics, an international sporting event for the deaf and hard of hearing.

He visited Izu Oshima Island in the Pacific with Crown Princess Kiko to watch a competitive event and said he was delighted to be able to interact with the athletes using the sign language he had learned, the agency said.
A close aide said the prince “carries out each event with care and converses wholeheartedly with the people he meets.”
After turning 18 in September 2024, the prince became the imperial family’s first male member to reach adulthood since his father, Crown Prince Fumihito, in November 1985.
But the official coming-of-age ceremonies were postponed by a year to avoid disrupting his university entrance exam preparations. /dl

articles.title: Bukidnon IP coffee farmers get boost from national, local officials
articles.summary: QUEZON, Bukidnon — National and local officials met with indigenous coffee farmers at the municipal farm in Barangay Salawagan, Quezon, Bukidnon on Friday to bolster the town’s expanding coffee…

blocks.text: QUEZON, Bukidnon — National and local officials met with indigenous coffee farmers at the municipal farm in Barangay Salawagan, Quezon, Bukidnon on Friday to bolster the town’s expanding coffee industry and review ongoing agricultural support programs.Executive Secretary Ralph Recto, Senate President Juan Miguel Zubiri, Bukidnon Governor Rogelio Neil Roque, Quezon Mayor Pablo Lorenzo III, and Pangantucan Mayor Manolito Garces led the engagement, meeting directly with local growers to discuss their challenges, needs, and industry prospects.For generations, local farming communities relied heavily on traditional monocrops like corn, abaca, and root crops.In response to changing market demands, the municipal government has promoted coffee as a high-value alternative crop.The Municipal Agriculture Office (MAO) has turned its 4.2-hectare municipal farm into a propagation center, distributing thousands of Robusta and Catimor coffee seedlings to rural and Indigenous People (IP) farming communities.Manobo Datu Kennedy Linongcay, chairman of the Gamot-Dumasilag Tribal Agriculture Cooperative, Inc. (GDTAC), welcomed the government support, stating it provides local growers with vital momentum to sustain their livelihoods and boost the industry.During the visit, officials highlighted national financial support tied to a broader P250 million fund designated for coffee farmers nationwide this year.Meanwhile, Mayor Lorenzo appealed for additional farm-to-market roads and upland infrastructure to help farmers transport their produce more efficiently from remote communities to commercial markets. /gsg

articles.title: No cars, no condos: CHED sets limits on student-athlete perks
articles.summary: While the Student-Athletes Protection Act features ‘detailed regulation against commercialization,’ enforcing it is another matter

blocks.text: Philippine collegiate leagues have long made decisions and rules with minimal government regulation. But in 2015, the government passed the Student-Athletes Protection Act (Republic Act No. 10676) that mandated “the protection and promotion of the rights and welfare of student-athletes.”
Although it took the Commission on Higher Education (CHED) a decade to operationalize this law, with the Memorandum Order No. 13 released only last June 1, it’s notable for its clear guidelines.

“The memorandum does not only pertain to protection of student-athletes from unsafe training and competition environment that might result in injury or even fatalities. It also protects the student-athletes from commercialization, from exploitation, from unfair residency rules, from mental health issues, and even academic neglect,” said Dr. Lorenzo Lorenzo, the National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA) representative who helped draft the memorandum.
“For instance, the section defining commercialization enumerates what items schools can extend to [student-athletes].”

For decades, there have been rumors that highly touted recruits in collegiate leagues get lavish offers beyond the standard scholarship and stipends, with cars, houses, condominiums, and excessive cash allowances among the alleged perks.
This time, the CHED Memorandum Order (CMO) lists specific benefits and incentives that student-athletes can receive, including:

items: Tuition
Board and lodging
School and athletic uniforms, equipment
Reasonable monthly living allowance
Medical services and insurance
Other benefits “to enhance academic and athletic performance”

blocks.text: “Anything beyond those items enumerated is defined as commercialization,” said Lorenzo.

“For example, if the financial incentives extend to the family, or extravagant gifts and gadgets were given, or a car and a condo were given — those are items that are beyond what is provided for by the Republic Act. So, this is defined as commercialization.“
The CMO also specifies what cannot be given to student-athletes, with Section 18 prohibiting the following:

items: Excessive cash allowances or stipends beyond what is reasonably necessary for educational, training, or living expenses
Lavish gifts or incentives such as high-value gadgets and luxury items
Luxury housing or accommodations, personal vehicles or similar privileges not ordinarily available to students
Unjustified academic exemptions, automatic passing grades, or unauthorized privileges inconsistent with academic standards or procedures
Preferential treatment such as priority access to resources or services creating inequity with the general student population

blocks.text: “Perhaps one of CMO No. 13’s strongest innovations is its detailed regulation against commercialization,” said NCAA basketball commissioner Rico Paolo Quicho said.

“Section 19 likewise regulates commercial endorsements involving a student-athlete’s name, image, or likeness by requiring written consent from both the student-athlete and, where applicable, the parents or legal guardians,” he added. “These provisions reinforce the amateur nature of collegiate athletics.”
League officials, however, admit that supervising each school will be a difficult task.

“It’s hard to monitor, so that’s the challenge with regard to policing the incentives. But we have actually already drafted [a rule] on maximum benefits that we parked because of this challenge,” said Rebo Saguisag, executive director of the University Athletic Association of the Philippines (UAAP).

“Suffice it to say, right now, for lack of enforcing power or monitoring power, or investigative body, in the meantime, we can start complying with CHED requirements insofar as the reportorial requirements are concerned.”
Quicho said documentation of the benefits, and communicating it “through official institutional policies or handbooks” can be a good start.
“This promotes transparency and prevents arbitrary or discriminatory distribution of benefit,” he said.
According to Article 5 of the CMO, a student-athlete must have a minimum of 12 units per semester in a two-semester school year, or nine units in trimester setups.
The CHED also requires student-athletes to have an academic standing of at least 60% to be considered eligible.
A student-athlete’s status, however, will be terminated upon signing any contract to play professionally, as determined by the rules of the Games and Amusements Board (GAB).
During the 2020 pandemic when varsity action got shelved, GAB issued special guest licenses to collegiate athletes to allow them to play in pro sports leagues.
By 2024, however, the NCAA discontinued the practice, while the UAAP never adopted the policy.
“One of the most persistent issues confronting student-athletes is the tendency of some institutions to prioritize athletic success over academic achievement,” said Quicho.
“Student-athletes often miss classes due to training camps, tournaments, and travel schedules, resulting in learning gaps, delayed graduation, and academic underperformance.’

“In some instances, institutional pressure to maintain competitive sports programs may inadvertently encourage academic compromises,” he added. “This undermines the fundamental principle that participation in collegiate sports should complement, rather than replace, higher education.”

Another issue top collegiate leagues deal with is “poaching,” or the sudden transfer of a student-athlete to another school within the league, which usually frustrates the alma mater that initially trained and honed the players’ skills.
Back in 2012, Jerie Pingoy, a former two-time UAAP juniors’ basketball MVP with the FEU Baby Tamaraws, spurned his high school and transferred to a stacked Ateneo Blue Eagles team for college.

Pingoy had already committed to play for the Tamaraws in the UAAP, but surprisingly left for the Blue Eagles. This led to bitter disputes, and eventually, the league crafted the so-called “Pingoy Rule,” which required high school transferees to sit out for two years before playing for their new college team.
The UAAP had since revised its rule on transferees.

“First and foremost, the freedom to transfer cannot be curtailed, especially if the student-athlete is after quality education. Another legitimate reason would be the sports program or the coach,” said Saguisag.
“Other than that, we want to address exploitation or commercialization, as incentives seem to poison the decisions of these young student-athletes.”
Another controversial transfer involved Mason Amos, who starred for Ateneo for one UAAP men’s basketball season before suddenly transferring to rival La Salle in 2024.
The move prompted the UAAP to again revise its transfer rule, where an athlete will have one year of eligibility deducted, on top of the existing one-year residency rule.
“If you sat out two years, we see how the skills of student-athletes have regressed, as well as physical fitness,” Saguisag said.

“I believe that the lawyers have studied [our rules], it’s permissible under current law, but the reason why we did that is when a person transfers, not for the legitimate reasons that I said, aside from commercialization, is to address the collegiality among member schools,” he added.

“The respect for other [schools]. Kung magkakasama tayo dito, sana wala namang ganyanan (We are all here together, let’s not do things like that)…because it leaves a bad taste in the mouth of each of the member schools.”
The CHED memorandum also gives student-athletes space to air grievances, as it requires schools to set up a complaints mechanism and policy.

In 2013, Mikee Bartolome, a decorated UAAP high school swimmer from the University of Santo Tomas, challenged a league rule after UST refused to allow her transfer despite passing the University of the Philippines’ college admission test.
With nowhere else to go, Bartolome sought a temporary restraining order and a Quezon City court granted it, allowing her to compete in UAAP Season 76.
But this time, student-athletes can now “report misconduct or exploitation.”
“An athlete’s grades, credentials, or academic documents cannot be withheld during a transfer, especially if they have no outstanding financial obligations to the school,” said Lorenzo.
Quicho added that CMO No. 13 subjects leagues and schools to “greater accountability.”

“They must register with the CHED, establish grievance mechanisms…investigate complaints, and comply with annual reporting requirements. These measures reinforce transparency and responsible governance throughout collegiate athletics,” he said.
CHED said student-athletes, parents or guardians, member schools or their alumni, and other stakeholders may file a complaint.
“Upon notice and hearing, CHED may impose the appropriate penalties under relevant laws, rules or regulations,” the memorandum states.
After an investigation, a school found guilty of violating the rules will merit a maximum fine of P1 million and/or a ban from participation in their respective leagues.
The leagues themselves may be fined a maximum of P1 million if found liable for any violation.
“There’s a continuous review of our policies. And again, it’s a matter of enforcing them, which is really a big challenge, but we have to start somewhere,” said Saguisag.

Quicho agreed that “the effectiveness of the memorandum will depend on consistent implementation, adequate institutional resources, meaningful enforcement, and ongoing monitoring to ensure that its protections translate into tangible improvements in the lives of student-athletes.”

CHED notes that the memorandum applies to all public and private schools, varsity leagues and inter-school competitions nationwide, off-campus activities, all persons involved in athletic programs, as well as foreign student-athletes.
Schools and athletic organizations have six months to comply with the required initial documentation after the memorandum rollout in June.
But as Saguisag reminded: “Legislating on that matter is one thing. Enforcing and policing it is another matter.” – Rappler.com

articles.title: Saxony-Anhalt's state election will have a nationwide impact
articles.summary: The parliamentary election in the small eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt could have dramatic consequences for Germany's federal government, further raising dissatisfaction with Chancellor Friedrich…

image.caption: Chancellor Friedrich Merz (center) made few campaign appearances in Saxony-Anhalt to support CDU Premier Sven Schulze (right)Image: Kay Nietfeld/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Only 1.6 million eligible voters are called to choose a new state parliament in Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday. The region between the Elbe River and Harz Mountains in eastern Germany is outnumbered in population by 10 of Germany's total 16 federal states.

Nonetheless, the vote has become a major challenge for the federal government coalition of the conservative Union — of the Christian Democrats and their Bavarian sister party the Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) — and the center-left Social Democrats (SPD). In the last few months, there were even rumors in Berlin that German Chancellor Friedrich Merz of the CDU could step down following this vote — or that he would be forced to by his own party.

This is because the in-part right-wing extremist Alternative for Germany (AfD) party leads the polls in Saxony-Anhalt, far ahead of the centrist parties governing at the federal level, the CDU and SPD. Even an absolute majority for the right-wing populists cannot be ruled out. If that came to pass, the election would have serious consequences for the federal government in Berlin.
A threat to Chancellor Friedrich Merz?
Political scientist Carsten Koschmieder from the Free University in Berlin does not believe Merz will give up.

"I do not have the impression that he is a person who would resign," Koschmieder told DW. "Rather, he is very glad to be chancellor and has long worked toward that." In addition, there is currently no ready successor to Merz in the CDU and CSU, he added.

An absolute majority for the AfD could, however, plunge the governing coalition in Berlin into crisis, Koschmieder said. It would also intensify pressure regarding the correct way to deal with the AfD, which is in parts right-wing extremist.

Before he was elected chancellor in May 2025, Merz set the goal of halving support for the AfD, in part by adopting a tough migration policy. The fact that this has not succeeded, and instead the CDU has lost support, has yielded him much criticism within his party. His Union of the CDU and CSU has categorically ruled out working with the AfD, as have all other established German political parties.
Could a CDU government get support from the Left Party?

It's also possible that the CDU in Saxony-Anhalt ends up forming a minority government with the SPD and the environmentalist Greens. But even such a three-way coalition is unlikely to have a majority in parliament.

This would mean it has to be tolerated, ironically, by the socialist Left Party. Ironic, because the CDU also wants to avoid any cooperation with the Left, as the chancellor reiterated in an interview with regional newspaper the Mitteldeutsche Zeitung: "Both the AfD and Left Party have such fundamental differences with the Union that cooperation is out of the question," Merz said on Tuesday.
Saxony-Anhalt election: Can the CDU stop the AfD?

Here, Koschmieder said, a double problem arises for Merz: Many local-level CDU politicians, especially in eastern Germany, consider cooperation with the AfD quite possible, and have categorically rejected working with the Left Party.

But many other conservative politicians fear the opposite: that engaging with the right-wing populists would massively damage the CDU/CSU. "There are many conservative democrats in the CDU who say: We have nothing to do with the AfD. They want to abolish our democracy; they support Russia's President Putin and oppose Western integration and European unity," Koschmieder explained.
Merz: Government stability not at risk

In other words: It is mainly for the chancellor's party that the election result in Saxony-Anhalt could become a crucial test. Merz has already identified this issue, and has made recent calls for calm.
"Outsiders are trying to drive a wedge into the Union. The result of a state parliament election does not endanger the stability of the federal government," he told the Mitteldeutsche Zeitung.
Amid far right's rise, is Germany at a breaking point?

The chancellor seems resolved to carry on with his government, even amid growing dissatisfaction and rising pressure. This year, he still plans to bring his controversial reforms of the old age pension system through parliament, which have been heavily criticized by members of his own party on the campaign trail in Saxony-Anhalt.
But that hasn't discouraged Merz. "The pension system is no longer sustainable because of demographics, and we have known this for years," he said.
AfD state government feared to be a security risk

Political scientist Koschmieder also thinks many CDU politicians at the state level will continue their criticism of the pension reform plans, but he added: "I do not think they will completely fail, but there will be amendments in some places."

Pressure from his own party, problems with upcoming reforms — all of this could be in store for the chancellor. And that's not all: Interior policy and security experts at the federal and state levels have warned of high risks if a possible AfD government in Saxony-Anhalt has access to sensitive data — when it comes to counterintelligence, for example.

Georg Maier, the SPD interior minister in the eastern state of Thuringia, told German media outlet RND: "If an AfD politician becomes the interior minister of Saxony-Anhalt, that would be in my view a glaring security risk for Germany."
What if Germany's far-right AfD party wins in Saxony-Anhalt?
SPD hopes for success in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania

What about the Social Democrats? A possible result of 8% or 9% of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt, as recently calculated by pollsters, sounds terribly low, but it would be a great improvement on what was being predicted six months ago.

In addition, the Social Democrat premier of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Manuela Schwesig, has good odds of a renewed mandate in state parliament elections there on September 20. The SPD has made a strong comeback in the polls in the coastal state since last year; with around 30% of the vote, they could form a government with the Left Party, the CDU or potentially both.
But also here, in northeastern Germany, the AfD is the strongest polling party, at around 35%.
Why voters are so unhappy with leadership in democracies
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Labor plans crackdown on social media algorithms as Taylor says he’s ‘deeply sceptical’
articles.summary: Anika Wells expected to release legislation creating a digital duty of care in parliament this week, but Coalition argues it is ‘attempt to censor the internet’

blocks.text: Labor’s plan to crack down on social media algorithms faces significant opposition in federal parliament, with the opposition leader, Angus Taylor, warning against efforts by the government to “censor” free speech online.
The communications minister, Anika Wells, is expected to release draft legislation creating a digital duty of care for social media users in Australia as parliament returns this week.

Among new rules being considered are functions requiring popular social media platforms to allow users to turn off algorithms controlling the content in their feeds, and to better identify problematic or illegal content to protect vulnerable users including children.

Labor wants to better protect social media users from being fed content that reinforces dangerous stereotypes and behaviours, including in areas around body image, women’s safety and child protection.
Fines of more than $100m would be created for breaches, with new powers given to the eSafety commissioner and researchers to investigate compliance by big platforms.
The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, is expected to spruik the plan at the United Nations general assembly in New York later this month.
Taylor told News24 on Sunday the government should focus on fixing problems with its under 16s social media ban before taking on new rules like the digital duty of care.
“I think everyone’s very disappointed at the way the government has implemented the initiatives to stop young Australians from getting access to social media,” he said.
“It’s something like a 4.4% reduction we’ve seen, which is just immaterial in the scheme of things. What we want to see is parents having more control over what the kids get to see on social media.
“We’ll wait and see this legislation. I’m deeply sceptical. I fear that this is just going to be an attempt by the government to censor social media.”
He warned against the communications minister having “enormous” discretion in any new powers.
“I fear, given Labor and the minister’s past biases, that this will just be an attempt to censor the internet, and that’s not what we should be doing.”

The shadow home affairs minister, the outgoing Liberal senator Jonno Duniam, likened the government’s plans to dumped anti-misinformation legislation introduced during Labor’s first term in government.
after newsletter promotion

“Empowering individuals to make a choice about what they consume is absolutely where we should be at,” he said. “Empowering parents to do the same for those that are in their custody, their kids, should absolutely absolutely do something.”
Duniam told ABC TV the Coalition would only support the plan if “it doesn’t necessarily impede on people’s rights and freedoms.”
“I think that we probably already have in terms of our broadcast, free to air, film, and cinema, and other forms of media classification program, a good sort of baseline to go from.”
The One Nation leader, Pauline Hanson, has already criticised the government’s plan, warning Labor should not have control over what Australians see online.
“Australia should be moving away from government censorship, not building the Orwellian machinery for it,” Hanson posted on social media last week.
Given the opposition from the Coalition and One Nation, any new legislation would require support from the Greens to pass the Senate.

The Greens have called for opt-in rules, like those supported by campaigner Chanel Contos. That model would require social media users to give explicit consent to platforms before being subject to algorithm-based content in their feed.

articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Tropical storm Pilandok (international name: Krovanh) may reenter the Philippine area of responsibility (PAR) on Sunday, according to the state weather bureau. In the 5 a.m.…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Tropical storm Pilandok (international name: Krovanh) may reenter the Philippine area of responsibility (PAR) on Sunday, according to the state weather bureau.

In the 5 a.m. weather forecast of the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (Pagasa), weather specialist Obet Badrina said that as of 3 a.m., Sunday, Pilandok was tracked some 875 kilometers northeast of extreme Northern Luzon.

“Halos nasa boundary ng PAR at hindi inaalis ang posibilidad na muli itong pumasok within the day. Kung papasok man ito, posibleng lumabas din within the day, lalabas din ng Philippine area of responsibility,” Badrina said.
(It is almost within the PAR’s boundary and its possibility of reentering the PAR within the day is not ruled out. Once it does, it may also exit the PAR within the day.)
He also said that once it reenters the PAR, it will move northward and will weaken into a tropical depression by Monday.
“Pumasok man o hindi, inaasahan na magpapalakas ito ng southwest monsoon bagamat hindi magkakaroon ng direktang epekto sa bansa,” Badrina added.
(Whether or not it re-enters the PAR, it is expected to enhance the southwest monsoon, however, it will not directly affect the country.)
Rainy Sunday
Meanwhile, Badrina said that the southwest monsoon will continue to bring rains over the western section of Luzon and Visayas.
He noted that heavy rainfall is expected over Zambales, Bataan, parts of Cavite, Batangas, Occidental Mindoro.

He added that Metro Manila, and the rest of Luzon, including the Ilocos region, Cordillera Administrative Region, rest of Central Luzon, Mimaropa (Mindoro, Marinduque, Romblon, and Palawan), and Calabarzon (Cavite, Laguna, Batangas, Rizal, and Quezon) may experience cloudy skies with chances of light to moderate rainshowers.
Fair weather forecast
Western Visayas is forecast to have cloudy skies while fair weather is expected in the rest of the Visayas and Mindanao.

articles.title: Indonesia uses water bombing to contain wildfires near future capital
articles.summary: JAKARTA — Indonesian authorities carried out a water bombing operation on Saturday to prevent wildfires from spreading in the future capital city Nusantara, a city official told AFP. The…

blocks.text: JAKARTA — Indonesian authorities carried out a water bombing operation on Saturday to prevent wildfires from spreading in the future capital city Nusantara, a city official told AFP.
The archipelago is constructing a new capital city in Borneo, home to vast tropical jungle, to replace sinking and traffic-clogged Jakarta.

The country is also fighting to contain wildfires that have burned large swathes of Sumatra and Borneo, which caused choking haze that has drifted across the border to Malaysia, Singapore and the Philippines.

Fires have been intensifying since mid-August in buffer areas outside the core area in Nusantara, where the city’s development is concentrated, Nusantara authority environment and natural resources deputy Myrna Asnawati Safitri said.
It prompted authorities to carry out a water bombing operation to complement on-the-ground firefighting efforts, she added.
“The function of water bombing is not only to extinguish fires but also to accelerate cooling in areas that have been extinguished by ground firefighters,” Myrna said.
The operation will last until Sunday, but Myrna said it can be extended if necessary.
So far, Nusantara’s construction has not been hampered by wildfires or haze, she said.
Then-president Joko Widodo revived the long-proposed capital move from Jakarta when he won a second term in 2019.
But construction has slowed down under his predecessor Prabowo Subianto, as the former general prioritised his welfare programmes including a free meal scheme for students.

As president-elect, Prabowo said he wanted to “continue, if possible finish” the capital move, but since taking office in 2024 he has yet to express any plans to sign the presidential decree needed to shift from Jakarta.
His spokesman Prasetyo Hadi said Nusantara should be ready to host the executive, legislative and judicial branches of the government before the move can take place, local media reported. /dl

articles.title: 43 reported dead due to Habagat, cyclones Luis, Maymay, Neneng, Pilandok --NDRRMC
articles.summary: Forty-three individuals reportedly died after the monsoon rains and tropical cyclones Luis, Maymay, Neneng, and Pilandok battered parts of the country, the National Disaster Risk Reduction and…

blocks.text: Published September 6, 2026 9:19am

Forty-three individuals reportedly died after the rains from the Southwest Monsoon (Habagat) and tropical cyclones Luis, Maymay, Neneng, and Pilandok battered parts of the country, the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council (NDRRMC) said.
In the latest NDRRMC data issued at 6 p.m. of September 5, most of the deaths were due to landslide and drowning. There were also deaths caused by electrocution and fallen tree.

The fatalities were recorded in Benguet (15), La Union (1), Pangasinan (3), Zambales (3), Pampanga (2), Rizal (6), Batangas (4), Quezon (2), Oriental Mindoro (1), Occidental Mindoro (2), Negros Occidental (1), and Caloocan (3).
On the other hand, 20 were reported injured. These were logged in Ilocos Sur, Benguet, Abra, Quezon City, Rizal, and Cavite.
There were also five individuals reportedly missing. They were from Quezon City, Manila, Batangas, Rizal, and Pampanga.

The weather disturbances also affected 2.9 million families or 10.2 million individuals. They were recorded in Ilocos Region, Central Luzon, CALABARZON, MIMAROPA, Bicol Region, National Capital Region, and Western Visayas.
In 814 evacuation centers, there were 18,299 families or 62,791 currently seeking temporary shelter.
When it comes to damaged houses, 3,882 are partially torn while 585 others were totally destructed.
According to PAGASA, the Southwest Monsoon or Habagat will continue to affect Luzon and Visayas, bringing occasional rains and thunderstorms over several areas on Sunday. —KG, GMA News

Charles, 77, who is being treated for an undisclosed form of cancer but maintains a packed schedule of engagements, released a statement mourning the loss of his “dear cousin” King Harald last week.

blocks.text: Three people have been taken to hospital with life-threatening injuries after an alleged axe attack in Victoria, with police still searching for the suspect.
The alleged attacker, who is known to the victims, came to an address in the Gippsland town of Tyers at about 12.30pm on Saturday, according to a spokesperson for Victoria police.
He is believed to have attacked an elderly man and woman, and a third person with an axe, causing serious injuries.
The man, who is in his 50s, fled the address and the victims were able to call emergency services for help, police said.
A specialist air ambulance and road paramedics were dispatched to the scene and all three victims were treated at the scene.
A spokesperson for Ambulance Victoria said a man in his 70s and a man in his 40s were transported to hospital in a critical condition.
A woman in her 70s was transported to hospital in a serious but stable condition, the spokesperson said.
The man is believed to have left the property on foot.
Victoria police launched a large-scale search for the man yesterday and were continuing to look for him on Sunday.

articles.title: 'He was a lifeline' - Families at a loss after Haitian caregivers let go in US
articles.summary: Haitian immigrants make up a large portion of the already overburdened home-care workforce.

blocks.text: Long Island mother-of-two Linda Mancuso has been "praying on a daily basis" that her disabled son's Haitian caregiver will be able to come back to work.

It was "horrifying," she says, when Jean, who had a temporary work permit, was laid off from work at the end of July from his position at a nonprofit supporting individuals with developmental and intellectual disabilities. Her son Michael is a 5ft 10in, nonverbal 23-year-old.
"Showering, sleeping, eating, tying his shoes - Michael can't tie his shoes - I mean, there's so much hands-on involvement, and Jean did all of that," she says.
Mancuso was a ball of nerves when she finally agreed to send Michael to residential care, at the age of 19, calling it "the hardest thing I've ever had to do".
When he met Jean in the adult home, however, she felt a sense of peace.
"Certain people just have it," she says of Jean. "He's literally a lifeline."
But Michael lost that lifeline weeks ago, when his employer had to lay Jean off along with 18 other Haitians.
Their temporary protected status (TPS) - which allows eligible foreign nationals from unsafe countries to work in the US - had expired.
The Trump administration first announced in June 2025 that it would be removing the TPS for Haitians, and the ensuing legal battle went all the way to the Supreme Court.
But America's top judges ruled in favour of the administration, paving the way for 350,000 Haitians to lose their status at the end of July.
The stripping of that status meant that holders can no longer legally work in the US and are at risk of deportation.
The healthcare industry, with a robust Haitian workforce, has been hit particularly hard - with legions of employers forced to fire TPS holders who work directly with patients.
Trump cancelled TPS amid a wave of measures restricting immigration, a central plank of his successful 2024 election campaign.
Immigration was one of the top concerns for voters in that election and, in Long Island, both counties decisively backed Trump.
More than a dozen countries have had their TPS terminated in Trump's second term and Haitians make up nearly a third of all TPS recipients affected.

items: Families face separation as Haiti TPS scheme ends
How US guns flow to gang-ravaged Haiti

blocks.text: The care industry is feeling the effects.

Haiti numbers among the top five countries from which immigrants in the direct-care workforce come, says Kezia Scales, vice-president of policy and research at the Paraprofessional Healthcare Institute.
The industry was already under-staffed and waitlists for many care services - from home health aides to assisted living - were already long.
"We simply do not have enough people in our domestic market, when you exclude immigrants, to fill those jobs," she tells BBC News.
National advocacy groups are campaigning for policies that would strengthen the long-term workforce - including ones that "would expand legal pathways for international caregivers".
When asked about the impact of TPS termination, a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security told the BBC that "Temporary Protected Status is exactly that - temporary".
"The assertion that the only way we can support the healthcare industry is by allowing unvetted illegal aliens to remain in the country is grossly false and lazy," the spokesperson said.

At AHRC Nassau, which employed Jean, CEO Stanfort Perry sounds exasperated and exhausted. The organisation let go of 19 Haitian staff this year and 22 last year, amidst other immigration crackdowns, he says.

"It takes us months to recruit one individual to work in this field, train them and prepare them to provide compassionate, caring support to a person with an intellectual and developmental disability," he says.
"I'm competing with fast-food restaurants, grocery stores and retail for staff, because they pay more than what we are able to pay," he adds.
It's an issue across the country. At Jewish Community Services of South Florida, which lost 18 Haitian TPS holders, the remaining aides are also working overtime.
"That is a huge financial strain on a nonprofit like us," says Sarah Katzenstein, the organisation's director of strategic communications and marketing.
The loss of TPS caregivers has been especially damaging to seniors served by the Jewish organisation, as many of them are Holocaust survivors, says Katzenstein.
"They had relationships with these home care aides for years - some of them for decades," she says, adding that Holocaust survivors especially can have difficulty trusting strangers.
"It's a very intimate relationship, so to these clients, the loss of having their Haiti TPS-holding caregivers truly is devastating."

Jewish Community Services has been writing to elected officials to advocate for proposed Senate Bill 4814, which would match a bipartisan bill already passed in the House to extend TPS for Haitians. The effort has currently stalled in the Senate, blocked by Republican opposition.

Hundreds of Haitians have been deported since the Supreme Court ruling, despite widespread gang violence in the country. White House czar Tom Homan defended the deportations in a recent CNN interview.
"The judges made a decision they must go home. And they need to go home... we're just enforcing the law. And we're doing it in a way that the American people voted for."

According to polling released last month by AP-NORC, external, support for Trump's overall immigration policy has fallen 10% since the start of his second term but remains relatively strong compared with other issues like the economy. On deportations, about half of US adults surveyed said Trump had gone too far, which is about the same number as the start of the year.
A Pew Research survey in June 2025, external, before the TPS provision was withdrawn from Haitians, suggested 39% of Americans supported the ending of TPS but 59% disapproved.
Back on Long Island, Mancuso is grieving the loss of a carer who had actually managed to connect with her high-needs son.
"That's one of the things that, as a parent, you worry [about]. Does this kid know that there are other people in the world, other than me, that love him?
"And I think he sensed that from Jean - that it's not just a job."
Her son might not be able to say it, but she knows he misses Jean and doesn't understand why he's no longer there. For Mancuso, her already-high anxiety about her son's well-being is skyrocketing.
"With Jean, I had not a care in the world," she says.

She's worried not just for her son but also for the other families served by the local non-profit - and, of course, for Jean and TPS holders like him who are living with uncertainty, unsure if or when they will be deported.

"I'm hoping against hope that this thing gets resolved," she says. "I care about [Jean] as a human being, he needs a livelihood - and this has been a livelihood for him, and he's good at it, helping my son.
"And it's directly impacting my son by his lack of presence here - and I want him back."

articles.title: Majority Russian-speaking city in Ukraine considers language ban in the arts
articles.summary: Ukraine's third-biggest city Odesa decides this week whether to ban Russian-language content in music and literature in public.

blocks.text: Ukraine's third-biggest city Odesa will decide this week whether to back a controversial plan to ban the Russian language in the arts.
The proposal being considered by councillors in Odesa on the Black Sea coast aims to add to existing restrictions on Russian imposed by national legislation.
It is particularly significant because Odesa is overwhelmingly Russian-speaking, although the ban would only affect public spaces and everyday usage of Russian would remain unaffected.

For millions of Ukrainians, Russian is their first language including many of the troops defending the country in its war with Russia. But Ukrainian is the only state language and spoken by the majority, and some see Russian as a tool of Russian influence.

The proposal in Odesa, which is targeted daily by Russian drone and missile strikes, calls for a complete halt to Russian-language content in music and literature, in streets, parks, public institutions and state-run arts and entertainment venues. It would also recommend a ban in privately owned spaces.
In a city famous for Russian-language writers and musicians, it has provoked strong passions.

The ban would extend in public spaces to old Odesa songs almost universally known throughout the former Soviet Union. All Russian-language books would be removed from display in public libraries. Currently, they can be shown, but not prominently.

"The Russian language is a weapon of Russia, and we need to try to fix that," says Odesa lawyer Artem Kartashov, who has advised local authorities on an official programme to "decolonise" the city of its historic Russian legacy.
"With Russian-speaking music and other things, Russians try to deconstruct Ukrainian identity and influence especially young people, because they grow up in a Russian-speaking environment."
But comic actor Borys Barsky, one of Odesa's best-known entertainers, says: "Russian isn't [only] the language of Putin, it's the language of [writers like] Dostoyevsky and Bulgakov.
"Who benefits from setting people against other people who love Ukraine just as deeply, only love it in a different language? Only Putin benefits from this."

Russian President Vladimir Putin has often referred to what he falsely describes as repression of the Russian-speaking minority in Ukraine as one of his justifications for launching his invasion of the country.
Russian and Ukrainian are closely related, but distinct in many ways. Many in Ukraine speak a mixture of the two, known as surzhyk.
Russian is the native language of President Volodymyr Zelensky, which he used often in his election campaign but has since used only Ukrainian in public.
But a 2019 law requires use of Ukrainian in many public and professional contexts including education, public services and customer service.
Public-facing workers - including waiters, shop assistants and doctors - must address customers or patients initially in Ukrainian, though they can later switch to Russian if the client prefers that.

Odesa's Mask Theatre, run by Barsky, has been fined for infringements of the legislation including using Russian in publicity materials. A later inspection found further violations such as a cafe sign with the Russian word for coffee.
"This isn't even like Orwell or Kafka, it's just madness," he says.

Public playing of songs by Russian citizens is already illegal across Ukraine, with exceptions for some artists who have publicly condemned the war, but Russian-language songs composed or performed by Ukrainians are still allowed.
Under the proposals they would also be banned in public places.
Anna Nerush said it would not affect someone celebrating their birthday in Russian in a private room in a restaurant, as it could not be heard outside.
"But on the streets, [hearing] the Russian language can be a real trigger, for example to [former] prisoners of war and people who've come from occupied territories," she said.
Many native Russian-speakers in Ukraine have switched to Ukrainian in recent years, particularly since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.
Photographer Natalia Mykhailenko switched even earlier. She has led tours of Odesa highlighting non-Russian elements of its history.

These include landmarks such as a Cossack cemetery that dates back to before 1794. That is the year Russian empress Catherine the Great is said to have founded the city, although it has been widely questioned in recent years.
A statue of Catherine was removed from a central Odesa square after a council vote in 2022, and streets have been renamed to commemorate some Ukrainian writers and activists.

"We must understand we were a colony," said Mykhailenko. "And these [language] laws are very important. I understand it's maybe sometimes not democratic. But without it, there will be no normal Ukraine in the future."

Anthropologist Anastasia Piliavsky, part of a group called Ukrainian Cosmopolis which aims to defend freedom of thought and speech, believes Russian-speakers are being made to feel like second-class citizens who are deprived of their heritage.
"In Ukraine, the vast majority of people understand both Russian and Ukrainian. So the question is not really one of language, it's one of liberty," she said.

"Ukraine has been fighting for freedom. The point of this war is not to be under authoritarian rule. That's what Russia has to offer. So when fines, or the threat of being fired [for breaking language laws] arrives, then people start wondering: what are we fighting for?"
It is unclear how much support the new language proposal has. It is opposed by an influential group of councillors linked to former mayor Hennadiy Trukhanov.

Beyond Odesa, a national poll showed 80% support for Ukrainian dominating "all spheres of communication" in 2022. However, a more recent survey of students in Kyiv found that 82% chose to speak Russian during break times, even though Ukrainian is enforced in classrooms.
One famous Odesan who found himself at the centre of the language controversy is Pavlo Viktor, a physics teacher whose online lessons have been followed by millions around the world.

Ukrainian language campaigners criticised him for putting the videos out in Russian, his first language, although he later translated them into Ukrainian. He was later criticised for saying he would talk to scared children in Russian during missile attacks, if that was the language they preferred.

Viktor is keen to take the heat out of the argument, explaining that currently about 10% of the Odesa population spoke Ukrainian in the street: "But if we wait 50 years, maybe 90% will speak Ukrainian."

"Ukrainianisation must be polite and soft… not to persuade children to move from Russian to Ukrainian, but to make an atmosphere when they want to do this. It's the best way. And I hope that gradually we'll move in that direction."
You can hear more about the language controversy in Odesa in the Crossing Continents podcast Ukraine: Fighting Russia, Fighting Russian, available from Tuesday 8 September.

articles.title: LOOK: 2026 Bar exams kick off on Sunday, September 6
articles.summary: Aspiring lawyers trooped to their testing centers early Sunday, September 6, as they take the first day of the 2026 Bar Examinations.

blocks.text: Published September 6, 2026 7:28am Updated September 6, 2026 7:33am

Members of the Manila Police District provide security on Sunday, September 6, 2026, at the University of Sto. Tomas as aspiring lawyers arrive to take the Bar Examinations. More than 14,000 examinees will take the exam in 15 testing centers nationwide. Screenshot from video of OLAN BOLA/Super Radyo dzBB
Aspiring lawyers trooped to their testing centers early Sunday, September 6, as they take the first day of the 2026 Bar Examinations.
As early as past 4 a.m., Bar takers arrived at the University of Santo Tomas (UST), one of the seven testing centers in Metro Manila. Their families also came with them to show support.
The Manila Police District said that 180 policemen were deployed in UST's vicinity. Meanwhile, 168 cops were securing the nearby San Beda University in Mendiola.
Manila Mayor Isko Moreno Domagoso also personally inspected the areas around UST on the first day of Bar examinations.
The Supreme Court earlier said 14,291 applicants have registered for the 2026 Bar Examinations, the highest number in the history of the Bar Exams.
The 2026 Bar Examinations will be conducted on September 6, 9, and 13 in 15 testing centers nationwide, with seven located in Metro Manila, three in Luzon, three in the Visayas, and two in Mindanao.
The San Beda College in Alabang, Muntinlupa City will serve as the national headquarters.
Several roads in Manila and Quezon City were also closed for the examinations. —Vince Angelo Ferreras/KG, GMA News

articles.title: Falling ceiling debris at Kennedy Center may mire debate over renovations
articles.summary:
Preservationists worry board may seize on incident ‘to make the point that the whole thing needs to be shut down’

Falling debris from a ceiling in the grand foyer of the John F Kennedy…

blocks.text: Falling debris from a ceiling in the grand foyer of the John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts may have complicated a battle over renovations of the Washington DC arts center that could result in the building being demolished.

A portion of the ceiling collapsed on Friday evening after heavy rain swept through the area, prompting officials to temporarily close the Edward Durell Stone-designed building. No one was injured by the debris.

Kennedy Center officials posted online on Saturday that the incident showed renovations to the building were urgently needed – an argument that Donald Trump has made in concert with a broader second-term agenda to reshape Washington.

“Another warning we can’t ignore,” the Kennedy Center said in the post. “A section of the Grand Foyer ceiling collapsed after this week’s storms. Thankfully no one was hurt. Decades of deferred maintenance made this inevitable.”

blocks.caption: The grand foyer at the Kennedy Center in Washington DC on 27 August. Photograph: Pablo Martínez Monsiváis/AP

blocks.text: Roma Daravi, the center’s vice-president for public relations, said in a statement that the collapse was “another example of the urgent need to close for renovation and revitalization, as our Chairman President Trump has championed”.

Alongside the White House ballroom, a proposed triumphal arch, fitful renovations to the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool and a remodeled golf course on the banks of the Potomac, the Kennedy Center has become a significant project for the president.
The Trump-aligned board has proposed adding Trump’s name to the building’s facade and to close the center for two years as it undergoes $250m in renovations.

Last month, a federal judge expressed doubts about the Kennedy Center’s stated intention to return Trump’s name to the building after a district court blocked the renovations and said Trump’s name had been added to the center illegally and ordered it to be removed.
The board voted earlier this month to inscribe “The John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts Restored and Renovated By President Donald J Trump” on the facade by 8 September.

If a fund for the renovations reaches $100m, another inscription would be added, reading: “Endowed by the Trump Kennedy Center Fund.” Congress has approved $257m for the project, and the Trump administration wants to raise an additional $500m through private donations.
Administration attorneys have argued that without Trump’s name on the building it would struggle to raise money for renovations.

Without the Trump-backed funding, they argue, the building “will deteriorate further into an unsafe, decrepit structure that will be required to be taken down, with a determination to follow on what to build on the site, such as a large outdoor amphitheater overlooking the Potomac River that has been proposed, by some, for many years”.

Last week a sculpture titled Blue by American post-minimalist Joel Shapiro was taken down. The Kennedy Center offered no reason for its removal, but said in a statement “we are honored to have been stewards” of the work.

Friday’s debris shower may strengthen the center’s position that the building needs a complete overhaul. Grace Terpstra of Keep the KC, a group fighting the center’s closure, told the Associated Press that the board may seize on the incident “to make the point that the whole thing needs to be shut down, that it’s going to fall on everybody”.
“I think they’ll try to make it into a bigger thing and show that they’ve found a lot of other things,” said Terpstra.

articles.title: Aviation faces hotter, stormier skies – and passengers might have to accept more disruption
articles.summary: Are people going to have to increasingly accept more delays and diversions as the effects of climate change intensify?

blocks.text: ByTheo Leggett
International business correspondent

blocks.caption: Theo Leggett

blocks.text: As the country sweltered through one of the many heatwaves of a baking summer in late June, towering thunderclouds were gathering over the south of England and across much of northern Europe. It was a Saturday, and with the holiday season getting under way, thousands of passengers were heading to London's Heathrow and Gatwick airports to catch flights abroad. It was always going to be a very busy day.

What followed, however, was chaos for travellers. As air traffic controllers struggled to route aircraft around the storms, airspace became heavily congested and many planes due to fly were simply forced to wait on the ground. In the end, some 900 flights to and from both airports were delayed, some by up to 11 hours. Dozens more were cancelled. At airports across Europe, passengers expecting to fly into London also faced long waits and uncertainty.
The weather in the UK may now have cooled, and passengers may soon forget their experiences. But some within the industry believe what happened in June should be seen as a warning.

The timing in this case was clearly unlucky. But there are concerns that such incidents are only going to become more common as the effects of climate change mount up around the world and weather systems are likely to become increasingly unstable, making disruption more likely and adding to costs for airlines, airports and travellers.
Tim Atkinson, an airline risk consultant and former pilot, says the very crowded skies over the UK and northern Europe mean the region is particularly exposed.
He thinks there is a real risk, for example, that all of London's airports could be affected by storms at the same time, potentially with major consequences in the air and on the ground.
"What we're seeing now is very rapid climate change," he says.

"We're going from the kind of weather activity which takes out an airport, and which the system kind of copes with… to a situation where, with very little predictability, it would be possible to lose all of the London airports from real-time operation quite swiftly and with little notice".
Such a scenario, he thinks, would make the disruption for passengers caused by the incident in June seem relatively minor – and could even put lives at risk. But how likely is it?
Intense activity

For controllers at National Air Traffic Services's (NATS) main control centre in Swanwick, Hampshire, thunderstorms are a major preoccupation. When I visit, it is a hot and humid day, there are ominous dark clouds in the sky, and heavy, thundery downpours are hitting the surrounding region.

In Terminal Control, the part of the building responsible for flights heading to or from airports in London and southern England, those same storm cells are being monitored continually. Their progress is tracked on large radar screens, while at the same time weather forecasts are carefully scrutinised.

Air traffic tends to come in waves during the day. Right now, at lunchtime, it is relatively quiet and the storms have yet to affect major routes. But with activity expected to intensify in the afternoon, staff are already preparing for what could be a tricky few hours.

Stormy weather can shrink the available airspace, meaning traffic has to be restricted and rerouted. If planes are unable to land at one airport, for example due to high winds, they may need diverting to another. But that can create its own problems; if too many unscheduled aircraft land at an already busy airport, it might not have sufficient infrastructure to accommodate them all.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Heavy rain and storms can make flying harder

blocks.text: Image source, VCG via Getty Images
Heavy rain and storms can make flying harder
Planes need fuel and somewhere to park. Passengers need food and facilities. Ultimately, if there isn't space, it can simply refuse to accept all but emergency traffic.

This is where the scenario set out by Atkinson comes in. He warns of a situation where traffic is diverted from Heathrow, Gatwick, Luton and Stansted at the same time, leaving aircraft coming in across the Atlantic and a large number of European flights all looking for somewhere to land at the same time, and some with dwindling fuel reserves.

This would at the very least create serious disruption for passengers, who might end up hundreds of miles from their destinations. But it could also, he thinks, create "a very serious risk event, such as an aircraft running out of fuel in the sky".
Aircraft are legally required to carry enough fuel to take them to an alternative airport if necessary, and to allow them to fly for an extra 30 minutes on top of that.
Not everyone shares Atkinson's concern. Former airline executive Andrew Charlton, who manages the Swiss-based consultancy Aviation Advocacy, thinks the risk is low.
"You've always got to imagine the worst-case scenario", he says. "But I also think we need to keep that worst case in context.

"Yes, it's possible to imagine it. But I'm also fairly comfortable with the ability of this industry to react well and make good decisions… of all the things that wake me up at 3am…this is not the top of that list."
Convective weather

Thunderstorms are caused by what is known as convective activity, where moist air close to the ground warms rapidly and rises quickly. As it rises, it expands and cools, allowing the moisture it carries to condense, forming large clouds. More heat means more convective energy, potentially creating instability. In addition, for every degree the Earth warms, the atmosphere can hold about 7% more moisture, increasing the probability of heavy rainfall.

It is not clear whether this means we will actually get more thunderstorms in the UK and across Europe, as so many variables are involved beyond the simple matter of energy and moisture. Some parts of the world may even get fewer. However, studies have shown that higher latitudes, particularly in the northern hemisphere, will see the biggest increases in favourable conditions for storms to form, and those that do may be more violent. According to the UK's Met Office, "while we may not see more thunderstorms overall, the ones we do experience could be more impactful".

Where possible, pilots will avoid flying through convective weather. Even though aircraft are designed to cope with severe conditions, storms can produce intense turbulence, capable of damaging the structural frame of the plane, as well as throwing people around the cabin if they are not strapped in. Hail can also be a big problem, potentially cracking windscreens or causing engine problems. So, however much inconvenience it may cause passengers, crews will invariably put safety first.

blocks.caption: Image caption, New technology helps pilots navigate tricky flying conditions

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
New technology helps pilots navigate tricky flying conditions

Onboard weather radars can help aircrew to see up to 320 nautical miles ahead. They also have access to live weather forecasting resources online. But thunderstorms can move quickly and, according to Prof Guy Gratton, an expert in aeronautics at Cranfield University, these systems are essentially "tactical rather than strategic". In other words, although they enable pilots to see storm cells on their screens from a relatively short distance away, and request a diversion, they do not allow for detailed long-distance planning.

The result is that unplanned diversions often happen late in flight, which is likely to mean burning more fuel. If storm delays do become more common, says Andrew Charlton, then aircraft will have to load more fuel as a matter of course, in case there is trouble brewing ahead. "Aircraft are going to have to fly further, and they're going to have to factor in the assumption they're going to fly further," he says. For an airline, fuel is one of its major costs – and if the fuel bill goes up, he says, it is inevitable passengers will pay more.

More intense storms would be likely to make air traffic management in busy regions harder and potentially lead to more delays and cancellations. However, it is possible some of this could be mitigated using new technologies.

Both Heathrow and Gatwick, for example, have moved away from mandating minimum distances between incoming aircraft in favour of a system which continually calculates spacing times based on wind speeds and aircraft types. In practice, this is meant to allow controllers to reduce the distance between landing aircraft, particularly in high winds, and get them on the ground more quickly. According to NATS, it has successfully improved landing rates and reduced delays by a significant margin.

However, there could be other effects from more severe storms as well. Heavier rainfall, for instance, increases the likelihood of flooding. In a worst case, this can paralyse airport operations, as happened in April 2024 when torrential downpours hit Dubai International Airport. It briefly had to close its runways, while disruption lasted for two days. More than 1,200 flights were cancelled, affecting tens of thousands of passengers.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Passengers were delayed during the floods in Dubai

blocks.text: Passengers were delayed during the floods in Dubai
But even if runways and taxiways themselves are clear, and aircraft are able to fly without any difficulty, passengers may struggle to catch their flights if roads, railways or car parks are flooded.

Protecting against such risks can be expensive. Gatwick Airport, which experienced severe flooding over the Christmas period in 2013, has spent tens of millions of pounds on mitigation strategies in recent years – although those figures are dwarfed by the more than £2bn it is expecting to invest in its current expansion plans.
Clear-air turbulence
The problem of clear-air turbulence is also a real one. It cannot be seen, and is becoming increasingly common as the climate warms.

This is when air moves violently at high altitudes with no clouds or other visual cues to help a pilot avoid it. For passengers, it usually only means a little bit of bumpiness, but occasionally it can be a lot more serious. On 1 March 2023, for example, a Lufthansa flight from Austin, Texas to Frankfurt encountered what the airline described as "brief but severe" turbulence.

Those aboard described how passengers and flight crew were thrown around the cabin as the plane suddenly lost altitude. After it made an emergency landing in Washington DC, seven people were taken to hospital.
While still rare, this kind of turbulence is already much more prevalent than it used to be and is likely to become even more so.

"You know the projections are pretty dire: doubling, trebling or worse in the amount of severe turbulence on many busy flight routes around the world," says Paul Williams, a professor of atmospheric science at the University of Reading. He says incidents over the North Atlantic have increased by 55% since 1979.
Nevertheless, he remains confident solutions can be found, including improvements to forecasting and making use of laser-based technology.
Sea levels rising

There is another climate-related threat to aviation, which may prove challenging to overcome: rising sea levels. When Hurricane Sandy arrived off the US East Coast in October 2012, it provoked a storm surge that flooded the city. The two runways at New York's LaGuardia airport were left under water for several days, preventing it from reopening even after the winds had subsided.

Significant flooding that would have affected the New York City area once in every 500 years in pre-industrial times is now experienced every 25 years or so – and could occur every five years by the middle of the century, according to one major study. That makes LaGuardia, built on reclaimed land next to Flushing Bay, appear highly vulnerable.

blocks.caption: Image caption, LaGuardia could be at greater risk of flooding and future closures

blocks.text: LaGuardia could be at greater risk of flooding and future closures

It is not alone. With some 40% of the world's population living within 100km of coastlines, many airports have been built on low-lying areas near the sea. According to research by Newcastle University, 269 airports around the world are already at risk of flooding due to rising sea levels, and that total is expected to rise. Among those potentially most exposed are the likes of Amsterdam Schiphol, London City, Bahrain International and Newark Liberty International.

Many airports do already have some degree of flood protection, especially larger ones. But stopping the flood risks from rising over the next century means expensive investment in flood defences, raising runways, or even moving airports. It could cost up to $57bn (£42bn) according to the Newcastle report. Such costs are ultimately likely to be met by taxpayers or by travellers.

The aviation industry is often criticised for its own contribution to climate change emissions. It faces a forbidding challenge in attempting to meet a target of being carbon neutral by 2050, while also accommodating growth that is expected to see the global aircraft fleet double in size over the next two decades.
Yet it is clear the impacts of climate change will also be felt by airlines, airports and inevitably by passengers -
"I think the best we can do is mitigate", says Andrew Charlton.
"We need to make sure we have enough space at air terminals for people whose flights are being disrupted and delayed, that we have enough hotel rooms and parking space and so on."
But ultimately, he says, "disagreeable moments are going to happen more".
Passengers, he thinks, will have to accept it as a fact of flying life.
