articles.title: Sydney reaches 33C in potentially warmest start to spring since mid-1800s, while snow forecast in southern NSW
articles.summary:
A total fire ban is in place for greater Sydney with extreme fire danger exacerbated by hot and windy conditions

  • Get our
articles.byline: Australian Associated Press with Guardian staff

blocks.text: Summer heat is due to arrive early across much of eastern Australia with potentially record early September temperatures predicted for Brisbane and Sydney, while snow was expected in southern New South Wales.

Maximum temperatures in Sydney during the first days of September were on track to match the city’s midsummer average of 26.4C, warmer than any other start to spring since the city’s Observatory Hill station opened in 1858.
Suburbs across Sydney were expected to reach up to 33C on Saturday afternoon, smashing average September records by up to 13C.
The temperature in Badgerys Creek reached 33C shortly before 2pm, while Observatory Hill hit 32.1C a short time later.
The meteorologist Tom Saunders said a gusty north-westerly airstream blowing south from the northern interior would lift maximums this weekend by as much as 13C above the average.
The highest anomalies were set to affect the NSW coast.

“For Sydney, it’s likely to be the hottest day this early in spring on record and for the first five days of September we’re on track to average a top of 27 degrees that matches the midsummer average,” he told ABC News.
“Temperatures this spring will average as much as three degrees above the baseline from recent decades, potentially the hottest spring on record.”
The warm, dry and windy conditions would cause fire dangers to spike. A total fire ban was in place for the greater Sydney region, where extreme fire danger was forecast.

The dramatic – and potentially dangerous – start to Australia’s spring extended across much of the continent, with damaging winds that could bring down trees and roofs in South Australia, and minor to moderate flooding for parts of Victoria and Tasmania.
Meanwhile, in southern NSW, live cameras appeared to show snow falling late on Saturday morning in Thredbo in the Snowy Mountains.
The Bureau of Meteorology had forecast snowfall to hit Thredbo top station by 4pm on Saturday, with a daytime low temperature of -1C.
The new falls won’t do much to help the parlous cover remaining on Australia’s ski fields after a warm winter, however.

The Weatherzone journalist Anthony Sharwood on Friday wrote: “September snowfalls are meaningful when there’s a decent remnant snowpack from winter onto which the new snow can bond. But … the Australian snowpack is at a historic low for the first week of September, even at the highest elevations of the mountains.”
after newsletter promotion
Across the border, southern Queensland would see temperatures peak in the mid-30s in another unseasonably warm start to September.
In South Australia’s Mount Lofty and Flinders ranges, wind gusts of up to 110km/h were possible late Saturday into Sunday morning.
Heavy rains were forecast for north-east Victoria and northern Tasmania, with up to 60mm expected in some parts.
“The catchments in those areas are really wet,” the BoM meteorologist David Crock said on Friday. “They’ve seen multiple rounds of flood warnings this winter already.
“So we’ve got a flood watch current again for these catchments across northern Victoria … and across parts of northern Tasmania as well.”

The dramatic start to spring comes against the background of a “supersized” El Niño weather phenomenon to Australia’s east, one that is already breaking heat records, and could comfortably surpass previous events.

On Thursday, the UN’s weather agency said the event in the Pacific was continuing to strengthen and would probably persist until early 2027, warning it had the “potential to deliver a massive blow to communities and economies across the world”.
El Niño events tend to mean hotter and drier conditions for Australia’s south and east in winter and spring, and can increase the risk of heatwaves, drought and bushfires.

Australia’s national council for fire and emergency services said fire authorities were predicting a heightened risk of fire across northern and south-eastern NSW, south-east Queensland, north-eastern Tasmania, parts of Western Australia, South Australia and Victoria, and large parts of the Northern Territory.

articles.title: Tate brothers officially indicted with trafficking and sex crimes in Romania
articles.summary: Andrew and Tristan Tate are currently in a Miami jail fighting extradition to the UK over separate charges and deny all the allegations.

blocks.text: The brothers - former kickboxers with dual US and British citizenship - have been under criminal investigation in Romania since December 2022.
They have been mainly based there since 2017, drawing a large social media audience - many of them young men - through misogynistic messages and images of a luxury lifestyle.
Romanian prosecutors described a case as centring on a vulnerable female who was 15 at the time of the alleged offence, in information released on Friday.

She is alleged to have been recruited by Andrew and housed in a building in Luton, Bedfordshire, so he could sexually exploit her. Tristan is alleged to have been an accessory, prosecutors say, using physical aggression to coerce the victim.
DIICOT investigators allege Andrew controlled her through surveillance and physical aggression, and coerced her to perform sex acts on video chats for his financial gain.
Andrew is also accused of moving her to Romania to carry on exploiting her in two of his homes.
He is separately charged with having sex with a minor, who was 15, in Romania.
Prosecutors have also requested four of the brothers' luxury cars worth £710,000 be confiscated. They believe money was laundered through their purchase.
The two brothers were previously indicted in Romania on trafficking charges, but in 2024 an appeals court in Bucharest sent the case back to prosecutors after deeming some evidence inadmissible.
It is not yet clear if DIICOT will seek their extradition from the US and the indictment has to be examined by a judge before any trial can begin.
The Tates have denied all the allegations and say their online personas are not their real personalities.

Their lawyer in Romania, Eugen Constantin Vidineac, said: "Today's decision by DIICOT does not determine guilt and it should not be presented as though it does. It represents the prosecution's latest attempt to bring this case before a court following the failure of its previous indictment to proceed to trial.

"The history of these proceedings matters. The previous indictment was subjected to judicial scrutiny and the court identified significant irregularities which prevented the case from moving forward to trial.

"DIICOT has now chosen to file a new indictment. We will examine every aspect of it with the same level of scrutiny and we will challenge any evidential, procedural or legal deficiencies through the appropriate judicial process.

"Our clients continue to reject the allegations against them. They have the right to the presumption of innocence, the right to properly examine the evidence relied upon against them and the right to mount an effective defence."

Correction 5 September: A previous version of this article incorrectly stated that the Tate brothers were charged with further offences. The article has been updated to make clear they have been officially indicted with offences of which they had already been accused. It has also been updated to reflect that Andrew, not Tristan, was alleged to have recruited the 15-year-old.

September 5, 2026
Nepal floods: India says tally of missing Indians at 275
India has said that 275 of its nationals remain missing, ten days after flash floods ravaged areas along the Nepal-Tibet border.
A total of 169 Indians have been rescued so far from the flood-affected areas in Nepal, India's foreign ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said on Friday evening.
Jaiswal said that in the latest rescue three Indians, including a five-year-old, were pulled to safety from Trishuli Bazaar in Nepal.
"Our Embassy in Nepal is assisting in their return to India by air," he said on X.
The spokesperson told a press conference in New Delhi that 1,907 Indian nationals have safely crossed over to Nepal from China.
No Indian travelers are now stranded in the Tibet Autonomous Region, Jaiswal announced, citing official Chinese sources.
Nepal's official death toll from the deluge now stands at 1,294, with 5,053 still missing.
A frantic rescue effort has gone on for days to search for survivors, especially at mud-filled hydropower tunnels, where hundreds of workers are believed to be trapped.
Indian team assists in Rasuwa tunnel rescue
On Saturday, New Delhi's envoy to Kathmandu said that an Indian tunnel rescue team, working with Nepal's defense forces at the Chilime hydropower plant in Rasuwa, had stepped up operations.

"The Indian tunnel rescue team working alongside with Nepali Army dug deeper into Chilime tunnel yesterday draining out water. A temporary track is also being made to allow more heavy equipment to reach tunnel," Indian Ambassador Naveen Srivastava said.
He added that doctors accompanying the Indian rescuers had also held a health camp for the local community.
India has also supplied nearly 95 tonnes of relief material to Nepal since the floods hit the country on August 26, Jaiswal said on Friday.

articles.title: Gamified abuse: How a PH forum rewards submissions of non-consensual intimate content
articles.summary: The forum’s gamified system rewards users for uploading intimate content, while traffic and advertising turn exploitation into profit

image.caption: — Dana Batnag, data privacy lawyer

blocks.text: Content Warning
The following story contains descriptions and discussions of sexual violence, image-based abuse, and the non-consensual sharing and explicit sexualization of women. Reader discretion is advised.
Second of two parts
Shortly after discovering that intimate videos of her had been uploaded online, Mishy kept returning to a question.
"I am hurt by the fact that they took something so private, deeply private, to gain attention or to make money," she said.
"Why would someone share something that was never theirs in the first place?"
It's because there is something to gain. For the operators of NSFWPH, it is traffic.

The forum, which now boasts more than 430,000 registered members, has evolved into far more than a repository of intimate images and videos. It is a structured online community where users are rewarded for posting content, climbing membership ranks through participation, and, in some cases, monetizing the very intimate images they upload.
Rewarding exploitation
Unlike a conventional pornographic website, NSFWPH is an internet forum.
Members create threads. They comment. They react to posts. They earn points. And every interaction contributes toward a merit system that unlocks additional privileges.
Users who accumulate enough points are promoted through ranks such as "Established Member," "Elite," "Contributor," and eventually "Legendary," the forum's highest status.
Higher-ranked members may gain access to locked content, including additional information attached to posts such as the names of victims or links to their Facebook and Instagram accounts.
Participation and contribution are rewarded.
On NSFWPH, however, those incentives revolve around something more concerning: the non-consensual sharing of intimate content.

By its structure, the system has the effect of encouraging members to find material worth posting, whether by obtaining videos from former partners, redistributing Telegram content, or manipulating women into sending intimate images. The more active a member becomes, the more they stand to gain within the community.
It is a structure that transforms participation into exploitation.
“A person can consent to documentation, but not for posting.”
From internet points to real money
The rewards do not end with forum status.
Rappler identified one of the platform's most prolific contributors: a user known as Mikey Kun.

Kun holds the rank of "Legendary," the highest attainable status in the forum. He has amassed 4,902 posts — the third-highest post count on the site. Included among those uploads are sexually explicit videos of Filipina women, ranging from livestreamers on livestreaming platform BIGO to content described as "leaks" and "scandals."
Majority of Kun's posts use a service called shrinkme.io for monetization.

To download one of Kun's videos, a user clicks on a shrinkme.io link associated with a specific post. The user is then redirected to a series of pop-up ads before they eventually reach the actual download link. For every 1,000 users that click the link, Kun is given a payout.
Shrinkme.io's official payout rates vary by country. In the Philippines, the rate is US$4 per 1,000 views.

In our scan, Kun had more than 200 posts with corresponding shrinkme.io links just in July and August 2026. In our random sampling of these posts, the majority reach at least 1,000 views on the forum, with one post reaching at least 12,000, while a few reach only 600 or 700 views.
Theoretically, if 100 of those 200 posts reach at least 1,000 clicks on shrinkme.io links, that would mean Kun earned $400 or roughly P24,000 (at $1 = P60).
What this illustrates is that content is not simply exchanged; it also generates income for some, in this case, Mikey Kun.
“Why would someone share something that was never theirs in the first place?”
Beyond that, Kun also redirects audiences outside NSFWPH.

Under the same identity, he maintains Facebook pages and Discord communities where followers are directed toward additional content. In one Facebook post, he reminded users he had referred to NSFWPH to follow the forum's rules because violations could affect his own account. In another, he told followers he would focus less on updating NSFWPH and instead devote more attention to his Discord server, The Nowhere.

His two Discord servers — Mikey's Vault and The Nowhere — collectively host nearly 6,000 members. One advertises a VIP-only section offering "Exclusive" and "SHS" (senior high school) sets to paying members. His Facebook page has 4,400 followers.
Access costs P500, according to a post by Mikeykun on his Discord channel called Mikey's Vault, payable through GCash. In return, members receive download links to additional content.
The result is a multi-layered monetization model.
Users gain prestige in the forum. They earn advertising revenue through download links and also by selling access to the seller's collections directly on other channels.
The forum profits too
The NSFWPH platform itself is designed to capitalize on traffic.
According to analytics service Semrush, NSFWPH receives more than 10 million page views each month, with users viewing an average of 25 pages per visit and remaining on the site for over 14 minutes.

The website displays multiple advertisements on every page using ExoClick, an advertising network commonly used by adult websites. ExoClick estimates earnings of roughly $500 for every 3-5 million ad views, although actual revenues vary, depending on factors such as location and conversion rates. Each page on NSFWPH displays around five advertisements.
The figures do not reveal exactly how much the site earns but they do show that this amount of traffic has commercial value.
Together, they sustain a platform whose popularity depends on the continued circulation of intimate content — the origin of which are often questionable.
What the law says
Despite the apparent business built around these images and videos, Philippine law already prohibits much of the conduct taking place.

The Anti-Photo and Video Voyeurism Act of 2009 makes it illegal not only to record sexual acts or private parts without consent, but also to copy, distribute, publish, sell, or broadcast such recordings without the written consent of everyone involved — even if the recording itself was initially consensual.

The later Safe Spaces Act further strengthened protections by penalizing gender-based online harassment, including the non-consensual uploading or sharing of photos, audio, or videos with sexual content.

Lawyer Dana Batnag, data privacy expert and human rights advocate, discussed further the elements of proper consent. "First, consent has to be informed. You need to tell me your purpose [for recording or documenting]. Consent has to be specific. A person can consent to documentation, but not for posting. If you were manipulated [to share intimate content], then was that consent freely given? Consent must also be freely given."

Consent to take a photo or record a video doesn't mean that the person has also given consent to have the content distributed, shared, or posted by any means. Persons also have the right to retract that right at any time they want.

Respicio Law also states: "A person who receives leaked private photos and forwards them may also face liability. 'I only shared it' is not always a defense… Group chat members, page admins, channel operators, and social media users should not repost, save, mock, or circulate intimate images."

Based on data privacy laws, Batnag said that since the forum is trafficking sensitive personal information in the form of intimate photos and videos, the administrators and owners of the site should be identified.

"For example, I'm one of those women. I have the right to know, under the data subjects right, who looked at my picture, who gave it to you, how you got it, your source of information. And I have the right to know to whom you shared those. As the data subject, I can demand that right. I can demand it from the owner of the website," the lawyer explained.

The site allows users to request for a content takedown, but since these are intimate images that are considered sensitive personal information, that would also mean that when the thousands of users get to see them without the clear and express permission of the subject, it can be argued that a violative breach of privacy has occurred.

Batnag also said that even if the website was hosted in another country, the owners of the website would face consequences under the Data Privacy Act, as the site deals with information of Filipinos, not just of the potential women victims, but also the very users registered on the site.

According to Liza Garcia, executive director of the Foundation for Media Alternatives, who advocates against the non-consensual sharing of intimate images, a massive platform like NSFWPH inflicts "a lot of harm" on victims, particularly young women, who often suffer profound "emotional harm" and "psychological harm."

Beyond the immediate trauma, victims face severe "harm to reputation" and even "financial harm" because the public nature of the exploitation can result in a victim being unable to work: "hindi ka na makapagtrabaho, ayaw mo na kasing lumabas ng bahay, nahiya ka na" (you can no longer work, you no longer want to leave the house, you are already ashamed).
This "profound shame" often causes victims to "tend to isolate" themselves, which means the "economic aspect of [their] life" is deeply affected.
This is the potential damage that can be caused by the operation of such a website.
For Garcia, those harms are not hypothetical. They are the foreseeable consequence of a platform built around the circulation of intimate content.
For the Philippine National Police Anti-Cybercrime Group (PNP-ACG), NSFWPH is part of a broader landscape of online sexual exploitation and non-consensual sharing of intimate material.

The police have been actively pursuing perpetrators. From 2025 through August 2026, the PNP-ACG conducted 138 operations involving cyber warrants, entrapment operations, arrest warrants, and rescue operations, resulting in the arrest of 160 individuals involved in violations of the Anti-Photo and Video Voyeurism Act.
Authorities also rescued minors and apprehended seven children in conflict with the law (CICL) related to these cases.
But going after NSFWPH itself presents a different challenge: jurisdiction.

A quick check on forensic tool Domaintools.com showed that the IP address of NSFWPH is connected to a Cloudflare server in San Francisco, California. Asueta said since the forum is hosted outside the Philippines, it is difficult for Philippine authorities to directly compel the platform to act. "So this is a jurisdictional issue," he said.
Requests for takedowns can also be circumvented through new sites and VPNs.

Asueta said these activities have existed for "medyo matagal-tagal na rin" (for quite a long time already). Recently, the PNP-ACG has seen fewer reports about the non-consensual spread of intimate images within its unit but cautioned that this does not necessarily mean the problem is declining because some victims may simply not be reporting.
Server accountability

Victims still have some recourse with content found on NSFWPH. The PNP-ACG said victims can file a complaint, and investigators can attempt to trace the source of the material found on the forum, identify an individual suspect, and pursue a case.
The police can also apply for a cyber warrant to search and examine the suspect's cellphone or computer for evidence.

But again, going after the actual platform is harder. Right now, if investigators can gather sufficient evidence, Asueta said they can coordinate with the relevant jurisdiction through Interpol and the International Mutual Legal Assistance mechanism — a formal method for international cooperation under the Department of Justice.

However, in the longer term, Asueta called for laws requiring foreign platforms operating in the Philippines to establish local offices and submit to Philippine court processes such as warrants and subpoenas.

To other women who may one day find themselves in the same position, Mishy offered fighting words: "Your body is not your shame. You deserve to take up space in this world without apologizing for what someone else did to you. There are countless women standing beside you, silently carrying the same wounds — but all of us are still worthy of every beautiful thing life has to offer. What happened to you is not a reflection of your worth."
Mishy said that if she had enough proof or evidence on who leaked the videos, she would attempt to pursue a legal case. — Rappler.com
Lance Ariel Bustos is an Aries Rufo Journalism Fellow for 2026, currently studying at the De La Salle University Manila.

If you or someone you know has been targeted by online abuse, intimate-image abuse, harassment, or the non-consensual sharing of private content, tell us what happened. Your story could help expose how these abuses happen—and who enables them.
You can reach us at desk@rappler.com.
You may also report online abuse to the PNP Anti-Cybercrime Group at 0998-598-8116 or (02) 414-1560, or to the NBI Cybercrime Division at (02) 8523-8231 to 38, local 3454 or 3455.

articles.title: Germany news: Thousands march at Saxony-Anhalt rallies
articles.summary: Ahead of Saxony-Anhalt's state election on Sunday, a democracy festival by civil society groups has been held in Magdeburg. The far-right AfD organized its final campaign rally in the state capital.…

image.caption: Police estimate that 6,000 people turned out at one demonstration in MagdeburgImage: Jan Woitas/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: September 5, 2026
Thousands turn out at 'Democracy Festival' in Saxony-Anhalt

blocks.caption: Police estimated that 6,000 people turned out at the demo in MagdeburgImage: Jan Woitas/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Thousands of people joined a "march for democracy" on Saturday in Magdeburg, the capital of Saxony-Anhalt.

Organized by a coalition called "Saxony-Anhalt: Open to the World," the march was called to uphold values of democracy, diversity and inclusivity ahead of a state election in which the far-right Alternative for Germany party (AfD) is comfortably leading opinion polls.
Germany's federal intelligence service has labeled the AfD state branch in Saxony-Anhalt as a right-wing extremist organization.
At the demo on Saturday, attendees carried signs that read "more love, less hate," "a better life without Nazis," and "the potato is also of foreign origin," among other slogans.

blocks.caption: Signs included slogans such as: 'A better life without Nazis'Image: Jan Woitas/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Police estimated that some 6,000 people participated in the march from Magdeburg's central station to Cathedral Square, where another 3,000 people joined them.
Among them were contingents from trade unions, church groups and other civic organizations.
"As initiatives, clubs, associations, and individuals, we are taking a stand and advocating for respectful coexistence in our state," the organizers stated in their call to action.
According to police, eight gatherings had been registered to take place in Magdeburg on Saturday. Others included a human chain for democracy and a democracy-themed cycling tour.

In an interview with German daily the Tagesspiegel, right-wing extremism expert Heike Kleffner praised the organizers' "paradoxical confidence" in being able to mobilize democratic masses despite being under attack.

blocks.caption: The demonstrators marched to Magdeburg's Cathedral SquareImage: Jan Woitas/dpa/picture alliance

articles.title: Lindsay Clancy murder trial has divided US on whether she's victim or criminal
articles.summary: Some say the case shed light on the mental health struggles of mothers, while others argue it's no excuse for murder.
articles.byline: Ana Faguy, Brandon Drenon, Sheila Flynn

blocks.text: Inside court as judge declares a mistrial in Lindsay Clancy case
ByAna FaguyReporting fromreporting from court in MassachusettsBrandon Drenon and Sheila Flynn
Warning: This story contains distressing details and discussion of attempted suicide

Jodi Fournier spent 15 days at the courthouse - sitting, listening and waiting. It was a personal duty, she felt, to show support for Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts mother charged with murdering her three children.
Katelyn Kazmirci, from North Carolina, convinced her mother to make a detour to the courthouse in Plymouth on their way to a family funeral, intrigued by the case she had followed on TikTok.

All around them, dozens of women wearing pink rallied in support of Clancy. Not everyone felt the same and across the country, on social media and at dinner tables, Americans have been debating the case with passion.
For nearly seven weeks, the trial transfixed and divided the nation on whether Clancy was a victim or a criminal who deserved to be behind bars.

The 36-year-old nurse's defence team argued she had been suffering from postpartum psychosis when she strangled her young children and so could not be held criminally responsible. The prosecution alleged the killings were intentional and calculated.
The judge declared a mistrial on Friday after jurors - who had heard the testimony of dozens of witnesses and deliberated for 40 hours - failed to come to a uninanimous decision.
Their inability to agree mirrored the wider discourse around the trial - one that trial attendee Maryanne Drysdale, 65, saw play out within her own family.
She and her 28-year-old daughter believe Clancy needs mental health treatment, not prison, while her three adult sons, who have children of similar age to Clancy's, completely disagree.
"It's black and white for them, [Clancy] killed the kids and that's that," she said. "I brought these kids up - how can we think so differently about this?"

blocks.caption: Image caption, Jodi Fournier spent more than two weeks outside the courthouse to show support for Clancy

blocks.text: Jodi Fournier spent more than two weeks outside the courthouse to show support for Clancy
Fournier believes Clancy was wronged by the US health system and felt compelled, as a woman and a mother, to show up for a case that has given a spotlight to postpartum struggles.
"It only takes one person to change the narrative," she said. "This is a global issue. This isn't just Massachusetts-small-town. This is... women everywhere."

Clancy claims she experienced hallucinations and delusions before strangling her three children - five-year-old Cora, Dawson, three, and Callan, who was eight months old - and then jumping from a second-floor window, leaving her paralysed.
The court heard testimony from more than 10 expert witnesses on Clancy's mental and postpartum health during the trial.
But some of them seemed to dispute the defence's claim that postpartum psychosis - a rare post-childbirth condition characterised by mania and depression - precluded Clancy from criminal liability.
Jennifer Tufts, who treated Clancy during more than a dozen sessions over five months, testified that she had not shown signs of psychosis.
Psychiatrist Avram Mack later testified that the American Psychiatric Association did not recognise postpartum psychosis as a diagnosis.
These declarations only deepened staunch opinions for many - on both sides.

Texas mother-of-four Nicole Russell, who followed the trial remotely, noted the prosecution's presentation of how much medical care and support Clancy had received - from doctors, her husband, nanny and family - calling it "way more help" than most mothers receive.

Clancy's struggles were said to have begun following the birth of her youngest child. She repeatedly sought care, visiting a hospital emergency room, different medical professionals and even calling a suicide hotline.
Many observers took that as evidence that Clancy had been proactive and done everything within her power to heal but had been failed by the system, prompting sympathy from some.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Melissa Merrill says she, like Clancy, suffered suicidal ideation after giving birth

blocks.text: Melissa Merrill says she, like Clancy, suffered suicidal ideation after giving birth
Melissa Merrill had been treated at the same hospital as Clancy after the birth of her son.
"I see myself in her, as a mum who had suicidal ideation," she told the BBC outside the Plymouth courthouse.

Throughout the weeks of emotional testimony, the now wheelchair-bound Clancy could be seen crying, holding her attorney's hand and making agonised utterances in court as sometimes harrowing details were shared.

After one of the trial days, Merrill rushed to Clancy's defence attorney outside the court and gave him a pink envelope holding a message of support and hope for his client, believing Clancy was a "sad, defeated woman".
But other parents, like Texas mother Russell, railed against "toxic empathy", insisting Clancy was "not a martyr or a symbol for tired mums".

"Lindsay Clancy cannot be the poster child of what difficult motherhood looks like, because millions of mothers give birth to children and endure all kinds of hardship, and they do not hurt their children," Russell argued.
The moment judge declares a mistrial in Lindsay Clancy case

The discourse around the Clancy trial was prominent on social media, with many users being hard-pressed to find a platform where the case was not being mentioned, if not being subject to myriad conspiracy theories.

Clancy's mother, sister and former husband all testified to her deteriorating mental state in the run-up to the murders, but her ex Patrick Clancy was singled out online for wild vitriol and cover-up accusations.

There were claims that he was to blame for the murders, despite his wife never denying killing their children, nor that she had been the only adult at home at the time. This thrust him into the limelight, with tabloids snapping photos of him travelling and with his new wife.
His lawyers issued a statement to CNN in August calling the facts "indisputable".

"Patrick Clancy has suffered an unspeakable and unimaginable loss," they said. "Unfortunately, the tragedy Patrick has experienced has been compounded by patently false, defamatory and injurious public statements."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Clancy supporters - many wearing pink - huddled outside the courthouse

blocks.text: Image source, The Boston Globe via Getty Images
Clancy supporters - many wearing pink - huddled outside the courthouse

blocks.caption: Image caption, Those who believed Clancy should be held accountable for the killings also had a presence outside the court

blocks.text: Those who believed Clancy should be held accountable for the killings also had a presence outside the court
The case became a flashpoint for gender discussion, too, with opinions often divided along gender lines.

Father-of-three Vincenzo Vazquez, who followed the trial from Illinois, believes gender has a lot to do with Clancy's treatment, doubting that the public would show similar sympathy if a father were on trial for the same charges.
"Whatever someone is dealing with, I don't think there's ever an appropriate time or an excuse or a justification to, you know, kill children of your own, or kill any children," he said.

He said he felt "very sad and a little disgusted to see how many people are rallying behind her", adding: "I think people should be out there rallying for justice for the children. They're three beautiful kids that had a future in front of them."

The decision to declare a mistrial after seven days of deadlocked jury deliberations has left the status of the case - and Clancy's future - unclear. A hearing at the end of the month could establish whether prosecutors will move ahead with second trial or attempt to reach a plea deal.
For now, the debates elsewhere will no doubt continue.

If you are suffering distress or despair and need support, you could speak to a health professional, or an organisation that offers support. Details of help available in many countries can be found at Befrienders Worldwide, external.
A list of UK organisations that can help is available here.

articles.title: No final decision yet to drop bribery article in Sara Duterte impeachment trial, says Tolosa
articles.summary: The House prosecution panel has yet to make a final decision whether or not it will be dropping the bribery charge under Article III of the Articles of Impeachment against Vice President Sara Duterte.

blocks.text: Published September 5, 2026 2:30pm

The House prosecution panel has yet to make a final decision whether or not it will be dropping the bribery charge under Article III of the Articles of Impeachment against Vice President Sara Duterte.

At a news forum on Saturday, House prosecution legal spokesperson Atty. Jay Tolosa said the prosecutors are still deliberating on the matter as they consider both the sentiments of the senator-judges and the public to expedite the impeachment proceedings and not let it continue up to next year.
“To be clear, wala pa namang ganung pinal na desisyon kasama po yan sa pinaguusapan, pinagdedesisyunan ng panel of prosecutors sa ngayon,” Tolosa said.
“Sabin naman natin mula noon kaisa kami doon sa hangad na as much as possible i-expedite natin ‘tong proceedings,” he said.

(To be clear, there has been no final decision, it is included in the discussions of the panel right now. We've said that since the beginning, we are one in the objective of having the proceedings expedited.)

The Article III refers to the allegation that the Vice President must be impeached for committing bribery by giving monetary gifts or payments to Department of Education (DepEd) officials to induce the violation and circumvention of procurement and other related laws.

So far, the prosecution has presented Article IV —which alleges that Duterte committed an impeachable offense by contracting for the assassination of President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos, Jr., First Lady Liza Marcos, and former speaker of the House and incumbent Leyte Representative Martin Romualdez, by making grave threats, and by actively inciting sedition against the republic— and Article I which alleges that the Vice President committed an impeachable offense due to systematic misuse, misappropriation, and irregular liquidation of confidential funds amounting to P500 million released to the Office of the Vice President (OVP) and P112.5 million released to the DepEd during her tenure as Education chief.
“Dalawa na lang ang matitira bribery and unexplained wealth (Only two remains, bribery and unexplained wealth),” Tolosa said.

He said that the House prosecution team has already collated records from the Bureau of Internal Revenue and the Anti-Money Laundering Council for the Article II, which argues that Duterte amassed unexplained wealth.
“Meron tayong nakuhang maraming dokumento na sa tingin namin talagang importanteng maipakita to sa proceedings and it will go to waste kung ‘yun naman ang hindi namin mapu-pursue,” Tolosa said.
(We have many documents which we think are really important and it will go to waste if we cannot pursue it.)
However, he said that the prosecution may opt to present first Article II to be followed by Article III. — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: What would an AfD government in Saxony-Anhalt really mean?
articles.summary: Detention centers for deportation, mandatory work for asylum-seekers, vigilante groups — the AfD wants to drastically overhaul Saxony-Anhalt. What does the party have planned?

image.caption: Ulrich Siegmund, top candidate for the far-right AfD in Saxony-Anhalt, is confident he will get the mandate to form a governmentImage: Annegret Hilse/REUTERS

blocks.text: The Alternative for Germany (AfD) could bring in massive changes should it form a government in Saxony-Anhalt. The far-right party, currently way ahead in opinion polls, is hoping to form a single-party government and have its lead candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, serve as state premier.
The Saxony-Anhalt chapter of the AfD is classified by the domestic intelligence agency as "confirmed far-right."
Radical tightening of asylum laws

In its draft government program, the AfD has promised "deportation from minute one!" if it wins the election in Saxony-Anhalt. The stated goal, according to the party's election program, is simply to deport as many immigrants who have no residency permits as possible.

The party has also pledged much stricter asylum rules at all levels: It wants more detention pending deportation, mandatory work for asylum-seekers, and intends to cut all state funding for integration programs, which it refers to as an "asylum industry."
What if Germany's far-right AfD party wins in Saxony-Anhalt?

Furthermore, it wants to exclude children and adolescents who do not have permanent residency in Germany from attending regular schools. On top of that, a "Remigration Task Force" is to be established within the state government to coordinate the state's asylum policy.

Exactly how many of these measures an AfD state government would be legally able to implement remains unclear. Creating special classes for refugees could, for example, be a violation of international and European law.
And the question of who can and can't be deported falls under the jurisdiction of the federal government, not that of an individual state.
Anti-immigration policy

The AfD opposes immigration to Germany. In its government platform, the party calls for a "180-degree turnaround in migration policy," and its stated goal is to reduce the number of immigrants in Saxony-Anhalt.

However, the region has been suffering for years from a shortage of skilled workers, particularly in nursing and care for the elderly. The AfD's plan to end this shortage is to encourage Germans who live abroad to come back.

To this end, it plans to launch a "return program," including a proposed "return bonus" to help find housing and daycare spots for children. It is unclear how many returnees the AfD anticipates and how much money it has budgeted for the "return program."
Germany looks to India to address skilled labor shortage

Saxony-Anhalt has been severely affected by depopulation for over 30 years. No other German state population has shrunk more since reunification in 1990 — from around 2.9 million people then to 2.1 million today.
Economic researchers like Reint Gropp, president of the Halle Institute for Economic Research, have warned that an AfD government is likely to exacerbate the skilled worker shortage.
"Highly qualified professionals, in particular, have options," he told Die Welt newspaper on Tuesday. "If they feel they are unwelcome or can expect hostility, they will choose other regions."
Rapprochement with Russia

The 16 state governments have virtually no authority over Germany's foreign and defense policy, though they can influence political debates via the Bundesrat, the chamber of parliament that represents the states. In that context, an AfD state premier would carry considerable political weight.

For example, since the start of Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine in 2022, Germany has largely halted oil imports, but the AfD's election platform calls for a rapprochement with Russia and an end to sanctions.
The call is largely symbolic, as Saxony-Anhalt is bound by federal sanctions, but an AfD state premier could set a new tone in the Bundesrat.
Threat from the far right: Never quite German enough?
The AfD also wants to expand Russian language instruction in schools and specifically recruit native Russian speakers for this purpose.

On Ukraine, meanwhile, the AfD is taking a harder line, calling for a "return offensive" for Ukrainian refugees. Again, a state government cannot deport Ukrainians from Germany — that is regulated by federal policy.
Establishing citizen patrols

Particularly controversial is the AfD's call for a kind of auxiliary police force. The regular police are "overwhelmed" by the task of ensuring security, according to the AfD's program for Saxony-Anhalt: "We will therefore establish a voluntary citizen patrol as a third pillar of the local security architecture."

Legal scholar and criminologist Thomas Feltes, of Ruhr University Bochum, warns against the idea. "It is the police's duty to ward off dangers and ensure the protection of the public. Only the police are authorized to use force in doing so," he wrote in a column for the outlet Legal Tribune Online.
Germany's freedom of art under threat?

A "citizen patrol," he said, would basically be a vigilante group that would have a negative effect on public safety: "Where such groups are active, the fear of crime is only stoked — not only among the participants, but above all among everyone else, and not just among 'concerned' citizens," he wrote.
Radical change in social policy

A central tenet of the AfD's governing platform is so-called identity politics. It aims to promote a positive image of German history, and advocates a fundamentally different view of the country's past. The party describes the process of coming to terms with German crimes during the Nazi era as the "perpetuation of a guilt complex" and wants to change school curricula accordingly.

It has also declared war on social diversity: Rainbow flags, as symbols of diversity, are to be banned in schools. It rejects the world-famous Bauhaus architecture — which flourished in Saxony-Anhalt — as "too globalist" and calls for a "patriotic cultural policy."

To that end, it wants to redirect funding away from the many pro-democracy projects that receive state funding for their work. In its platform, the AfD has rejected any continuation of these payments.
Between homemaking and hate: Undercover with far-right women
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Sara Duterte posts bail for grave threats case
articles.summary: The Vice President posts bail a day after a Quezon City court issued warrants for her arrest over three counts of grave threats

blocks.text: POSTING BAIL. Vice President Sara Duterte, along with legal counsels, arrives at the Quezon City Regional Trial Court, following the issuance of an arrest warrant against her over a grave threats case, on September 5, 2026.
Jire Carreon/Rappler
The Vice President posts bail a day after a Quezon City court issued warrants for her arrest over three counts of grave threats

items: Vice President Sara Duterte posted bail of P360,000 after being charged with three counts of grave threats related to alleged assassination threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and others.
The Quezon City Regional Trial Court issued warrants for her arrest, which were upheld despite her legal team's arguments regarding her status as an impeachable official.
Duterte expressed concerns for her safety and that of her children, citing documented threats and harassment since 2023.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Vice President Sara Duterte posted bail on Saturday, September 5, in connection with the three counts of grave threats filed against her over her alleged assassination threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Marcos, and former House speaker Martin Romualdez.
Her lawyer, Paul Lawrence Lim, confirmed that Duterte posted P120,000 bail for each count of grave threats before Quezon City Regional Trial Court Branch 98.
Lim said Duterte underwent booking process inside the court, which includes taking of her fingerprints.
“Kailangan pa rin (It’s necessary)…. [She did the booking process] in front of court staff,” Lim told reporters outside the court.
Duterte’s impeachment lawyer and spokesperson Michael Poa was also present in court with Duterte and Lim.
Before entering the hall, Duterte talked to journalists where she aired concerns over her security.

“I have documented threats and harassment since 2023. I fear for my children. I do not feel they are safe if I am with them. Umalis na nga ako kung nasaan mga anak ko para pumunta sa korte pero pumunta pa rin ang pulis. I do not feel safe. Pakiramdam ko papatayin nila ako,” Duterte said in a statement.
(I left the place where my children are to go to the court but the police still came… I feel like they will kill me.)

On September 4, the court issued a warrant after it found probable cause to hold Duterte for trial. It also denied her motion to defer or recall the warrants and quash the information for lack of merit.

Duterte’s camp had argued that she could not face a criminal case while serving as Vice President because she is an impeachable official. Several legal experts, however, have said that unlike the President, the Vice President is not immune from suit.
The Department of Justice filed the three counts of grave threats in August following complaints from the National Bureau of Investigation over Duterte’s November 23, 2024, midnight press conference.

During that press conference, Duterte said she had already talked to someone who would kill Marcos, his wife, and Romualdez if she herself were killed. Duterte said at the time that she was not joking. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Is Russia proving better at protecting friends than fighting enemies in West Africa?
articles.summary: Russian forces were brought in to help defeat jihadists but they also defend the military leadership in Niger.

blocks.text: When mutinous soldiers seized a strategic military base in Niger's capital last Saturday, the country's ruling junta turned to a foreign partner it has increasingly relied on since coming to power: Russia.
Following a night of intense fighting in Niamey, Russia's Africa Corps helped Nigerien loyalist forces to regain control of Air Base 101 at Diori Hamani International Airport.

Africa Corps, unlike its predecessor the Wagner Group, is directly under the control of the defence ministry in Moscow. It provides combat support and military training and is thought to have some 200 to 300 men in Niger.
Russia's ambassador to Niger, Viktor Voropaev, publicly acknowledged the weekend intervention, saying his country's forces had helped "repress a mutiny".

"This is seen as a symbolic victory," according to Beverly Ochieng, senior analyst at Control Risks. "[One] that will continue to put them at the centre of not just the counter-insurgency campaign, but even in the protection and prolongation of military rule."
The attempted coup offers perhaps the clearest evidence yet that Africa Corps' role in three Sahel countries extends beyond its stated mission of helping governments fight jihadist insurgencies.
Russia is increasingly demonstrating that it can provide something perhaps even more valuable to the military rulers of Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso: protection for the governments themselves.
"It was not sufficient to bring stability," said Ochieng, "but it's enough to allow these military governments to have a political lifeline."
The thwarted mutiny also highlights something the ruling junta may not want to admit - just how dependent on Moscow it has become for security.
In January, Africa Corps personnel also played an important role in repelling an attack at the same airport.
"We saw videos of the jihadists walking around the airport basically completely unimpeded," said Jacob Boswall, a security analyst who tracks jihadist activity for the BBC's media monitoring service.

"Probably there is some substance to the claim that Africa Corps was able to restore power in that case [in January]. And I think, again, in this case as well, that intervention was very significant."

One of the Nigerien military's central justifications for the July 2023 coup, which saw Gen Abdourahamane Tiani seize power, was the deteriorating security situation and alleged failure of Niger's civilian authorities, under elected President Mohamed Bazoum, to tackle it.
They also blamed Western partners at the time for their inability to contain jihadist violence.
Yet, three years later, that insurgency remains unresolved.
Militants linked to al-Qaeda and Islamic State have continued to launch attacks, including in the Tillabéri and Dosso regions. Some, inflicting heavy casualties on security forces.
Ochieng described this latest mutiny as evidence of longstanding grievances within Niger's own military, compounded by the pressure the soldiers have been facing.
"Counter-insurgency forces do not feel adequately supported by the military government," she said. "There have been challenges in providing equipment and replenishments."

Niger's government is facing threats on two fronts: extremist militant groups attacking the state, and grievances within its armed forces responsible for fighting them. Africa Corps may have helped contain the latter this past weekend, but it has yet to resolve the former.
Unlike Wagner mercenaries, whose status in a private military company allowed Moscow some deniability, Africa Corps is more clearly an instrument of the Russian state.
"The whole point of Africa Corps is that it brings the power back under the control of the Russian Ministry of Defence," said Boswall.
Officially, its forces are deployed to help Sahel governments combat Islamist militant groups.
But dissidents contemplating moves against military governments elsewhere in the Sahel region may now have to factor Russian forces into their calculations.
Despite the struggle to contain the jihadists, no-one anticipates Africa Corps leaving the Sahel any time soon. Keeping those governments in power protects Russia's investment.
"Wagner - and now Africa Corps - have always had a very transactional interest in Africa," Boswall said.

"If they can get mineral resources in exchange for providing protection and defence, then they will. We see that in Mali with gold… and then in Niger, it really is uranium [that] seems to be the main resource that Africa Corps is protecting."
Analysts say Russia also benefits from having friendly governments that could support it in international forums.
"Having that kind of international group of supportive countries, Russia sees as giving Russia credibility - diplomatic credibility," Boswall explained.
Like Mali and Burkina Faso, Tiani's government has built much of its legitimacy using the language of sovereignty, pan-Africanism and liberation from former colonial powers.

All three governments ordered French troops to leave. They also formed the Alliance of Sahel States (AES) and subsequently withdrew from the West African regional bloc Ecowas, presenting the new alliance as an assertion of regional independence.
Some analysts regard this as at odds with its growing reliance on Africa Corps.
"The military governments argue that they have selected Russia on their own terms," said Ochieng.
"Russia is seen as a partner that respects that sovereignty, unlike their previous partnerships with France or even the EU and, to some extent, with the US."

An army captain on Niger state television accused foreign powers, including France and Chad, of being behind last weekend's unrest, while Russia's foreign ministry described the mutineers as "extremists seemingly incited by European former colonial powers".
France has repeatedly rejected accusations that it is attempting to destabilise Niger. Chad's government did not respond to a BBC request for comment.

"[Niger is] underplaying the role that Africa Corps has in these countries, and they're overplaying the resource-nationalism narrative - the idea that the government is in control and fighting back against the jihadists," explained Boswall.
"There is a huge media war going on in the Sahel to control the narrative around that."
Russia's war with Ukraine is another important factor shaping its strategy in the Sahel.
The conflict continues to consume Russian personnel and military equipment, limiting how far Moscow can expand its operations in Africa.
"It's quite a tightrope for Russia because ultimately its priority will always be Ukraine," Ochieng said.

"It will maintain at least enough numbers to allow it to reassure the military governments in the Sahel that it continues to be a reliable partner. They'll continue to deploy just enough weapons and supplies and logistics… to continue supporting Africa Corps."
But there are limits to what that support can achieve. "Russia cannot afford a sustained counter-offensive anywhere in the Sahel," Ochieng said.
This may help explain why protecting allied governments appears to have become such an important part of Russia's regional strategy.
Defending a capital or helping loyalist forces defeat a mutiny requires fewer resources than recapturing and securing vast areas affected by an insurgency.
"These are quite limited interventions, but with an outsized impact," Boswall said.
"I think at that level they'll be able to sustain that over the foreseeable future, even with the war in Ukraine."
Russia may have helped Tiani survive this latest security challenge, but it has not removed the conditions that could produce the next mutiny.

articles.title: Prosecution: Poa testimony yielded key admissions in impeachment trial

articles.title: Tunisia: Judge orders arrest of journalist Mohamed Yousfi
articles.summary: A journalist and vocal critic of the Tunisian president, Mohamed Yousfi has been taken into custody ahead of an interview. A union called the arrest an attack on all journalists' rights.

image.caption: Tunisians took to the streets in August to call for the release of jailed activists and journalists and the president's resignationImage: Jihed Abidellaoui/REUTERS

blocks.text: A judge in Tunisia ordered the detention of prominent journalist Mohamed Yousfi on Friday. Police had taken him into custody as he arrived at a radio station to give an interview, according to Zied Dabbar, president of the journalist syndicate SNJT.
Dabbar said it was unclear why Yousfi was detained outside Radio Express FM, but he believed it was related to Yousfi's criticism of the authorities.
The judge ordered Yousfi detained on charges of illicit enrichment and money laundering, the state news agency reported, citing a judicial source.
No reason provided for detention

Yousfi, editor-in-chief of investigative news website Al-Qatiba, has been an outspoken critic of President Kais Saied. Al-Qatiba is known for investigative reporting and coverage of political, economic, social and environmental issues.
Radio Express FM host Walid Ben Rhouma said no reason was given for Yousfi's detention.
"He was barred from entering to participate in the program as a guest and was taken away for questioning, according to those who stopped him," Rhouma said in a Facebook post.
The SNJT said Yousfi's detention shows the erosion of press freedoms in Tunisia, where reporters, lawyers, opposition figures and activists have recently faced prosecution.
Attack on freedom of the press
SNJT called Yousfi's arrest not only an attack on him but also on all journalists and Tunisians' right to a free and independent media.

Rights ⁠groups ​warn of efforts to close Tunisia's remaining independent ​voices since Saied suspended parliament in 2021 and dissolved it in 2022. Saied says he will not be a dictator and that freedoms are guaranteed in Tunisia.
In August, protesters took the streets to demonstrate in support of jailed activists and journalists, as well as to call for Saied's removal from power.
Media figures jailed this year include Zied Heni, Mourad Zghidi and Borhen Bsaies. Khaoula Boukrim was sentenced in June to four years in ​absentia.
On Thursday, lawyer Ghazi Mrabet, known for handling politically sensitive and civil liberties cases, was arrested and placed in custody, according to local media reports.
The case reportedly involves alleged drug trafficking, although there are conflicting accounts of the circumstances.

articles.title: Bolivia: Deadly explosion rocks military base in Viacha
articles.summary: The explosion occurred at an army base where fireworks were stored. The exact cause of the blast is under investigation.

image.caption: Firefighters have been deployed at the site of blast in ViachaImage: APG Noticias/AFP

blocks.text: At least 10 people were killed, and 59 were injured after an explosion occurred at an army barracks in Bolivia on Friday, local authorities said.
Earlier, the police reported at least two deaths and several missing persons.
What do we know about the blast?
According to authorities, the blast occurred at around 2:30 p.m. (1830 GMT) local ​time in an area used to store pyrotechnic materials.

The explosion occurred in the western city of Viacha, about 30 kilometers (19 miles) from the capital, La Paz, at the military base where fireworks were stored. However, the authorities have yet to determine the cause of the explosion.
In a Facebook post, Defense Minister Ernesto Justiniano said that 52 of the injured were civilians and the rest were military personnel.
The fatalities could be between 10 and 15 people, Viacha health director Rita Nebraska told ‌local television.
Fourteen of the wounded were transferred to hospitals ​in La Paz, including a girl with third-degree burns, she said.
Several homes were damaged as windows broke in the blast, according to the police.
Threat of another blast looms
Nebraska ⁠said firefighters had warned that a heat source remained at ⁠the site, raising ​the risk of another explosion, and urged residents to stay at least 150 meters away.
Rescuers, medical teams and ambulances have been deployed at the site to help the injured and assess the damage.

articles.summary: Authorities fear the death toll in Viacha will rise and warn people to stay away from the barracks due to a risk of further explosions.

blocks.text: At least two people have been killed after an explosion at a military barracks in Bolivia but authorities fear the toll could be higher.

Bolivian Defence Minister Ernesto Justiniano said at least 58 people had been injured when "pyrotechnic material" detonated at the barracks, where an artillery regiment is stationed, about 14:30 (18:30 GMT) on Friday.
Health official Rita Nebraska told local television between 10 and 15 people were believed to have died in the incident in Viacha, about 30km (19 miles) from La Paz, according to Reuters.
Police said dozens of homes had been damaged - largely windows shattered in the blast - and emergency workers are searching the rubble.
Nebraska said there was a risk of further explosion and urged people to stay at least 150m away from the military base.
Police spokesman Roger Roca told AFP news agency that fireworks had been stored at the barracks, and the cause of the blast remained under investigation.
Viacha's authorities have declared three days of mourning.

articles.title: Why are European countries moving their gold out of North America?
articles.summary: The Netherlands has relocated 86 tonnes of the shiny stuff - what's going on?

blocks.text: When the central bank of the Netherlands confirmed this week that it had moved tonnes of the country's gold out of North America, it said the relocation would make it "better prepared for severe crises".

Some 86 tonnes from the combined total of about 313 tonnes held in the US and Canada were relocated to London "in view of increasing geopolitical unrest", it said, so the shiny stuff could be "readily available for use in a crisis situation".
Questions were bound to follow. Why were the Dutch doing this? Were they anticipating some major economic shock on the horizon?

It seems not, but the move was clearly in response to the unstable and uncertain state the world finds itself in, with trade and military wars prompting countries to take precautions and hold their gold closer to home.

Earlier this year, France announced it had removed its gold reserves from the US to home shores. Meanwhile, Germany's Bundesbank transferred more than 216 tonnes of the metal from storage locations abroad - 111 tonnes from New York and 105 tonnes from Paris - over a few years ending in 2016., external

It is a strategy which has played out before in times of global instability. "Some European central banks moved part of their gold holdings to New York during the Cold War," said research analysts Lina Thomas and Daan Struyven of Goldman Sachs.

Joseph Cavatoni, senior market strategist at the World Gold Council, told the BBC while wars and trade tensions were "playing into some of these decisions", it didn't "top the list" of motivating factors.
Inflation, interest rates and just having gold in a place where it can be traded quickly also played a role.

"I don't get a sense that there's an impending doom," Cavatoni said, "but what I do think is people are being better educated around how to manage their reserve assets, growing their reserve assets, and actually thinking more effectively around how to make the most of those assets."
De Nederlandsche Bank said the gold removed from the US and Canada between March and August this year was now being held in the vaults of the Bank of England.
"We expect that we will never need to use them, but we do need to strengthen our resilience and preparedness," said the governor of the Dutch central bank, Olaf Sleijpen.

London was seen as the best choice due its position in the world as a major trading centre. If you want to be able to buy or sell gold fast in a crisis, London is the place to be, which makes the Bank of England a popular storage spot.
The Bank is one of the largest custodians of gold in the world. Underneath the 300-year-old institution in central London sits about 400,000 bars worth more than £200bn.

According to industry surveys by the World Gold Council, the Bank of England remains the most popular vaulting location, but central banks are increasingly diversifying where they store the precious metal.
Where to store your country's gold is "increasingly top of mind for reserve managers", according to Thomas and Struyven of Goldman Sachs.

In the modern world, there are many ways to shift your treasure around. The Dutch sold about 59 tonnes in New York and then bought more stocks in London, meaning that amount didn't need to be hauled across the Atlantic.
But more than 27 tonnes were "physically transferred" from the US and Canada to the Dutch town of Zeist. A similar quantity was also sent from Zeist to London.

Companies that perform such services are tight-lipped on how operations are carried out, but it's fair to say the security measures and planning are extensive to avoid the risk of a real-life Italian Job.

Cavatoni, of the World Gold Council, said one standard approach to move gold stocks was to sell the commodity in one place and buy it in another. "Let's say I want my gold in New York and I have it in London. I could sell it in London, buy it in New York, same day, same time, effectively book transfer without actually having to put it on any other logistical change."

There are only a few select companies which handle gold shipments across borders, one of which is Brink's Global Services, who told the BBC it had seen "increased demand" from the likes of central banks in recent times.

"Heightened geopolitical and economic uncertainty, along with gold's growing role as a strategic reserve asset, appear to be contributing to this trend," said Nader Antar, Brink's executive vice president.

The reason gold storage is such a topic in the minds of central banks is because they have been increasingly buying the stuff. But storing it at home comes at a cost, said Thomas and Struyven of Goldman Sachs.
"Domestic storage requires investment in physical security, audit infrastructure, and insurance; costs that can be disproportionate for smaller central banks," they said.

Over the past four years, central banks have accumulated an annual average of 1,000 tonnes of gold, up significantly from the 500 tonnes average over the preceding decade, according to the World Gold Council.
The trend stretches back to the global financial crisis. And that is only expected to go up in the next year.
Gold has been having a moment in recent years. Its price has surged to hit a series of record highs, passing $5,000 an ounce in January.

There are several reasons behind its value jumping, but a major factor has been the precious metal's position in the human psyche as a so-called safe haven asset, to invest during periods of financial and geopolitical turmoil caused through trade and military wars.

Inflation and interest rates also influence gold's popularity. Due to the commodity's scarcity and the value placed on it across thousands of years, it is somewhat resistant against rising prices, and so is seen as a good investment.
"Over the past half-century, gold prices have risen much faster than the Consumer Price Index (CPI) - the most closely watched measure of inflation," according to investment bank Charles Schwab.
While the price of gold has fallen from the record high seen early this year, it still remains at a high level historically.
According to researchers at Goldman, the price is forecast to rise to $4,900 (£3,624) per troy ounce by the end of 2026, $300 more than it was in August.
The demand for gold from central banks is one key reason why prices are surging, according to Thomas and Struyven.

articles.title: Friend holds out hope for Canadian runner missing on Matterhorn
articles.summary: A friend of a Canadian athlete who went missing on the Matterhorn says Squamish, B.C.'s mountain running community is hoping for her safe return.

image.caption: The Matterhorn, seen from Zermatt in December 2020. Kalie McCrystal, an elite athlete from Squamish, had previously completed a solo ascent of the mountain in August starting from this village. (Jamey Keaten/Associated Press)

blocks.text: British Columbia
A friend of a Canadian athlete who went missing on the Matterhorn says Squamish, B.C.'s mountain running community is hoping for her safe return.
Helicopter crews suspended search for Kalie McCrystal, a Squamish, B.C., resident
Kalie McCrystal, an elite mountain athlete from Squamish, was last seen on Sept. 1 above the mountain's Jean-Antoine Carrel hut, located at an altitude of roughly 3,830 metres.
Search and rescue crews were mobilized to find her, but recently declared they would suspend the helicopter operations after a full day of aerial searches on Thursday turned up no trace.
"We just want her to come home safe," said Duncan O'Regan, a friend of McCrystal. "And we miss her here. So we're just crossing our fingers."

items: Helicopter search suspended for Squamish, B.C., mountain runner missing on Matterhorn

blocks.text: He described her as a fixture in the local mountain running community.
Speed record in sight

McCrystal, a 38-year-old lawyer, was training to climb and descend the Matterhorn in less than five hours via the Lion Ridge, the main route from the Italian side. She had her eye on attaining the fastest known time.

"I know that this objective was well within her capabilities," said O'Regan, who is a mountain runner. "She's done much more difficult things, and this is not something that is beyond her capabilities. She's comfortable in this terrain."

O'Regan said the Matterhorn objective is something she's been training and rehearsing. One of the most recognizable peaks of the Alps, the Matterhorn straddles Italy and Switzerland, standing 4,478 metres tall.
McCrystal is known as an expert skyrunner — a discipline which combines trail running and mountaineering.

"It's sort of like blending running a very long distance with scrambling," said Jacob Cook, a professional climber based in Squamish. "Sort of like rocky mountaineering terrain. And it quite quickly, often blends into, like, real climbing."
Cook said he doesn't know McCrystal personally but is aware and impressed with her accomplishments on the local circuit.

items: Hiker missing from B.C. gondola made call to 911 saying he's 'stuck on the mountain'

blocks.text: An accomplished athlete

In July, McCrystal bagged the fastest known female time of Squamish's Tantalus Traverse at nine hours and 40 minutes, crushing the previous record by three hours, according to the Fastest Known Time database.
"To do the Tantalus Traverse in the time that she did represents a really incredible level of athleticism," said Cook, who'd done the route a day after her.
McCrystal tested herself in competitions and mountains abroad.
Recently, she placed fourth in the women's division of the Trofeo Kima skyrunning race, which forces athletes through 52 kilometres of extremely technical mountainous terrain in Italy.
On Aug. 14, McCrystal completed a solo ascent and descent from Zermatt via the Swiss Hörnli Ridge in six hours, 47 minutes and 33 seconds, according to the Fastest Known Time database.
Global Affairs aware of situation
Capilano University, where she is a faculty member, expressed its sympathy.

“Our thoughts are with Kalie’s family, friends and colleagues, and with everyone involved in the search efforts during this incredibly difficult time," said Jason Dewling, president and vice-chancellor of the university.
Global Affairs Canada says it's aware of a missing Canadian and is in contact with local authorities.
"Everyone here in Squamish is just really missing Kalie and hoping that she comes back soon," said O'Regan.
