articles.title: Nepal rescuers try to reach dozens trapped in tunnel after two found alive
articles.summary: More than 1,300 people have died and thousands are missing, but rescuers' hopes have risen after finding survivors in a tunnel.

blocks.text: The full impact of the flood in Tibet is unclear. China has released information through state media outlets showing the devastation around the border, but has given few details about the victims or the impact on local villagers.
In Nepal, however, rescue operations are taking place at seven hydropower tunnels in which more than 150 people are feared trapped - as well as in 19 other areas.
In the early hours of Friday morning, rescuers heard what they thought could be voices at the Trishuli 3A hydropower site.
According to local reports, they called out "don't worry, we're here to rescue you" - and heard back a faint "okay".

Crews clambered in to find Sanjaya Shah and Kabir Maharjan - both had injuries on their hands and legs, "possibly" from crawling through the tunnel. Both were airlifted to the Army Hospital in the capital, Kathmandu.
Maharjan, who was rescued second, is in a critical condition, the prime minister's office said. Shah was also undergoing medical tests.
The body of a third person was found in the same tunnel later. A local official said it was swollen and could not be immediately identified.
Officials believe another 39 people are in the Trishuli 3A tunnel, although it is not clear if all are alive.
Col Jhabindra Reshmi said that his teams had rescued more than 400 Nepali nationals and 270 foreign citizens following the flash flooding on 26 August.
He has said mud and rocks have made entering tunnels difficult and rescuers were having to dig access holes to get underground.
Engineers have been pumping air into the tunnels.
Last week's floodwaters washed away a lot of heavy machinery, making it harder for rescuers to unblock tunnels, says a representative for Nepalese power companies.
Uttam Bhlon Lama, vice president at Independent Power Producers of Nepal, told the BBC's Newsday programme that the rescue of the two men on Friday would "motivate the rescuers to do more".
"The flood level is still very high," Lama added.
Nepalese authorities have warned that rainfall may cause additional flooding in the region.
At least 1,287 people are known to have died in Nepal, with 5,083 still missing.
On the Tibetan side, the death toll reported by Chinese media on Friday was 31, with 531 people unaccounted for.
Emergency teams in Tibet appear to be focusing on helping the living rather than holding out hope for more survivors.

articles.title: Bystanders rescue SUV occupants who crashed into Rideau River in Ottawa
articles.summary: Two occupants of an SUV that crashed into the river near Mooney's Bay on Friday morning had to be pulled from the water to safety. The rescue shows how important it is to have basic swimming skills,…

image.caption: Emergency crews respond to Friday morning's single-vehicle crash at the corner of Riverside Drive and Walkley Road. Thanks to the quick efforts of several bystanders, two people inside an SUV that crashed into the Rideau River were able to safely make it to shore. (Gabrielle Huston/CBC)

blocks.text: Ottawa·Updated

Two occupants of an SUV that crashed into the river near Mooney's Bay on Friday morning had to be pulled from the water to safety. The rescue shows how important it is to have basic swimming skills, according to one of the women who rushed to help.
Shows how important it is to have basic swimming skills, says one rescuer
Two people whose SUV crashed into the Rideau River on Friday morning are safe after several others who were in the area rushed into action to rescue them.
Emergency services responded to the single-vehicle collision around 5:50 a.m. at the corner of Riverside Drive and Walkley Road near Mooney's Bay, according to Ottawa paramedics.
They said an SUV went into the water and that two people inside had made it back to shore. They were assessed by paramedics and released at the scene.
CBC News saw a long silver pole on the road and boats labeled "Ottawa Fire" on the water around 6 a.m. on Friday.
Lesley Tomlinson had been out for a run that morning and was near the intersection when she heard the sound of a car braking and skidding.
She told CBC the SUV had skidded through the intersection, hit the light pole, went over the embankment and crashed into the water.
"I was dumbfounded," she said.
'He can't swim!'
"There was definitely a moment of panic as to, how do I help these people?" Tomlinson said.

Two other people emerged on the scene to help, she said. One woman came out of a house nearby and called 911, while another woman who'd been in a car behind the SUV pulled over and jumped into the water.
Tomlinson said she watched her help the driver out of the car and then go around to the passenger's side, yelling: "He can't swim!"
A former lifeguard, Tomlinson dove into the water. When she reached the car, it was mostly submerged and the passenger was holding onto it.
"I was very assertive and I told him that he was not to touch me, he was not to put his arms around me, that that would mean we would both drown," Tomlinson recalled.
"I told him that he is going to lie on his back and I am going to hold his head and I'm going to bring him in. ... We got him into that position just as the car completely submerged."
'You really need basic swimming skills'
Tomlinson said she swam with him to shore while supporting his head.
Speaking to CBC News afterwards, she said it didn't hit her how extraordinary the situation was in the moment.

items: Do you know what to do if someone is drowning?
How to know when someone is in trouble in the water

blocks.text: Tomlinson emphasized that it was a group effort to help, saying the woman who had pulled over and jumped in first was "the real superstar."
Later that day, Tomlinson went to work as a teacher and told her students about what happened.

"I felt it was so important to impress upon them the ability to swim. The driver was not a strong swimmer but he could keep his head up ... the other person couldn't swim and didn't know what to do," she said.
"I really think the takeaway from this whole thing is that you really need basic swimming skills because you never know what situation you're going to be in."
Police told CBC on Saturday that the SUV had been recovered from the Rideau River.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Gabrielle is a journalist for CBC News in Ottawa and Sudbury who loves to learn new things. She has a bachelor's degree in the humanities and journalism from Carleton University and has previously written for tech outlets like TheGamer and MobileSyrup. Reach out to her for any reason at gabrielle.huston@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Majority of Germans see Russia as a threat
articles.summary: More than half of German citizens believe that Germany's security is threatened by Russia, according to the latest ARD Deutschlandtrend survey.

image.caption: The German government has accused Russia of hybrid attacksImage: Florian Gaertner/photothek/picture alliance

blocks.text: In the past few weeks, Germany has seen a drone attack on Leipzig Airport and an arson attack near defense contractors in Bavaria, while explosive devices and pyrotechnics were found at two substations in Brandenburg and North Rhine-Westphalia.
As the country enters a September featuring three vital state elections, attacks on critical infrastructure appear to be on the rise, and defense contractors are apparently in the crosshairs.

After some initial hesitation, the German government has now publicly blamed Russia for the Leipzig attack, but could the Kremlin also be behind the other attacks? "We are not at war, but we are no longer at peace either," said Chancellor Friedrich Merz of the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU).

Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, of the Bavaria's conservatives, the Christian Social Union (CSU), has also warned that Germany has now become a "daily target of hybrid warfare," referring to measures that are not military, but are nonetheless meant to destabilize a country and unsettle the population — including cyberattacks, espionage, propaganda, disinformation, and acts of sabotage.

The developments seem to have alarmed the German people. Some 56% of the eligible voters polled now see Germany's security as threatened by Russia, according to the latest Deutschlandtrend, for which the polling firm infratest-dimap conducted a representative survey of 1,319 German voters for public broadcaster ARD between August 31 and September 2.
East Germans are significantly less concerned

But not all Germans feel this way. Nearly half of citizens in eastern Germany, for instance, feel only slightly threatened, or not at all, by Russia. The same goes for supporters of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), some of whose prominent figures have expressed support for Russia. The survey found that two-thirds of AfD supporters consider the threat from Russia to be low.

The same divisions in the German population emerge on the question of arms exports to Ukraine. Just over half of Germans consider the country's military support for Ukraine appropriate, or think it should even be expanded, but for just over four in ten Germans, that support goes too far. Opposition to sending weapons to Ukraine predominates in eastern Germany and among AfD supporters.
AfD holds steady lead nationwide

The eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt will elect a new state parliament on Sunday, and the AfD continues to be way ahead in the polls and could even win an absolute majority — usually unheard of in German elections.

The party also continues to enjoy strong support at the national level. The new poll suggests that if a general election were held this coming Sunday, the AfD would receive 27% of the vote, one point less than in August, which would make it the largest party in the lower house of parliament, the Bundestag.

The CDU/CSU, meanwhile, remains in second place at 21%, well below the 28.5% it managed in the Bundestag election in February 2025. The Greens would receive 15%, while the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) and the socialist Left Party have seen slight improvements compared to August, reaching 13% and 12%, respectively (+1 each). All other parties would fail to clear the 5% threshold.
Unpopular government, unpopular chancellor
The latest poll also suggests that the current governing coalition of the CDU/CSU and the Social Democrats would no longer have a majority if an election were held now.

Only 15% of those surveyed are satisfied with the government's performance, and even among supporters of the governing parties themselves, a majority is disappointed with the incumbent coalition's performance. Chancellor and CDU leader Friedrich Merz fares even worse: Only 13% approve of his work.
This is consistent with how citizens assess the CDU/CSU's competence.

Also notable is that significantly fewer voters believe the CDU/CSU is capable of finding solutions in key policy areas. While just over a year ago, 31% still considered those parties competent to ensure peace in Europe, that figure has now dropped to just 23%.
A similar loss of confidence in the CDU/CSU is apparent elsewhere: On asylum and refugee policy, on pension reform, and on climate and environmental policy.
On the topic of the economy, the CDU/CSU still enjoys the highest level of public confidence at 24%, but here too, the figure has dropped significantly from 31% in February 2026.
In eastern Germany, the AfD is now the party in which citizens place the most confidence across all policy areas surveyed, with the exception of climate and environmental policy.
Is Germany's weak economy boosting the right-wing AfD?
Economy causing concern

For many months now, Germans have viewed the economic situation as the most pressing problem to be solved. As many as 79% of respondents in the ARD Deutschlandtrend survey say the economy is doing poorly or very poorly. Here, too, however, there are significant differences depending on party affiliation.

As many as 41% of SPD supporters view the economic situation as good or very good, and 37% of Green Party supporters say the same. In contrast, only 3% of AfD supporters share this view — they are much more pessimistic, with 96% saying the economy is poor or very poor.
This article was translated from German.

articles.title: The hidden environmental cost of AI data centers
articles.summary: As data centers multiply to meet AI demand, they're straining power grids, draining water supplies and reshaping the land and air around them.

image.caption: Rows of servers hum inside Google's data center in Douglas County, Georgia — one of thousands of facilities worldwide powering the AI boomImage: Connie Zhou/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Every question sent to AI models provides an instant reply that seems to appear out of nowhere, but answering queries requires physical infrastructure that consumes real energy, water and land.

Somewhere around the world — maybe in Virginia, Sao Paulo or Hong Kong — a massive warehouse filled with fiber-optic cables and seemingly endless rows of humming servers is working to provide the processing power for the more than 2.5 billion questions ChatGPT alone fields daily.

AI models, along with cloud storage, streaming, web hosting and social media, all have a very real physical footprint. If data centers were a country, their level of electricity use would make them the 11th largest electricity consumer in the world, according to researchers from the United Nations University.
From energy to water to land, here's the real toll data centers take on the environment.

blocks.caption: Every query typed into a chatbot like ChatGPT sets off a chain of physical processes in data centers around the worldImage: CHRISTIAN BEUTLER/KEYSTONE/picture alliance

blocks.text: An insatiable appetite for power

Data centers are becoming some of the world's fastest-growing consumers of electricity. These warehouses of servers, routers and internet-connected devices run 24/7, while cooling systems operate continuously to keep the tech from overheating.

In Frankfurt, Germany, the grid is currently so saturated that no new connections will be available until at least the 2030s. There, data centers consume about 41% of the city's electricity. In Dublin, it's double that.

And data center electricity consumption is growing rapidly — it's expected to double by 2030 to about 945 terawatt-hours, around what Japan consumes annually, according to the International Energy Agency.
How the AI boom could slow climate progress
All that energy has to come from somewhere, increasing reliance on fossil fuels.

One 2024 study found that more than half of the United States' data centers are powered by fossil fuels, emitting in excess of 105 million tons of CO2. Offsetting that would take more than 31,000 wind turbines running continuously for a year.

The build-out is also keeping old coal plants alive. Utilities in the US have delayed the retirement of 15 coal-fired plants nationwide to meet surging demand, plants that together emitted nearly 65 million tons of greenhouse gases in 2023 alone.

blocks.caption: A technician checks equipment at an Amazon Web Services data center in New Carlisle, Indiana, one of the facilities straining local power grids to keep up with demandImage: Noah Berger/REUTERS

blocks.text: And utilities are also constructing new gas-fired power plants, with more than 100 GW of additional facilities across the country already announced. That would lead to more carbon emissions than burning 111 million pounds (50.4 million kilograms) of coal.

Of course, data centers can also be powered by renewable energy. Pairing a facility with on-site renewables can ease pressure on the local power supply, and any surplus energy can even be sold back to the grid, making it more stable.
However, using green electricity for data centers means there is less available for electrifying transport or decarbonizing other emissions-heavy industries.
Hidden water demand

Many data centers consume millions of gallons of water to stay cool. Servers generate constant heat, and water is one of the most effective ways to absorb and carry that heat away through evaporation.

A single large facility can use up to 5 million gallons a day, roughly the same as a town of 10,000 to 50,000 people. About 80% of the water withdrawn for cooling simply evaporates; the rest becomes wastewater that can overwhelm local treatment systems never designed to handle that volume.

blocks.caption: Demonstrators in Fredericksburg, Virginia, joined a nationwide protest against data centers in July 2026, with many signs targeting the industry's heavy water useImage: Evelyn Hockstein/REUTERS

blocks.text: In northern Virginia, the almost 300 data centers clustered in one region of the US state supply about a third of the world's online traffic. There, in what is known as the world's data center capital, facilities collectively used nearly 2 billion gallons of water in 2023.

There are several more efficient ways to cool data centers. These include immersion cooling, where devices are bathed in a coolant, and closed-loop cooling systems which recycle water and can reduce freshwater use by up to 70%.
Data centers are making cities hotter
Cooling a data center doesn't get rid of the heat, it just moves it outside. That can exacerbate the urban heat island effect, which is when cities experience higher temperatures than rural areas.

Researchers in Phoenix, Arizona, found a single large data center can emit as much waste heat as tens or even hundreds of thousands of households, raising nearby land surface temperatures by up to 9 degrees Celsius (16 Fahrenheit) and air temperatures by up to 2 degrees Celsius. Those effects can be felt as far as half a kilometer away.

Since cities are already 0.5–4 degrees Celsius warmer than their surroundings, these higher temperatures can increase heat stress risks for nearby residents and push up air conditioning demand, requiring still yet more energy.

Not all of that heat goes to waste: a growing number of data centers are capturing and piping it into nearby homes and businesses. This process, called thermal energy networks, can reduce data center power demand by up to 30%.
Coal, gas and diesel all contribute to dirty air
Powering and running data centers pollutes the air on two fronts.
First, coal and gas plants release toxic particulate matter, which can lead to respiratory disease, heart disease, asthma and more health conditions for nearby communities.
On-site diesel generators, used as backup power when the grid fails, also release harmful air pollutants. These generators pump out 200 to 600 times more nitrogen oxides than natural gas plants.

One estimate found that when backup generators for all of Virginia's data centers were emitting at just 10% of their permitted level, they could contribute to 14,000 cases of asthma symptoms, more than a dozen deaths and up to $300 million in public health costs a year.
Data centers take over large swaths of land
Data center construction requires large plots of land to build on. Repurposing natural and agricultural areas into industrial zones can threaten biodiversity and disrupt local ecosystems.

In Hattersheim, Germany, for example, an 18-acre (7-hectare) parcel reserved for agriculture and groundwater protection — a local green space known for its rapeseed blossoms — was rezoned in 2024 to make way for a five-building data center campus.
The damage often extends beyond the site itself. Gas pipelines and power plants built to supply these facilities require their own land, fragmenting habitats and eroding soil along their routes.
Why does AI need so much energy?

articles.title: Serbia: How the funeral of Ratko Mladic is dividing a nation
articles.summary: As the Serbian government leaves the decision about Ratko Mladic's funeral arrangements to his family, international pressure on the country is mounting. How do Serbs feel about the matter?

image.caption: 'There is no small town in Serbia without at least one mural glorifying Ratko Mladic,' says Jasmina Lazovic, executive director of the Humanitarian Law CenterImage: Darko Vojinovic/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The body of the former Bosnian Serb army commander Ratko Mladic, who died last week in The Hague, where he was serving a life sentence for genocide and other war crimes in Bosnia and Herzegovina, has arrived back in Serbia.
Wrapped in the Serbian flag, Mladic's coffin was carried by members of the Serbian Armed Forces from the plane to a vehicle that transported his remains to the Military Medical Academy for autopsy.

Several groups of citizens gathered along the route from the airport to the hospital. Standing on overpasses, they greeted the motorcade carrying Mladic's body, holding banners that read "Thank you, General" and "Heroes never die."
Pro-government tabloids provided minute-by-minute coverage, referring to Mladic as a "Serbian general" and claiming that he had been "killed in The Hague."
A funeral with full state honors?

Ratko Mladic was sentenced in 2017 to life imprisonment by the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia in The Hague for the genocide in Srebrenica, in which more than 8,000 Muslim men and boys were killed, the years-long siege of Sarajevo during the 1992–95 Bosnian War, and other war crimes, including the establishment of detention camps for non-Serb civilians and prisoners of war.

blocks.caption: The body of former Bosnian Serb wartime general Ratko Mladic (in the red van) was transferred to the Military Medical Academy for autopsy after being flown to Belgrade from The HagueImage: Darko Vojinovic/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Belgrade media report that Mladic will be buried in Belgrade on Monday. Justice Minister Nenad Vujic had previously announced that the funeral would be held with the highest state honors.
Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic, however, says the decision will be left to the family.
Security agencies estimate that tens of thousands of people could attend the funeral.

"We will be there to provide all kinds of logistical and transport support and to maintain public order and security," said the president, adding, "It is very difficult to ensure and guarantee the safety of everyone."
Glorification that has continued for decades

For Jasmina Lazovic, executive director of the Belgrade-based Humanitarian Law Center, which has spent decades working on transitional justice and dealing with the past, none of this comes as a surprise.
She points to the long-standing glorification of Ratko Mladic in Serbia and his legacy.

"There is no small town in Serbia without at least one mural glorifying Ratko Mladic. The narrative that he was unjustly convicted has existed for years," she told DW. "Now a narrative has emerged that he was killed, despite the fact that he died at the age of 85 after suffering several strokes."

Lazovic says that these narratives suit the state leadership's portrayal of Serbia as a country that fought exclusively defensive wars and do not leave enough room for a discussion of the consequences of those wars and the victims they left behind — neither in the media nor in the education system and institutions.

"And there are hundreds of thousands of victims across Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina and Kosovo. Above all, these were crimes committed against civilians, crimes that left the countries of the region — particularly Bosnia and Herzegovina — with a completely transformed ethnic structure," she said.
Lazovic says that the list of victims also includes those who survived rape and torture, as well as those who were forcibly displaced. "The list is long, and our knowledge is limited," she added.
A general without a rank
The announcement that Mladic could be buried with the highest state honors drew swift responses from the international community.

"Glorification of war criminals is contrary to European values. There is no place for it either in EU member states or in candidate countries. I hope the government in Belgrade is aware of that," said European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos.

blocks.caption: Ratko Mladic was convicted of war crimes, including the 1992-95 siege of Sarajevo. This memorial features the names of 1,601 children killed during that siegeImage: Amel Emric/REUTERS

blocks.text: Aleksandar Vucic responded by accusing the West and the Hague Tribunal of blaming only Serbs for war crimes and failing to deliver justice for Serbian victims. But for now, he has officially left the decision on whether the deceased general will receive state honors to Mladic's family.

Jasmina Lazovic believes Vucic will once again take a pragmatic approach and that the final decision will depend on an assessment of what brings the authorities greater political benefit and what could cause greater damage.
She also points out that the issue is not only political, but legal.

"What is being overlooked here is the fact that Ratko Mladic was indeed a general, but he was sentenced to life in prison. Under the Law on the Serbian Armed Forces, anyone sentenced to more than one year in prison for a criminal offense loses their rank and, therefore, all the privileges that come with that rank," she told DW.
"If Ratko Mladic were buried with the highest state honors in accordance with the rank he held during the armed conflicts, that would be a direct violation of the law of this country," said Lazovic.
What do Serbs want?

On the question as to how they view Ratko Mladic, Serbian citizens interviewed by DW in several cities across the multi-ethnic autonomous province of Vojvodina expressed sharply differing views, ranging from those who are convinced that Mladic was unjustly convicted to those who accept the genocide designation without reservation.

blocks.caption: Mladic was also convicted of genocide in Srebrenica, where over 8,000 Muslim men and boys were killed in the summer of 1995Image: Samir Jordamovic/Anadolu Agency/IMAGO

blocks.text: "What was he supposed to do, let them kill all the Serbs? Thank you [Mladic], for everything," one man from Ruma told DW.
"For me, the matter was settled when the genocide verdict was handed down," said a student from Novi Sad.
But most people simply wave the question away. "I have enough of my own problems," said Svetlana from Zrenjanin.
Goran, from Novi Sad, believes that it is simply another political issue: "They've been making fools of us for years. Nothing is different now," he told DW.
Jasmina Lazovic believes that most Serbs are apathetic about the matter.

For her, this is a greater problem than just the pro-government media portraying Serbia as wanting to say goodbye to Mladic as a general. She argues that confronting Mladic's legacy and the past is essential if Serbian society is to move forward.

articles.title: Europe targeted by spiralling campaign of sabotage and Russia is the chief suspect
articles.summary: Germany has blamed Russia for an attack on Leipzig airport but there has been a series of suspicious incidents elsewhere.

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Germany said the attack at Leipzig airport was part of a pattern of "Russian hybrid operations" in Europe
BySarah Rainsford
Southern and Eastern Europe correspondent
As summer temperatures in Europe smashed records this summer and many politicians shifted to holiday mode, Russia remained focused on its war.
Not only did its military attacks across Ukraine intensify last month, becoming ever more deadly for civilians, Russia also appears to have escalated its sabotage campaign across Europe.
This time, military and defence sector sites were the prime target.
A full month after drones packed with explosives were found at Leipzig's airport, used by Ukraine to transport military goods, Germany's interior minister has declared that "Russia is responsible".
Russia's President Vladimir Putin is demanding proof, as always, and his officials call the accusation "absurd".
But the drones were just a dramatic start. August then brought a series of suspicious fires at defence facilities from Italy to Estonia.
Some of the affected countries have already blamed Russia; others are still investigating and some fires may eventually be ruled accidental, exactly as such attacks are designed to seem.
Poland's interior minister is clear.

"There are many, many signals that Russia is changing its strategy and intensifying its activities, including terrorist and sabotage activities," Marcin Kierwiński said, warning people to be on their guard.
August campaign across Europe
4 August Germany: The first drone at Leipzig airport is discovered.
10 August Bulgaria: A major fire breaks out at a factory of the defence firm EMCO, with initial reports that a truck ignited during a fuel delivery.
13 August Italy: A fire at KNDS Ammo Italy outside Rome triggers a large explosion.

The local prosecutor is looking into possible outside interference, La Repubblica newspaper reports. Publicly, his office will only confirm that a case has been opened for negligent disaster against "unknown persons".
15 August Estonia: The Milrem Robotics factory in Tallinn, which the Kyiv Post says supplies drones to Ukraine, goes up in flames. Two suspects are arrested.
Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal says the possibility of Russian sabotage is being "taking seriously" by investigators.

25 August Slovakia: Police announce they have averted an arson attack on a Ukrainian-owned drone manufacturer and seized a "large amount of incendiary mixture". The firm itself blames Russia and police arrest three suspects who they say were "following orders". Slovakia is Russia's close ally in Europe.
30 August Poland: A country which is heavily targeted for sabotage reports two more fires.
One is in Lublin at a company which produces helicopter components. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said arson "cannot be ruled out".
An attack on the drone producer, WB Group, is clearer cut. A masked man is caught on CCTV throwing incendiary devices. Tusk calls it a "continuation of Russia's escalatory activities".
The pattern has continued into September with two Bulgarians arrested in Munich, Germany, for suspected arson after throwing incendiary devices from a car at defence firm Rhode & Schwartz.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The 31 August fire at Skarżysko-Kamienna targeted one of Poland's biggest defence firms

blocks.text: Image source, EPA
The 31 August fire at Skarżysko-Kamienna targeted one of Poland's biggest defence firms
Why is this happening now?
Attacks on military and defence targets are not new, although previous acts of sabotage linked to Russia include more puzzling targets - such as an Ikea store and a Polish paint store.
The novelty now is the concentration of cases.
"The intensity of military sites being attacked we've seen over the past couple of weeks is unusual," Daniela Richterova of the Department of War Studies at King's College says.
She links the spike to developments in Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
"We've basically seen Ukraine take the war to Russia and strike deep inside Russian territory…They [Moscow] are under pressure, they have to do something."
Whilst some sabotage is staged to sow chaos or fear, Richterova believes the Kremlin's aim right now is "coercive signalling": pressuring countries to stop supporting Kyiv by raising the stakes.
After a slow start, Germany is Ukraine's biggest supplier of military aid.
There are other theories.
To some, Russia is less concerned about "turning off the taps" of supplies to Ukraine and more about testing Nato for weaknesses.

"Russia is probing the boundaries of what's acceptable and collecting information on the results. They find out what works, and what's vulnerable," argues Keir Giles from the Chatham House think tank.
He sees the sabotage campaign as preparation for the "next phase", as he puts it, of Russia's aggression in Europe.
"They're assessing the willingness of the victim country to actually do something about it."

The International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS), which tracks sabotage cases, points to a previous surge in 2024 when Ukraine's allies began allowing it to use Western-supplied weapons deeper inside Russia.
2024 was the year of the parcel bomb plot, when Russia was accused of sending packages containing liquid explosive to the UK and Poland.
One ignited shortly before it was loaded on to a DHL cargo plane. It is thought this was a test run for something significantly bigger.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Four parcels were sent from Lithuania to the UK and Poland in 2024 - two caught fire, at a warehouse in the UK and at Leipzig's airport

blocks.text: Image source, Police handout
Four parcels were sent from Lithuania to the UK and Poland in 2024 - two caught fire, at a warehouse in the UK and at Leipzig's airport
"That was a marked high in terms of their willingness to inflict mass casualties," Giles adds.
It was a step so serious, the White House contacted the Kremlin to tell it to stop. Russia had probed and found the limit.
But the attacks have continued. German media on Friday quoted a federal police report that lists more than 165 suspected sabotage cases nationwide this year, though they don't say who is responsible.
Who are the suspected saboteurs?
Reports from Germany suggest the men who loaded and launched the drones at Leipzig's airport were Russian, and at least one may have entered the country specially for this job.
That would be unusual.
The vast majority of sabotage attacks in Europe have been carried out by Russian proxies: its so-called "gig economy saboteurs".
They are usually Russian-speakers from former Soviet states, recruited online and driven by the cash, not political conviction.
In one case the BBC reported from Poland, the saboteurs-for-hire had previously fought for Ukraine as volunteers.
The "handlers" are generally thought to remain in Russia, co-ordinating operations online.
The IISS likened the proxies they used to kamikaze drones: cheap and easy to launch in large numbers, but disposable.
The amateurs can be sloppy or reckless, though. In the parcel plot, one man failed to find a pick-up point and the whole mission had to be aborted.
So if Moscow did send professionals for the Leipzig drone launch, it suggests it wanted precision - and success.
In fact, the devices appear to have malfunctioned.
Nato faced with Soviet-style campaign

Russia's sabotage operations seem to come from the Cold War playbook. Daniela Richterova's research shows very similar targets on Soviet sabotage lists, and agents-saboteurs were used in much the same way.
The idea, she says, was to have small, deniable attacks in peace-time that would escalate in times of war.
"I think we are still in the grey zone between the two, but the kind of attacks we've seen in the past weeks shrink that zone," she says. "And I think that increases the risk of what happens next."
As Nato scrambles to respond, questions like how many small, individual attacks add up to a sustained Russian assault - and demand action - remain unanswered.
Perhaps riskier than all is the potential for escalation by accident.
What if the exploding parcel had gone off mid-air and caused a crash? What if the Leipzig drone had brought down a plane?
"I think it could result in a big attack," Richterova says. "Then Nato, in this heightened security environment, would not be able to ignore that, and have to react."

articles.title: South Korea pushes back on reports it is readying Hormuz deployment amid US pressure
articles.summary:
Seoul reportedly seeking parliamentary approval to send military assets to Middle East but president’s office plays down claims

South Korea is reviewing a possible deployment of military…

blocks.text: South Korea is reviewing a possible deployment of military assets to the strait of Hormuz amid pressure from Donald Trump over Seoul’s reluctance to provide support in the region, according to domestic media reports.

Citing unnamed government and military sources, the reportspublished on Thursday and Friday said preparations were under way and that the government intended to seek parliamentary approval for a new deployment. The reports, which appeared in major South Korean outlets, said the exact scale and timing have not been agreed.

But the presidential office pushed back, telling the Guardian that such reports were “different from the facts” and that “nothing related to the matter has been decided”, though it said the review was “continuing”.

An official said: “Our government has been closely discussing with the international community ways to make practical contributions for the speedy restoration of free navigation in the strait of Hormuz and peace and stability in the Middle East.”

According to reports, the assets under consideration include a P-8 Poseidon aircraft, which would mark South Korea’s first overseas deployment of a maritime patrol aircraft, and a naval logistics support ship to provide rear support.
One outlet, Seoul Broadcasting System, additionally reported that an explosive ordnance disposal team from the navy’s underwater demolition unit was part of the package.
Any new deployment in principle would require review by the national security council, a cabinet resolution and approval from the national assembly.
South Korea is highly dependent on the strait of Hormuz, importing more than 90% of its primary energy, including roughly 70% of crude oil through the waterway.

blocks.caption: The office of South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, said ‘nothing related to the matter has been decided’ in response to the media reports. Photograph: YONHAP/EPA

blocks.text: In 2020, the government of the then president Moon Jae-in expanded the mandate of an existing anti-piracy unit off the coast of Somalia to cover the strait of Hormuz, rather than seeking parliamentary approval for a new deployment.

South Korea’s defence minister, Ahn Gyu-back, in March told parliament that any deployment to the strait would require the national assembly’s consent given how different the mission would be from the unit’s existing anti-piracy mandate.

The reports come amid growing strains in the US-South Korea alliance. Trump has repeatedly complained in public that Seoul turned down his request for help over Iran, claiming in August that South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, had told him “No, thanks” despite the US stationing tens of thousands of troops on the peninsula.
Days later, he ordered the Ulchi Freedom Shield joint military exercises to be scaled back, shortening the drills by six days.

Relations between the two allies have also been strained by delays implementing a $350bn investment package Seoul agreed with Washington last year, reports that the US had restricted intelligence sharing with South Korea, and by a dispute over a data breach at the South Korean e-commerce company Coupang.
Separately, Seoul has expressed interest in taking part in any renewed US-North Korea diplomacy, as Trump signals openness to another meeting with Kim Jong-un.

articles.title: President Javier Milei says ‘winds of change’ support Argentina’s claim to Falkland Islands
articles.summary:
President cites Donald Trump’s suggestion that he might reconsider US support for British sovereignty, and threatens swifter sanctions on British oil interests

President Javier Milei has…

blocks.text: President Javier Milei has said “winds of change favourable” to Argentina’s claim to the Falkland Islands were “blowing around the world” in a televised address, citing signs that Donald Trump might reconsider the US position on the islands’ sovereignty.
“Recently, President Trump declared that the US is re-evaluating its historic position in relation to the Malvinas,” he said, using the Argentinian name for the islands.

The Argentinian president said the UK was facing “multiple crises of a migratory, demographic and economic nature that are unlikely to be resolved. It is clear that they are on a path of decline. Argentina’s future, however, is flourishing and will prevail.”

Earlier on Thursday, Trump was asked by British outlet GB News if he would “come to the UK’s aid” during a potential territorial dispute over the Falkland Islands with Argentina, and hinted that he would not, adding that the UK “weren’t there to help me [with Iran]”.
Supporters had expected Milei to use his address to the nation on Thursday night to announce an unprecedented US endorsement of Argentina’s sovereignty claim over the Falkland Islands.

Instead, the self-styled libertarian, when asked whether he was reviewing the US position on the islands, repeated the US president’s words, saying: “I always review every position. That’s just one of many.”
The far-right president then portrayed Trump’s response as a “threat” that was “not innocuous”.

“The US is considering this change of position because it knows that Argentina has a reliable partner, aligned with western values, in a strategically important position that can be a valuable ally in the decades to come,” he said.

The US has formally recognised the UK’s de facto administration of the islands but has not taken a formal position on sovereignty. The first reports of a possible revision emerged in April, when an internal Pentagon email reported by Reuters raised the prospect of Washington reconsidering its stance as one possible way of punishing Nato allies that declined to join the Iran war.

In Thursday’s interview, Trump said of the UK: “Your country was not there to help me. We didn’t need help, but I did ask Nato, and I asked your former leader [Keir Starmer], ‘why don’t you send a couple of ships?’. He said, ‘We don’t have any’. It was pretty sad, the whole thing.”

Despite the expectations created by Milei and his supporters – the president summoned all his ministers to stand alongside him – the main new elements of the speech were a few decrees announced by the president.

One of them is to speed up sanctions “against those participating in oil extraction initiatives”, specifically citing an offshore oil project in the North Falkland Basin led by the Israeli company Navitas alongside its British partner Rockhopper. Milei claimed the project violated a UN call for neither Argentina nor the UK to take unilateral action in the territory.

Despite his “radical” austerity policies, Milei also said he would sign an emergency decree to increase resources for the defence ministry, prioritising the construction of an integrated naval base in Tierra del Fuego. The project to build a base there predates Milei, and construction began in 2022.

The UK said earlier this week that its position on the Falklands was “long-standing and unwavering”. It said in a statement: “Sovereignty rests with the UK, and the islanders’ right to self-determination is paramount. The UK’s position is clear. The islanders have repeatedly expressed their wish to remain a British overseas territory.”

Some analysts had already viewed Milei’s recent embrace of the Malvinas cause as another attempt to create a “smokescreen” at the lowest point of his popularity since taking office. He is expected to seek re-election next year.

Amid corruption allegations involving members of his government and poor economic results – his “chainsaw” austerity policies have brought inflation under control, but unemployment and poverty have risen – the far-right president has increasingly turned up the volume on controversial measures, including claims of an anti-Argentina campaign dating back to the World Cup, attacks on Brazil’s leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and an immigration crackdown modelled on the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

Many have also noted that his interest in the issue is recent. Milei had long described himself as a great admirer of Margaret Thatcher, the British prime minister during the 1982 Falklands war, and only began adopting a public pro-sovereignty stance a few months ago, after reports emerged that the US might be reconsidering its position.
The far-right leader also dismissed the principle of self-determination invoked by the UK – in a 2013 referendum, 99.8% of the islanders voted to remain a British overseas territory.
Echoing the same phrase used by Argentina’s national team on a banner celebrating their victory over England in the World Cup semi-final, Milei said that “The Malvinas are Argentinian.”

articles.title: Chinese man, 2 others nabbed in alleged P300,000 cellphone robbery
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — A Chinese man and two of his alleged cohorts were arrested in Makati City for allegedly attempting to rob two individuals during a deal to purchase P300,000 worth of cellphones,…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — A Chinese man and two of his alleged cohorts were arrested in Makati City for allegedly attempting to rob two individuals during a deal to purchase P300,000 worth of cellphones, the Southern Police District (SPD) said on Friday.
In a statement, the SPD said the suspects were arrested along Amorsolo Street in Barangay Pio del Pilar on Thursday night following a request for police assistance from one of the victims.
Police identified the suspects only by their aliases: “Lulu,” a 27-year-old Chinese man; and “Leif” and “James,” both residents of Barangay New Lower Bicutan in Taguig City.
The victims had supposedly met with the suspects along Amorsolo Street for the transaction to purchase the cellphones.

“During the transaction, the suspects allegedly forcibly took one of the victims aboard their vehicle. The other victim pursued the vehicle and shouted for help, alerting police personnel manning a nearby post,” the SPD said.

“The police officers immediately responded, proceeded to the area, intercepted a black Ford Territory and a silver Toyota Fortuner, and arrested the three suspects before they could leave the vicinity,” it added.

Police operatives recovered a Taurus 9mm pistol with seven live rounds of ammunition; a caliber .38 revolver with three live rounds of ammunition; an unidentified number of license plates bearing different plate numbers; several cellphones and other personal belongings.
The SPD noted that authorities also recovered 1.8 grams of suspected shabu (crystal meth) worth P12,240 as well as two glass tubes with suspected drug residue from the suspects.
The three arrested individuals were taken into the custody of the Makati City Police Station.

They await charges for attempted robbery, grave coercion and usurpation of authority as well as violations of Republic Act No. 10591 or the Firearms and Ammunition Regulation Act; RA No. 9165 or the Dangerous Drugs Act; and RA No. 4136 or the Land Transportation and Traffic Code. /jpv

articles.title: 2 trapped workers rescued alive from a tunnel in Nepal, officials say
articles.summary: KATHMANDU, Nepal — Rescuers in Nepal pulled two workers alive from a tunnel Friday during an ongoing operation at the Trishul 3A tunnel, officials said. Nepalese lawmaker Shri Ram Neupane posted…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU, Nepal — Rescuers in Nepal pulled two workers alive from a tunnel Friday during an ongoing operation at the Trishul 3A tunnel, officials said.

Nepalese lawmaker Shri Ram Neupane posted about the second rescue on his Facebook page shortly after army spokesperson Brig. Gen. Raja Ram Basnet confirmed the first trapped worker’s rescue during the operation at the tunnel. Officials identified the two men as a mechanical foreman and a mechanical supervisor.
The rescues come nine days after the Aug. 26 floods, likely caused by a glacier collapse, that devastated towns and valleys in Nepal.

Local television news channels showed images of the first rescued worker covered in mud and being carried from the site on a rescuer’s shoulder. Both men were under medical observation, the officials said.

At least 557 workers are missing from the Trishuli 3A hydropower project along the Trishuli River, with about 115 believed to be trapped in the main tunnel, according to the Independent Power Producers Association of Nepal. Officials present at the rescue site said rescuers believe some people may still be alive inside the tunnel.

At least 1,259 people were killed and more than 5,000 remain missing, according to the country’s disaster management agency. China, as of late Wednesday, said 21 people were killed and 541 were missing on the Tibet side of the border.
About 900 workers are missing from 12 hydropower projects in Nepal, with roughly 500 believed to be trapped in tunnels, according to local authorities. /dp

articles.title: Nepal-Tibet floods: two workers pulled alive from tunnel nine days after disaster
articles.summary:
Officials say pair were rescued from Trishuli 3A hydropower tunnel in Nepal after being trapped in depth of 170 metres

Two people have been pulled out alive from a hydropower tunnel in Nepal…
articles.byline: Hannah Ellis-Petersen and Gaurav Pokharel in Kathmandu

blocks.text: Two people have been pulled out alive from a hydropower tunnel in Nepal nine days after deadly flash floods buried the projects in deep mud and left them trapped.

The workers were rescued during an ongoing operation at the Trishuli 3A tunnel, a hydropower project in one of the areas worst-affected by last week’s deadly Nepal floods, according to army spokesperson Brig Gen Raja Ram Basnet.

Sanjay Shah was the first to be rescued and was taken to the Nepal army barracks in Trishuli. Another person, identified as Kabir Maharjan, was also rescued from the tunnel. They were rescued from a depth of 170 metres inside the tunnel, confirmed Basnet.
Sanjay Shah was foreman at Upper Trishuli 3A and Kabir Maharjan was a superviser.
Nepal’s army released images of Shah being pulled from the small dark entrance of a tunnel. He emerged covered in mud but conscious and was carried from the site on a rescuer’s shoulder.
Speaking to army officials after he was rescued, Shah’s first question was: “What day is it?”
Describing his ordeal, Shah said he had been in the tunnel’s control room at the time of the flood.

“Usually there would be only five or six people there but at this time there must have been around 40 to 45 people inside,” he said. “Since I was in the control room, my responsibility was to save everyone’s lives. After such an accident, I couldn’t just run away by myself. I had to save everyone.
“While trying to get everyone out, I told them that there had been a major accident at the dam and urged everyone to run. In doing so, I lost time. In the end, I couldn’t get out myself.”
To keep himself calm in the darkness of the tunnel, Shah said he spent his time chanting mantras. He said that while trapped, he had been communicating with only three or four others.
“They were communicating by shouting to each other from nearby. There could also be people inside the powerhouse. Some of them may not have been able to escape,” he said.
Officials said the two men were in stable condition and flown to a hospital in Kathmandu.
Nepal’s communication minister, Bikram Timilsina, said officials remain hopeful that more workers will be rescued. “We are waiting for the rescue of more and more people,”he wrote on social media.

Most of the hydropower projects along the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers were destroyed when a surge of water, debris and mud came coursing down the valley last week, triggered by ‌the collapse of a melting glacier on the border between Nepal and China-controlled Tibet.

blocks.caption: A survivor is carried out after being rescued from inside the tunnel. Photograph: Nepal Army/Reuters

blocks.text: At least 1,287 people were killed in the floods and more than 5,000 remain missing, according to the Nepal’s disaster management agency.

Rescue efforts have increasingly centred on the hydropower tunnels, where authorities believe workers may ⁠have survived for more than a week due to air pockets. So far, more than 270 people have been rescued across several projects.

Large boulders and flood waters had deluged the hydropower tunnels, blocking off the entrances, and some were buried deep in mud. At the Upper Trishuli 3A facility, it took rescue workers almost six days to find the tunnels.

Army and specialist teams have been working round the clock to try and clear debris from the tunnel entrance. It was confirmed that voices of many people had been heard inside after a breakthrough was made on early Friday morning.
After the rescue team called out, “Don’t panic, we are rescuing you,” they received a response from inside: “OK.”

At least 557 workers are missing from the hydropower project along the Trishuli River, with about 115 believed to be trapped in the main tunnel, according to the Independent Power Producers Association of Nepal.

Families of those missing in the tunnels have been gathering at hospitals in Kathmandu and at the Nepal electricity office for nine days, desperate for answers about their relatives. Posters of workers missing in Trishuli 3A and other projects line the wall of Tribhuvan University teaching hospital in Nepal’s capital.
In total, local authorities estimate about 900 workers are missing from 12 hydropower projects high up in the Himalayas, with about 500 believed to be trapped in tunnels.
Rescue efforts have also been focused on Rasuwagadhi hydropower plant where Nepal authorities said they are confident that 46 workers trapped in an underground chamber in the plant are still alive.

articles.title: Nothing left: Nepal flood survivors face loss and uncertainty
articles.summary: Rasuwa, Nepal – In Nepal’s flood-ravaged Rasuwa district, Yangee Tamang grapples with grief and uncertainty, days after deadly torrents swept away entire villages, leaving a landscape of mud,…

blocks.text: Rasuwa, Nepal – In Nepal’s flood-ravaged Rasuwa district, Yangee Tamang grapples with grief and uncertainty, days after deadly torrents swept away entire villages, leaving a landscape of mud, rock and debris.
From a helicopter flying up the valley of destruction, the ground below resembles a puzzle with missing pieces. Entire sections of settlements have vanished.
Picturesque villages of green paddy fields and houses sit beside vast chunks of land washed away.
Tamang’s house sits on a hillside in Syabrubesi in Rasuwa district, but the flood swept away the settlement below, where her relatives lived and markets were.
“It is all gone, nothing is left. No one is left,” Tamang told AFP, after tracing the route of the August 26 destruction by air on Thursday, with roads below washed out.
Rescue teams in Nepal have recovered more than 1,250 bodies, and more than 5,000 are missing, after the gigantic wave triggered by a rock and ice avalanche roared down the China-Nepal border.
What were once busy villages, markets, green hillsides and winding roads in Rasuwa have been transformed into vast stretches of mud, broken rock and debris.
“It wasn’t really water, it was gas-like, all black and it moved like boiling water,” she said.
“It was all so sudden, it was not possible for anyone to run away.”
About 100 people are feared trapped in hydropower tunnels.
Tamang’s husband is safe, but his workplace, the nearby Chilime Hydropower Project, which was smashed by the flood.
“I don’t know what we will do. Nothing is left here for us to live,” she said.
The river, still flowing brown, traces a path of destruction, and the enormous amount of debris has changed the shape and course of the waterways.
The floodwaters, carrying huge quantities of mud and rocks, rushed through river valleys with tremendous force.
In narrow gorges between the lush green hills, soil lies exposed where the flood stripped away trees and grass.
Roads that once connected remote communities have been washed away, while bridges lie destroyed or have completely disappeared.
Vehicles remain stranded on washed-out roads along hillsides.
Along the route, many surviving buildings are buried beneath thick layers of mud.
Some remain standing but are left empty, the people gone.
Risang Tamang, another resident, said for those left, the future is bleak.
“It is difficult — roads are is such a state, so many bridges have been swept away. Now, even if you have money, there is nowhere to buy anything,” he told AFP.
“Any hope that we can live here has died.” /dp

articles.title: Nepal says it will need billions in funding to rebuild after flash floods
articles.summary: BBC South Asia correspondent Azadeh Moshiri is in Nepal where authorities are trying to begin rebuilding amid the debris.

blocks.text: Nepal is one of the most vulnerable countries to the climate crisis, even though it is one of the lowest emitters of global greenhouse emissions.
In the deadly flash floods on the Nepal-Tibet border – which scientists are still studying the exact cause of – at least 1,200 people have died and thousands more are missing.
BBC South Asia correspondent Azadeh Moshiri is in Nepal where authorities are trying to begin rebuilding amid the debris and rubble covering villages and roads.

articles.title: Pacific leaders issue joint rebuke over China missile test
articles.summary: KOROR, Palau – Pacific Island nations condemned a Chinese missile test into their midst in a joint statement agreed Thursday, despite pressure from Beijing on Palau, the host of a regional…

blocks.text: KOROR, Palau – Pacific Island nations condemned a Chinese missile test into their midst in a joint statement agreed Thursday, despite pressure from Beijing on Palau, the host of a regional leaders’ meeting.

The Pacific Islands Forum summit communique, read by Palau’s President Surangel Whipps to a late-night news conference, calls for at least 24 hours’ notice of any intercontinental ballistic missile testing.
The statement was agreed by 17 of 18 forum members, with Naoero, formerly known as Nauru, dissenting.

China gave only a handful of nations short notice before test-firing the intercontinental ballistic missile in July, flexing its military might in a region where it has long sought to expand its influence.

The missile landed in international waters near Taiwan ally Tuvalu and Naoero, sparking immediate outrage from Pacific countries who hold bitter memories of nuclear testing by the US, Britain and France decades earlier, and have declared their waters a nuclear free zone.
The summit’s communique says leaders “register concern on the recent intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM) test which overflew a number of members without adequate notice”.

It called on “all states undertaking ICBM testing to ensure transparency and reassurance including through the provision of advanced notification of a test, at least 24 hours, in accordance with international practice”.
Beijing said the test launch was “a routine arrangement of China’s annual military training”, and that “relevant countries were informed in advance”.
Naoero switched diplomatic ties from Taiwan to Beijing two years ago, and has been reluctant to criticise China, a significant infrastructure lender to the region.
On Thursday, the Chinese foreign ministry accused Palau of “hijacking” responses from other Pacific nations.

“Palau has repeatedly hyped the issue, maliciously hijacking the positions of other Pacific Islands Forum member countries. This scheme will not succeed,” ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun told a news conference in Beijing, before the Pacific statement.
“I think the message from the forum is clear, transparency needs to happen,” Whipps responded.

The United States conducts ballistic missile tests in the Pacific under a defence agreement with the Marshall Islands, which Palau and Australia’s leaders said Thursday was “very different” to China’s test because adequate notice is given.

Palau invited its diplomatic ally Taiwan to the forum as an aid partner, among a dozen non-Pacific countries including China and the United States that participate in sideline events in different capacities.
Beijing bristled at the presence of Taiwan Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung at the opening ceremony.
Beijing claims self-ruled Taiwan as part of its territory, and China’s Pacific envoy Qian Bo told reporters on Monday there would be “consequences”.
Taiwan hit back saying its role in the Pacific, where it has three diplomatic allies, stops China from “having full control”.
The friction at times overshadowed Pacific nations’ focus on the region’s most pressing issues, tackling climate change and transnational crime.

Australia, the largest forum member and the Pacific’s biggest aid donor, pledged AU$600 million ($432 million) to boost satellite and drone aerial surveillance to help track and intercept “narco subs” bringing increasing volumes of methamphetamine and cocaine through island waters.

Papua New Guinea Prime Minister James Marape said he had raised concerns about new US visa bond charges for Pacific citizens travelling to the United States in a sideline meeting with US Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau.
Landau pledged $60 million to improve fuel security in the Pacific, to alleviate soaring prices caused by the Middle East crisis.
At the forum’s closing ceremony, secretary-general Baron Waqa said the Pacific faced significant challenges and had shown it would act together.
“The bonds between us must remain stronger than the forces that seek to divide us,” he said./dp

articles.title: UN to vote on adopting new world map that shows Africa’s true scale
articles.summary:
Togo-sponsored resolution calls to phase out traditional map that depicts continent as similar size to Greenland

The UN general assembly will vote on Friday on a resolution for the world to…

blocks.text: The UN general assembly will vote on Friday on a resolution for the world to formally phase out the traditional Mercator map of the globe in favour of one that more accurately displays Africa’s size.

Robert Dussey, Togo’s foreign affairs minister, said the resolution was sponsored by Togo and backed by countries including the African Union’s 54 other member states. He did not specify the total number.

blocks.caption: The 1569 map by Gerardus Mercator (1512-1594) has remained the global standard. Photograph: Stock Montage/Getty Images

blocks.text: “This discussion is not a political discussion [but] a scientific discussion, because there is scientific proof so we all have to accept the reality,” he said.

UN resolutions are non-enforceable but if the vote passes, it could lead to an update of classroom curriculums and everyday technology, given the wide usage of the Mercator projection in education, technology and governance.
The layout was introduced by the Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator in 1569 to help sailors navigate the seas. Almost five centuries later it remains the global standard.

Because of its projection style, however, regions near the equator appear significantly smaller than they are, whereas high-latitude areas look much larger. For example, the map shows Africa as being similar in size to Greenland, but the continent is 14 times larger than the Danish territory.

“You could fit the United States, China, India, Japan, Mexico and much of Europe into Africa and still have land to spare,” says a petition on Change.org for the #CorrectTheMap campaign, which has more than 11,000 signatures. The African Union endorsed the campaign in August 2025 and then asked Togo to spearhead its adoption.
Historians and geographers have said for years that the Mercator projection is rooted in western stereotypes. Activists have echoed this, with some coining the term “cartographic colonialism”.

Some argue that the map has subtly shaped international power dynamics by minimising the physical presence of the global south and visually inflating northern hemisphere nations while shrinking equatorial regions. This, they say, has reinforced systemic biases in international trade, development priorities and educational frameworks.

One of the Mercator projection’s most prominent critics was Arno Peters, a German historian, who launched the Peters world map based on the Gall–Peters projection in 1973. It has often been used as an alternative to the Mercator map.

blocks.caption: The 2018 Equal Earth Map. Photograph: equal-earth.com

blocks.text: Togo’s #CorrectTheMap campaign is promoting the use of the more accurate 2018 Equal Earth design, which was developed by an international team of cartographers. Supporters say it will help to reverse perceptions of Africa and decolonise global curriculums.

Some analysts agree too. JJ Enoch, a London-based senior associate at JS Held, a geopolitical risk advisory firm, said the Mercator projection visually diminished Africa’s true scale. He linked the campaign to a quest by African nations for “greater influence in global institutions and greater control over how the continent is represented”.

He added: “Adopting an equal-area map … would provide a more accurate basis for education and public understanding, while signalling that Africa’s demographic, economic and geopolitical importance should no longer be viewed through inherited and distorted conventions.”

blocks.caption: A map of Africa from Mercator's atlas dating between 1595-1602. Photograph: Royal Geographical Society/Getty Images

blocks.text: Togolese authorities hope the vote will go the same way as another African Union-backed decision at the UN this year. In March a Ghana-sponsored resolution to describe the slave trade as “gravest crime against humanity” passed, with 123 states voting in favour. Three states voted no and 52 abstained.

Ghana’s success has given supporters of the map cause to believe in a favourable outcome. Togo’s government is planning an event in Lomé, the Togolese capital, with Unesco, the African Union and tech brands such as Google Maps during the first quarter of next year to map out the implementation of the resolution.
Dussey said: “To those who say why now, I say, why not? When we look at the world map … it is time for us to change the narrative.”
He added: “It’s time for us in Africa to take responsibility to change what we can change ourselves.”

articles.title: Watch: Inside court as Lindsay Clancy's lawyer asks judge to remove juror
articles.summary: The jury now faces a seventh day of deliberations in the triple-murder trial.

articles.title: DMW: 2 Filipinos dead in Strait of Hormuz attack
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Migrant Workers (DMW) has reported the death of two Filipino seafarers on board the Saudi-flagged crude oil tanker SIDR which was hit by unidentified…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Migrant Workers (DMW) has reported the death of two Filipino seafarers on board the Saudi-flagged crude oil tanker SIDR which was hit by unidentified projectiles as it was about to cross the Strait of Hormuz.

Migrant Workers Secretary Hans Cacdac said in a press briefing on Wednesday that the victims were among 16 Filipino seafarers on the vessel when it was attacked on Aug. 31. The rest were unharmed with the vessel now off the coast of Oman.
“Unfortunately, we have two crew members who died as a result of the attack,” Cacdac told reporters, adding that a fire broke out on the tanker but it was contained by the crew.
“We are already working on the immediate repatriation of all the crew members, including the two fatalities,” he said.
According to the DMW chief, he would personally visit the families of the victims although he did not disclose where they reside, citing privacy concerns.

The DMW and the Overseas Workers Welfare Administration will also provide assistance to the families while government agencies coordinate with authorities in Oman on the repatriation of the Filipino seafarers, Cacdac said.
President Marcos has likewise ordered that assistance be given to the victims’ families, Palace Press Officer Claire Castro said on Thursday.

“First and foremost, the President and the administration extend their condolences to the families of the two seafarers from Cabuyao, Laguna, and Daanbantayan, Cebu. The President has also ordered immediate assistance for the families of our two fellow citizens who perished, as well as the provision of all necessary support—including the benefits, compensation and insurance proceeds—rightfully due to them,” Castro said in a briefing at the Malancañang.
“The government will not neglect the families left behind by our two fellow citizens. Once again, we extend our condolences to the families of our two seafarers,” she added.

The DMW, meanwhile, remains on red alert amid continuing security risks in the Strait of Hormuz, Cacdac said. According to him, they were coordinating with the Department of National Defense and the Department of Foreign Affairs on the security situation involving Filipino seafarers in the region.
About 3,000 Filipino seafarers remain aboard vessels in the wider Persian Gulf, although they are not necessarily all within the Strait of Hormuz, Cacdac said.
High-risk area

Since Feb. 28, when the United States and Israel launched an attack on Iran, triggering the Middle East conflict, about 31 ships carrying 421 Filipino seafarers have been attacked while entering or leaving the strait.
Cacdac said that 268 of those seafarers have since returned to the Philippines. Of the 421, 406 were unharmed, 10 were injured but had recovered, three had died and one remains officially missing.

The DMW, however, is not imposing a blanket deployment ban on Filipino seafarers passing through the Strait of Hormuz unlike its policy covering the Northern Black Sea, because of the strategic importance of the waterway and the principle of freedom of navigation, he added.

Instead, shipowners must conduct risk assessments before voyages and ensure that adequate security measures are in place, including security protocols, possible escorts, armed guards and reporting mechanisms, he said.
“We are disallowing deployment to the extent that there is a refusal of sailing by the seafarer,” Cacdac stressed.
He said that the right of Filipino seafarers to refuse sailing in high-risk areas must be respected.
The DMW will investigate the incident, including whether the appropriate safety and risk-assessment measures were followed.

Cacdac said the SIDR appeared to have been heading toward the Strait of Hormuz after coming from the eastern coast of the United Arab Emirates and sailing northward off Oman, but the vessel’s exact route remains subject to further determination.
For now, it is still too early to provide details on how the two Filipino seafarers died, he noted.
“It is not yet clear how exactly that happened. Usually, when we are still 24 to 48 hours removed from the event, we will find out the details as we go along,” Cacdac said.

He added that the DMW remains in contact with Bahri, the Saudi shipping company in charge of the vessel, and would meet with its top management to discuss the incident and the safety of Filipino crew members. /das

articles.title: Iran war is not a war, US VP Vance says
articles.summary: WASHINGTON, United States — U.S. Vice President JD Vance said Thursday he would not categorize the Iran war as a war, despite continuing clashes with Tehran six months after the start of the…

blocks.text: WASHINGTON, United States — U.S. Vice President JD Vance said Thursday he would not categorize the Iran war as a war, despite continuing clashes with Tehran six months after the start of the conflict.
Vance’s comments came amid growing signs that President Donald Trump is trying to draw a line under the conflict that has bogged down his administration.
“I wouldn’t call it a war. Right now, there is no active shooting,” Vance told a White House briefing when asked if the war would be over by the U.S. midterm elections in November.
Vance added that “I recognize there have been places where this has flared up,” but said major combat operations only lasted for six weeks after the U.S.-Israel war started on Feb. 28.

“But when you ask when will this end, you’re asking me a question like when will the Iranians stop shooting at ships? I think the reality is I don’t know the answer to that question. You would have to ask the Iranians,” he said.
After several weeks of calm, fresh clashes began with U.S. raids on Sunday, deepening the impasse in the six-month war, as Iran maintains a stranglehold on the strategic Strait of Hormuz.
Vance insisted that the United States would not reopen talks with Iran until it ended attacks on commercial shipping.

But with fuel prices threatening to cost Trump’s Republicans their control of Congress at the ballot box, his administration has begun pushing the message that oil flows through the waterway are now returning to pre-war levels.
Wedding strike probe
“Their control over the Strait of Hormuz is effectively gone,” Vance said of Iran.

“If you go back three months ago, how much oil and gas was coming out of the strait under Iranian threats? It was virtually nothing. Now, it’s almost back to where it was before the conflict even started,” Vance said.
Trump’s approval ratings are near record lows as the president who vowed to keep the United States out of any more foreign wars finds himself in a quagmire with the Islamic Republic.
Eighteen U.S. troops and thousands of people in Iran and Lebanon have died in the conflict since February.
The Wall Street Journal reported that Trump was now discussing with senior aides whether to declare the Iran war over. He posted a photo of a banner saying “Mission Accomplished” last week.
Iran pressed on with fresh attacks on Thursday, saying it hit U.S. military bases in Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates to avenge a strike on a wedding that it blamed on Washington.
Vance said the United States was probing the wedding strike but cast doubt on Iranian reporting of the incident.

“I know that we’re investigating,” Vance said. “I will say that the Iranian state media has not been a very good source of information about what’s happened in the conflict thus far. So I’m extremely skeptical of this.”
The Iranian Red Crescent said the missile attack on the wedding in the Iranian coastal town of Kuhestak killed four people late Tuesday, including a child, and wounded more than 50. /das

articles.title: ‘Friend-for-hire’ services gain traction in Thailand
articles.summary: “Friend-for-hire” services have started taking off in Thailand as the country’s social landscape changes with an aging population and a rise in the number of unmarried people. The service is a new…

blocks.text: “Friend-for-hire” services have started taking off in Thailand as the country’s social landscape changes with an aging population and a rise in the number of unmarried people.
The service is a new type of gig work in which people are paid to act as companions, for instance accompanying someone on a trip to take photos or even joining them in indoor rock climbing.

Although no official figures are available, industry players say demand for professional companions has increased in recent years due to the rise in people living alone, changing lifestyles and the influence of social media.
According to global market research company Euromonitor International, 29.5 percent of Thai households were single-person households in 2025, exceeding the global average of 21.9 percent.
And that growing segment has created rising demand for products and services designed for independent living, such as single-seat restaurant tables and solo travel.
For many clients, however, the motivation for hiring a companion is convenience rather than loneliness.

Ainthuon Rattanawaraporn, a university student and content creator from Bangkok, said she initially used the service out of curiosity but soon found it solved a problem—friends were sometimes too busy to come with her on trips but she was not yet comfortable traveling alone.
“I also wanted someone to take pictures for me,” she said.
Unlike asking friends for favors, hiring a companion allowed her to freely request specific photo angles and compositions because photography was part of the service.
“I don’t want to bother my friends by asking them to take hundreds of photos during a trip,” she said. “With a hired companion, I can tell them exactly what kind of pictures I want.”
Growing demand
The growing demand has created new income opportunities for people like Thanaporn Charoenchuea, a 20-year-old university student who started her “Snap Like a Bestie” service.
Within about two months, she had served more than 50 clients. She said her customers are not simply looking for someone to take photographs.
“They want someone who can make them feel comfortable while capturing natural-looking photos,” she said.
Apart from taking photos, Thanaporn spends much of her time chatting with clients, helping shy or introverted people relax before posing for pictures.

“The biggest challenge is making sure every client enjoys both the experience and the final photos,” she said. “I love photography and meeting new people, so I find the job both enjoyable and rewarding.”
On busy days, she accepts up to three appointments, each lasting between one and three hours. She only accepts bookings in public places after screening clients through their social media accounts.
For another companion service provider, Penkawin Wangniwetkul, known as Ice, the business has evolved well beyond photography.

After leaving her full-time job as a television coproducer, Ice spent several years working as a presenter, master of ceremonies, and online marketing host before entering the companionship business about three months ago.
The opportunity came unexpectedly after relatives suggested she accompany two elderly women on shopping trips and outings.
“I realized there was genuine demand for someone who could simply accompany people,” she said, adding that she later began posting about the experience on social media, leading to more referrals.

Today, clients hire her for activities, including running, gym workouts, aerobics, shopping, spa visits, cafe hopping, and even indoor rock climbing. A typical booking lasts two to three hours, and she charges 1,000 baht ($30) per hour.
Ice has served more than 10 clients and intentionally limits bookings because she continues to work as an MC and presenter. She also screens every client before accepting an assignment.

Her clients have included public figures, including an actress she accompanied to a veterinary clinic. She has also received requests to attend wedding receptions as a companion, although she was too busy to accept.

Despite growing demand, Ice is selective. She turns down requests that could compromise her safety or make her feel uncomfortable, including accompanying male clients to late-night entertainment venues.
Outside city trips
The service has also expanded to trips outside the city. Company employee Sasiprapa Nookong is among those who hired a companion during a trip to Chiang Mai.

Sasiprapa said that while traveling with a friend, they decided to spend one day pursuing different interests. Her friend planned to go hiking, while she preferred visiting cafes around the city, so she contacted a university student offering the service after seeing reviews on TikTok.

“I believe this service meets the needs of people who occasionally want company, not long-term companionship,” she said, echoing others in stressing that safety should always come first when hiring strangers.
