Sociologist Narupon Duangwises of the Princess Maha Chakri Sirindhorn Anthropology Centre wrote in a report that interacting with hired companions may provide emotional comfort for people who find it difficult to make friends in everyday life.

But he noted that one feature distinguishing “friends for hire” from traditional friendship is the ability to choose a companion based on physical appearance, unlike friendships that develop naturally.
He therefore suggested that service providers establish clear rules and boundaries to protect themselves and prevent situations, such as sexual harassment or other forms of violence. /das

articles.title: El Niño could be strongest in decades, UN warns
articles.summary: GENEVA, Switzerland — El Niño is forecast to be the strongest since comparable records began four decades ago, the United Nations’ climate agency warned Thursday, with the UN chief saying the world…

blocks.text: GENEVA, Switzerland — El Niño is forecast to be the strongest since comparable records began four decades ago, the United Nations’ climate agency warned Thursday, with the UN chief saying the world was in the “danger zone of extreme weather.”
The weather phenomenon is set to become “very strong” in the months ahead and is almost certain to persist through February, the World Meteorological Organization said.
“If this trajectory continues, it may be stronger than anything since our monitoring began,” WMO chief Celeste Saulo told reporters in Geneva.
El Niño will peak toward the end of this year — though its knock-on effects on the climate will continue well into 2027, said the WMO.
El Niño warms surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, bringing worldwide changes in winds, pressure and rainfall.
Heat in the oceans is released more slowly into the atmosphere, pushing up global temperatures the year after it develops.
The powerful 2023-24 El Niño contributed to 2024 being the warmest year on record, and “we should not be surprised if this record is broken,” Saulo added.

“El Niño is firmly established and will intensify into a very strong event in the coming months, with big impacts on rainfall and temperature patterns and associated risks of floods, drought and extreme heat,” the WMO said.
Highway to the danger zone
El Niño is a naturally occurring phenomenon and is not caused by climate change.
But scientists expect it will exacerbate the heat of a planet already warming from burning fossil fuels, while amplifying weather extremes.
“El Niño is being supersized before our eyes,” said UN chief Antonio Guterres.

“The science leaves no room for doubt: The planet is in uncharted waters, and those waters are heating up. Sea surface temperatures are rising, temperatures keep climbing, and the world is in the danger zone of extreme weather.”
WMO chief Saulo urged disaster management authorities and climate-sensitive sectors like agriculture, fisheries, health, energy and water to prepare themselves.
“This exceptional El Niño … has the potential to deliver a massive blow to communities and economies across the world,” she said.
“We are already seeing disruption and devastation from droughts and floods, and we expect these impacts to increase as El Niño intensifies.”
El Niño typically takes place every two to seven years and lasts around nine to 12 months.
Conditions oscillate between El Niño and its opposite, La Niña, with neutral conditions in between.
El Niño can reshape weather and climate patterns thousands of kilometers away from the tropical Pacific.
Pacific Ocean heating up

Wilfran Moufouma-Okia, the WMO’s climate prediction chief, said some places would be affected before, some during and some after the peak later this year — though the strength of the peak is not an indicator of the severity of the impact.
For September-November, WMO forecasts indicate an increased likelihood of above-normal temperatures “across almost all land areas.”
The index, which measures sea surface temperature anomalies in the central eastern equatorial Pacific, has strengthened from an average 1.5°C above normal between May and July.
Weekly values between late July and mid-August ranged from around 2.2°C to 2.6°C above average, indicating continued El Niño intensification.
The UN agency classifies El Niño events as weak, moderate, strong or very strong — meaning this one is set to reach the highest level out of four.
Moufouma-Okia said the classification meant a sea surface temperature anomaly of more than 2°C.
“That category is open: We know where it starts; we don’t know where it ends,” he told AFP.
The average forecast is pointing toward an anomaly peaking at 3.6°C — way higher than the last two very strong El Niños in 1997-98 and 2015-16.
In some areas, subsurface ocean temperatures were more than 8°C above average during July and early August.
Saulo called this a huge reservoir of “very warm ocean waters that will fuel the intensity of El Niño.”
The UN’s International Organization for Migration agency appealed Thursday for $110 million to protect 4.9 million people from the potentially severe impacts of the phenomenon. /das

articles.title: Spacecraft bound for Mercury begins ‘tricky’ arrival
articles.summary: PARIS, France — After an eight-year journey, a spacecraft carrying European and Japanese probes began the months-long, high-risk approach to Mercury on Thursday to study the Sun-scorched planet. The…

blocks.text: PARIS, France — After an eight-year journey, a spacecraft carrying European and Japanese probes began the months-long, high-risk approach to Mercury on Thursday to study the Sun-scorched planet.
The BepiColombo mission set off from Earth in 2018 on a winding path to study the smallest and least understood planet in our solar system, with the aim of releasing the two probes into its orbit.
On Thursday, it began its arrival phase, described by the European Space Agency (ESA) as its “most operationally challenging planetary arrival sequence ever attempted.”

Mercury’s relatively tiny mass — it is only slightly bigger than the moon — means its gravitational pull is extremely weak compared with the Sun’s, making it complicated for spacecraft to approach the planet without ending up incinerated or lost in space.
“It’s a very ambitious mission,” Santa Martinez, the mission manager at ESA, told a press conference ahead of its arrival.
The spacecraft had to travel more than 10 billion kilometers (miles), executing a series of nine flybys, to speed up, slow down and perfect its trajectory.
The two probes, which are attached to each other, finally separated on Thursday from the transfer module that has propelled them — a crucial first step in the final approach.

It was the equivalent of “launching a new spacecraft. Only this spacecraft happens to be around a different planet,” explained Ignacio Tanco, ESA’s head of inner solar system mission operations, before the separation began.
All went to plan
On Thursday, Mercury was some 63 million km from the Sun and 200 million km from Earth.

“At these distances … any real-time operation becomes impossible,” Tanco said, explaining there was about a 30-minute delay between checks being performed and commands being executed from the ground to the spacecraft.
It meant the spacecraft had to check and execute the separation autonomously — a “tricky business,” Tanco said.
But all went to plan.
The spacecraft autonomously cut the four mechanical struts connecting the orbiters to the module.
Spring mechanisms then gently pushed them away.
The separation took place at a speed of 40 centimeters (16 inches) per second, leaving the two entities relatively close given the vastness of space.

Due to the distance between the probes and Earth, the signal confirming the operation’s success reached the control center in Darmstadt, Germany, nearly two hours later — at 1353 GMT — sparking rounds of applause and cheers.
“This is the best-case scenario, that the telemetry comes exactly at the moment we expect it,” said Elsa Montagnon, in charge of module operations at ESA.
“The spacecraft has completed its reconfiguration as expected,” she said with relief.
The probes are due to enter Mercury’s orbit on Nov. 21.
The next tricky phase will come on Dec. 9 and 10, when the two probes separate into their respective orbits.
From April, the ESA’s Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) will begin studying the planet closest to the Sun with unprecedented precision, passing just 480 km from its surface.
The Japanese Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (Mio) will focus on its space environment and magnetic field, following an elliptical orbit that will carry it as far as 11,000 km away.
New chapter
Mercury is the least studied of the four rocky, innermost planets in our solar system, which include Venus, Earth and Mars.
NASA’s Mariner 10 was the first probe to capture a close image of its lunar-looking surface in 1974.
The MESSENGER probe then orbited the planet in 2011.
But many mysteries remain about its magnetic field, iron core and surface marked by hollows.

With its 16 instruments and 1.7-billion-euro ($2.0-billion) budget, BepiColombo “is going to bring to humanity and to the scientific community unprecedented views of Mercury … and it’s going to open a new chapter in our understanding of the solar system,” Martinez said. /das

articles.title: Spain’s PM says no evidence ‘whatsoever’ Morocco behind Ceuta border breach
articles.summary: Pedro Sánchez continues to defend Rabat after police report claiming border forces helped 70,000 cross border

blocks.text: Spain has seen no evidence “whatsoever” that Morocco planned or facilitated a mass border breach into its north African territory of Ceuta, the Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has told parliament.

The address on Thursday followed the emergence of a police report, commissioned by a judge and widely quoted in the media, claiming Moroccan border forces had actively aided about 70,000 people to cross the border in late July.

“I ‌can assure you ‌that no institution – not the diplomatic service, nor the European Commission, ‌nor any international body – has provided the Spanish government with any solid evidence that Morocco planned or carried out the incident. None whatsoever,” Sánchez told parliament.

Speaking the morning after about 50,000 people marched in Madrid to protest his handling of the Ceuta crisis, the socialist prime minister also denied the government had received any warning of the mass breach, saying no reports to authorities had anticipated “the scale or probability of what eventually happened”.

blocks.caption: A protest against the Spanish government’s handling of the recent border breach at Ceuta. Photograph: Francesco Militello Mirto/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Sánchez has repeatedly defended Morocco during the crisis, highlighting Rabat’s cooperation in returning most of the migrants in the days after the surge.

But he said on Thursday that Spain had summoned Morocco’s ambassador on 21 August because of “unacceptable statements” made by two ministers over Ceuta and Melilla, another Spanish north African territory. Last month, Morocco’s justice minister, Abdellatif Ouahbi, publicly reiterated Rabat’s sovereignty claims over the cities.
Sánchez said he had “for now” ruled out Moroccan government involvement but conceded that Moroccan forces had allowed crossings to occur during a key 10-hour period on 30 July.
Many of those who crossed said in interviews they had been actively encouraged to do so. Moroccan officials have denied enabling the crossing.
Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the leader of the conservative People’s party, called on Sánchez to resign for his “incompetence and complicity”.

In response to Sánchez summoning the Moroccan ambassador to discuss the crisis, Santiago Abascal, the leader of the far-right Vox party, said: “Morocco doesn’t need an ambassador in Spain – you are its ambassador.”

blocks.caption: People who entered Ceuta from Morocco in late July on hunger strike last month to demand asylum.  Photograph: Laura Rincon/EPA

blocks.text: As many as 141 people are thought to have died trying to enter Ceuta at the end of July. The influx unleashed a political crisis, a humanitarian emergency and reignited tensions within the EU over immigration.

On Thursday, Sánchez appealed for European solidarity over the crisis. He did not single out any countries by name but, in a pointed passage apparently aimed at Italy and Denmark, the two countries that had led public criticism of Spain, said the principle of solidarity should apply to Ceuta as much as it applies to Greenland and Lampedusa.
Although 90% of the people had returned to Morocco within 24 hours, several thousand, including at least 500 minors, are thought to remain, either living on the street or in makeshift shelters.

Amid calls from Vox to return them to Morocco, Sánchez reminded parliament that under Spanish, European and international law, migrants had a right to be treated as individuals. “You can’t just grab someone by the arm and drag them across the frontier as though they were a sack of dirt,” he told MPs.

In reference to the hundreds of destitute minors, Aina Vidal of the leftwing group Sumar, said: “They’re children, not invaders, not soldiers. They didn’t come carrying bombs, they arrived wearing water wings, in tears.”

It seems likely the government will invest in facilities in Ceuta to accommodate the remaining migrants rather than risk the political backlash both in Spain and across Europe were they to bring them to the mainland.
There is also evidence that, faced with hunger as well as hostility from many local people, some migrants have already begun going back to Morocco.

However, as Sánchez told parliament, the per capita income of Ceuta is eight times that of Morocco and “even if we build a wall 100 metres high there will still be people prepared to throw themselves into the sea to get across”.
“We will not stop working until Ceuta emerges from this difficult situation: stronger, more prosperous, and more integrated with the rest of Spain and the EU,” he added.
Additional reporting by Jakub Krupa

articles.title: Yen soars as Bank of Japan tipped to raise interest rates
articles.summary: Jump lifts currency to highest level against dollar in a month, while global markets remain jittery

blocks.text: The Japanese yen has soared by more than 1.7% against the dollar amid speculation the Bank of Japan is set to raise interest rates.
The latest jump on Thursday lifted the yen to its highest level against the dollar in a month, at 155.85, and followed a 0.9% move the previous day.
Global markets remain jittery after this week’s dramatic government bond sell-off – caused by fears of a fresh inflation increase as a result of higher oil prices.
Investors have been reassessing their expectations for the future path of interest rates, in Japan and across other major economies.
Remarks by a Bank of Japan policymaker, Hajime Takata, suggesting it needs to move more “nimbly”, appeared to have heightened the prospects of a decisive move.

The chief executive of the financial adviser deVere, Nigel Green, said the scale of the yen appreciation over such a short time period underlined the febrile state of markets. “Markets this jumpy don’t need a shock to move hard, a rumour is enough,” he said.
Citi said in a note to clients: “(The) remarks are the strongest messaging we’ve heard from the board and reintroduces the idea of an expedited rate hike trajectory.”

The Bank of Japan has been incrementally raising rates for the past two years, after the economy finally shrugged off decades of deflation, or falling prices – but its main policy rate was left unchanged at 1% in July.
Markets now believe there is a 77% chance of a rate rise at the BoJ’s next meeting, which starts on 17 September.

Commenting on the latest market moves, Japan’s vice-finance minister for international affairs, Atsushi Mimura, said he was “neither satisfied nor reassured”, and policymakers “remain on a state of heightened alert”.
after newsletter promotion

The global bond market sell-off – pushing up the yield, or interest rate, on government borrowing – intensified earlier this week after the US Federal Reserve chair, Kevin Warsh, used a speech last Friday to indicate that he was determined to bring inflation back to target.

Warsh had previously baffled some investors by withdrawing the Fed’s approach of signalling future rate moves, known as “forward guidance” – but in Friday’s speech at the central bankers’ conference in Jackson Hole, he said that if inflation did not move towards the 2% target the Fed would have “more to do”.

The bond sell-off appeared to have eased on Thursday, with yields on 10-year UK government bonds, known as gilts, hovering at about 5.1% in morning trading – having touched the highest level since 2008, close to 5.3%, earlier this week.

articles.title: Dozens of trapped hydropower tunnel workers in Nepal could still be alive, official says
articles.summary: About 46 people believed to be trapped in ‘room-like’ structure inside hydro plant tunnel on Nepal-Tibet border
articles.byline: Hannah Ellis-Petersen and Gaurav Pokharel in Kathmandu

blocks.text: Nepal authorities have said they are “confident” that dozens of workers in Nepal’s Rasuwagadhi hydropower plant are still alive, more than a week after deadly flash floods left them trapped in an underground chamber.
Authorities said that at least 639 workers were still missing from hydropower plants built along Nepal’s Bhote Koshi and Triushuli rivers.

Most of the projects were destroyed when a surge of water, debris and mud came coursing down the river valley last week, triggered by ‌the collapse of a melting glacier on the border between Nepal and China-controlled Tibet.
The deadly flash floods reached up to 100mph (160km/h), according to scientists, and travelled more than 60 miles down the river valley, wiping away whole villages, bridges, and hydropower dams.
At least 1,252 people have been confirmed dead from the floods. More than 4,200 remain missing.

According to a preliminary estimate by the UN Development Programme, the disaster created at least 2.2m tonnes of debris, including parts of buildings, rocks and sediment. Large boulders and flood waters deluged the hydropower tunnels, blocking off the entrances, and some were buried deep in mud.

Rescue efforts have increasingly centred on these tunnels, where authorities believe workers may ⁠have survived for more than a week due to air pockets. So far, more than 270 people have been rescued from the hydropower projects.

blocks.caption: A turquoise-green house stands tall amid sludge near Trishuli River in the aftermath of flash floods.  Photograph: Arun Sankar/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Speaking on Wednesday, officials said they believed 46 people were still alive in an underground room in Rasuwagadhi hydropower plant, and efforts were ongoing to locate them using excavators and other heavy equipment.

“We are very confident that they must be alive after one week because … they have food and water over there in the building,” Amhsu Kiran Shahi, a board member of the Nepal ⁠electricity authority, told Reuters.

Durga Gurung, 60, said his brother Jhappad Bhujel was among those trapped in a hydropower tunnel. “Right now, we are just relying on God,” he told the Guardian. “We have not been given any information about whether the people inside are alive or not.

“Neither the army nor the people from the electricity authority are telling us anything. So many days have passed that we have reached a point where it feels like all we can do is hope for a miracle.”
“Our relatives are sitting inside a dark tunnel,” he added. “How long can they possibly survive?”

blocks.caption: The area around Rasuwagadhi hydropower plant before the flash flood.  Photograph: Maxar/DigitalGlobe/Getty Images

blocks.text: Major rescue operations were under way or planned at four hydropower projects. Two sites – the Rasuwagadhi hydroelectric project and the Upper Trishuli 3A facility – where about 90 people are missing, offered the strongest prospect of finding survivors because of the presence of air inside the tunnels, Shahi said.

The Rasuwagadhi hydroelectric project is located in Rasuwa district, about three miles away from the border with Tibet, which was one of the areas of Nepal hardest hit by the floods, and remains almost inaccessible except by helicopter. “This is the only project where it’s possible to walk through ‌the tunnel,” Shahi said. “The army tried doing that three days ago, but they didn’t find the room. We are going in again.”

At the Upper Trishuli 3A facility, another project hit by the floods, it took rescue workers almost six days to find the tunnels ⁠because of the thick mud. The authorities believe about 30 to 40 people may still be alive in the tunnel. “We are expecting [survivors] in there because we ​are told there is a ​dry space inside. We are ​trying to break into the tunnel now,” said the Nepali army spokesperson Raja Ram Basnet on Wednesday.

The army said the search and rescue operation would go on for as long as there was hope for survivors, but that efforts would also continue to recover the dead bodies. “We are using every technology ​available in Nepal ‌right now, and we ​are taking help ​from the Indians, Chinese, Koreans. We have experts from Australia too,” added Basnet.

Families of those still trapped in the projects have returned to the Nepal electricity office for the past eight days, in the hope for information. Laxmi Adhikari’s brother Jeevanlal Adhikari had gone to the Trishuli 3A Hydropower Project to test the machines, when the floods hit.

She accused the authorities of withholding information from the families, and of not acting fast enough to save their relatives. “We have been running from one ministry to another and from disaster management authority to another government office, trying to find my brother,” she said. “We keep going from place to place, but the rescue operation has not been accelerated.”

She said the lack of answers made the wait even more painful: “When the water came rushing in, where did he go? Did he manage to get to safety? They haven’t even given us definite information about whether our people are alive or not.”

Nepal has invested more than $9bn (£6.7bn) in building hydropower dams across the mountains, huge sums given the country’s small economy. According to preliminary surveys, the floods debilitated or destroyed 11 hydropower plants and knocked out about 10% of Nepal’s total electricity-generation capacity.
According to the authorities, more than 20,000 houses will have to be rebuilt in the aftermath of the flood. Nepal has put the cost of recovery at more than $5bn (£3.7bn).

articles.title: DOJ careful in evaluating US extradition bid for Apollo Quiboloy
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines—The Department of Justice (DOJ) said it continues to assess the request by the United States to extradite jailed evangelist and alleged sex offender Apollo Quiboloy, as it does…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines—The Department of Justice (DOJ) said it continues to assess the request by the United States to extradite jailed evangelist and alleged sex offender Apollo Quiboloy, as it does not want to take the matter to the court “half-baked.”

Justice Undersecretary Ian Dato said in a news briefing on Thursday that the main factor in determining whether the DOJ should proceed with filing a petition for extradition in a local court is whether the request is “thorough enough” to stand in court.

“The department is conscious of the fact that it should not be filing anything half baked,” Dato stressed. “It will not bound itself to a timeline, but it will make sure that whatever case or petition it will file in court will stand scrutiny by the judge.”

The DOJ received on Aug. 7 the vast amount of documents from the US to boost its request for extradition of Quiboloy, who is facing charges of sex trafficking, visa fraud and cash smuggling in the US.

Chief state counsel Dennis Chan had noted that once the DOJ completes its evaluation and finds that the extradition request was in compliance with the 1994 treaty between the Philippines and the US, a petition would be formally filed before a regional trial court.
However, this could still be challenged by Quiboloy, but only up to the level of the Court of Appeals, based on the Supreme Court’s new extradition rules.
The DOJ also earlier maintained that it is serious in its commitment to international law as well as to a fair judgment of the case. /mr

articles.title: Victims sue South African government over 1961 Sharpeville massacre that left 91 dead
articles.summary:
Claim relating to infamous apartheid-era shooting of protesters part of wave of litigation for apartheid-era crimes

The day dawned brightly on 21 March 1960, as residents of the South…

blocks.text: The day dawned brightly on 21 March 1960, as residents of the South African township of Sharpeville gathered to protest against pass laws, which forced “Black, Indian and Coloured” South Africans to carry documents at all times specifying where they were allowed to be.

Abraham Mofokeng joined the march, one of dozens organised nationwide by the Pan Africanist Congress (PAC), a breakaway group from the African National Congress. “The weather was very nice, the sun was out. You could not have suspected that the day would go so horribly,” said Mofokeng, who was then a 20-year-old factory worker.

blocks.caption: Abraham Mofokeng, who was shot in the foot and back while protesting against South Africa’s apartheid pass laws during the Sharpeville massacre on 21 March 1960.  Photograph: Rachel Savage/The Guardian

blocks.text: Mofokeng, now 86, was among the thousands gathered peacefully outside the police station in Sharpeville, which is about 40 miles south of Johannesburg in a heavily industrialised region known as the Vaal Triangle.
The crowd was singing, he said, when officers opened fire without warning. At least 91 people were killed and 238 injured, in what became known as the Sharpeville massacre.

As Mofokeng fled, a bullet grazed the inside of his right foot, ripping his shoe off. A woman fell to the ground before him; he jumped over her and kept running. Only later, when he noticed blood running down his legs, did he realise he had been shot in the back, where a bullet remains lodged in his spine.
Mofokeng is among three claimants suing the South Africa government, in a case filed on Thursday, for compensation for the massacre. If the case is successful, dozens more could file claims.

The case is part of a wave of litigation demanding justice for apartheid-era crimes, amid widespread disillusionment with ANC-led governments that have failed to rectify South Africa’s huge racial inequality and poverty since the end of apartheid over three decades ago.

blocks.caption: Dead and wounded South Africans lie outside the Sharpeville police station. Photograph: PN2

blocks.text: In January 2025, 25 survivors and relatives of victims of apartheid state violence sued South Africa’s government for failing to prosecute cases referred to it by the post-apartheid Truth and Reconciliation Commission. That May, the president, Cyril Ramaphosa, announced a judicial inquiry into potential political interference, which is still ongoing.
Spokespeople for South Africa’s justice department did not respond to a request for comment on the Sharpeville compensation case.

In the immediate aftermath of the Sharpeville massacre, police claimed that protesters had been throwing rocks at them. “I don’t know how many we shot,” said Colonel J Pienaar, the local police commander, according to a story published by the Guardian the following day. “It all started when hordes of natives surrounded the police station. My car was struck with a stone. If they do these things they must learn their lesson the hard way.”

In July 1961, in response to victims filing compensation claims, the white minority regime passed a law indemnifying the government and anyone acting under its authority for any actions taken “in good faith for the prevention or suppression of internal disorder, the maintenance or restoration of good order, public safety or essential services, or the preservation of life or property”.

blocks.caption: Members of a choir perform during the commemorations of the massacre, at the Phelindaba cemetery in Sharpeville, on 21 March 2026.  Photograph: Marco Longari/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The law, which was made effective retrospectively from the date of the massacre, is still in force today. The claimants’ legal team is arguing that the law is unconstitutional.

The claimants are hoping to get compensation of about 500,000 rand (£23,000), said Daniel Leader, a partner with UK law firm Leigh Day, which is advising the South African legal team, led by Lawyers For Human Rights, an NGO.
Mafokeng was awarded 30,000 rand as a one-off payment, after the TRC concluded in 2003. The TRC had recommended annual reparations payments of around 20,000 rand for six years.
“We continued to suffer,” said Mofokeng, who still lives in Sharpeville. “Especially now … I am struggling and my health is not up to standard.”

blocks.caption: Paulina Mathinye, whose father Samson was killed by police in the Sharpeville massacre Photograph: Rachel Savage/The Guardian

blocks.text: The other two test claimants were children when their fathers were killed in the massacre. Paulina Mathinye was five when her father Samson was shot. “Every time he came back from work, I would be so happy to see him that I would run to him, and then he would pick me up,” she said.
Mathinye didn’t initially understand what had happened that day in 1960. “I kept on asking my mum: ‘Mummy, why are you crying?’”

Mathinye’s mother struggled to raise her five children on a domestic worker’s wages and Mathinye, who had wanted to train as a teacher but couldn’t afford the bursary, had to leave education at 17 to find work.

Mathinye, who is now 71, said she hoped for compensation that would make up for some of what she lost when her father died. “Some of my friends are teachers, some of them are nurses, and I’m staying in the same house that my father did,” she said.

Sharpeville’s problems didn’t begin with the massacre in 1960, but with the dispossession of Black South Africans from productive land, their forced removals to townships and their exclusion from the economy, said Vincent Thamae, a PAC member who supports the massacre victims and their families.

“When people talk about compensation now,” he said, “compensation is a concept to them that includes all the land that they lost, the economy that they were taken out of and even how they have been treated in the new democracy.”

articles.title: Nepal PM warns of risks as scientists flag more glacial disasters
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — Prime Minister Balendra Shah has urged the international community to recognise the August 26 Bhotekoshi flood as a warning of the growing climate risks confronting the Himalayan…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — Prime Minister Balendra Shah has urged the international community to recognise the August 26 Bhotekoshi flood as a warning of the growing climate risks confronting the Himalayan region.

Briefing the House of Representatives on the losses caused by the disaster and the government’s response on Wednesday, he said the moment has come to bring these growing risks more urgently to the attention of the international community.

“Experts have said that the flood in the Bhotekoshi River in Rasuwa was triggered by a massive rockslide in the Himalayan region,” Shah said. “The incident is a serious indication that the risks we face in the Himalayan region are increasing.”
The prime minister said Nepal must tell the international community more forcefully that climate change is driving the disasters and risks it faces.
“Climate change is a global problem,” Shah said. “Mitigating and managing its impacts is a shared responsibility of the international community.”

His remarks come amid a massive search-and-rescue operation in the aftermath of the disaster, with scientists and climate experts on both sides of the Nepal-China border still working to determine the disaster’s trigger and whether such events could become more frequent.

According to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, the flood’s death toll rose to 1,204 as of Wednesday evening, while 4,216 remained out of contact. Around 1.6 million people in Rasuwa and Nuwakot were directly affected by the disaster.
The floods completely swept away 41 concrete bridges and damaged four others. In Nuwakot alone, 1,267 houses were completely damaged and another 1,253 partially damaged.

But beyond the immediate devastation, the disaster has raised a larger question about the increasing instability of the Himalayan cryosphere and the possibility of similar events occurring more frequently as temperatures rise.
According to the National Climate Centre (NCC) of China, glacier-related disasters could indeed become more frequent as global warming weakens glacier stability on the Qinghai-Xizang Plateau.
Gao Rong, deputy director of the Centre, said at a press conference on Wednesday that global warming was accelerating the melting of mountain glaciers worldwide.

“Mountain glaciers in China are concentrated mainly on the Qinghai-Xizang Plateau and surrounding areas. Against a backdrop of a warmer and wetter climate, glaciers across the region are generally undergoing accelerated melting,” Gao said.

He added that the internal structural stability of glaciers on the plateau is expected to decline further. “Glacier-related disasters could become more frequent and trigger cascading effects that amplify the scale of destruction and expand their impact,” he warned.
The warning comes as the global scientific community is increasingly linking the rise in extreme weather events to a warming planet.

The United Nations Environment Program said on Wednesday that global temperatures are set to cross the 1.5°C threshold, likely within the next few years, pushing climate risks and impacts to increasingly dangerous levels.

Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal has also blamed climate change for the increasing risks faced by Nepal and said the international community must recognize its responsibility towards countries such as Nepal that contribute little to global emissions but face disproportionate consequences.
The government has already approached the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage for immediate support and compensation for the devastation caused by the August 26 floods.

Manjit Dhakal, an adviser to the Least Developed Countries Group in UN climate negotiations, said the Loss and Damage Fund was established precisely to respond to catastrophic events affecting vulnerable countries.

“As someone involved in the Transitional Committee that helped establish the Fund, I clearly remember our discussions about making it more responsive to the realities and urgency of loss and damage,” Dhakal said.

“The FRLD now has an opportunity to demonstrate what it was created to deliver: timely, accessible and grant-based support when vulnerable countries face catastrophic loss and damage. We sincerely hope no country has to face such a tragedy. But today, Nepal needs solidarity translated into action,” he added. /dl

articles.title: India rejects Hague ruling on Indus waters: What’s next?
articles.summary: The Indus Waters Treaty is facing a fresh dispute after India rejected a Hague-based Court of Arbitration ruling that the 1960 agreement remains in force. Pakistan has welcomed the decision and said…

blocks.text: The Indus Waters Treaty is facing a fresh dispute after India rejected a Hague-based Court of Arbitration ruling that the 1960 agreement remains in force.
Pakistan has welcomed the decision and said India remains bound by the treaty.
India’s Ministry of External Affairs described the tribunal as a “so-called Court of Arbitration” that was “illegally constituted.”

It said the body had been established by the World Bank in breach of the treaty and that India “categorically rejects its so-called award, just as it has firmly rejected all prior pronouncements by this illegally constituted body.”
“The Court of Arbitration has no jurisdiction whatsoever to pronounce on India’s sovereign decisions,” the ministry said.
What to know about the treaty
The Indus Waters Treaty, brokered by the World Bank, governs the use of water from six rivers flowing through India and Pakistan.

The agreement largely gives India rights over three eastern rivers while Pakistan has rights over the western Indus, Jhelum and Chenab. India is allowed to use the western rivers for specified purposes including certain hydroelectric projects.
The treaty had endured wars and prolonged periods of intense hostility between the two nuclear-armed neighbors.

But India placed the treaty in abeyance in April 2025 as part of a package of diplomatic and economic measures announced after a deadly attack in India-administered Kashmir killed 26 people, mostly tourists.
New Delhi accused Islamabad of backing the attack. Pakistan has denied the charges.
High stakes for Pakistan
Millions of people in Pakistan depend on the Indus, Jhelum and Chenab rivers for drinking water, farming and daily life.
The rivers are particularly important to Punjab and Sindh provinces, whose agriculture is central to the country’s food supply and rural economy.
After India’s move to suspend the treaty, Pakistan approached the court in The Hague over the status of the accord.
Pakistani officials have repeatedly warned that any attempt to deny the country its share of the waters of rivers flowing across the border would be treated as an act of war.
Ajay Bisaria, a former Indian high commissioner to Pakistan, said India had challenged the treaty on both political and legal grounds.
“Politically, abeyance hands India a new point of leverage, one more lever to press Pakistan into changing its behavior on cross-border terrorism,” Bisaria told DW.
He also pointed to India’s earlier requests to renegotiate the treaty, citing climate change, new dam-building technology and the deterioration of relations between the two countries.
India chose to put the treaty in abeyance rather than formally abrogate it. Bisaria said the ruling in The Hague would not change that course.
“The tribunal will not alter this trajectory,” he said. “India’s course on the Indus Waters Treaty is set. The treaty will not be revived in its present form.”
Legal battle over water
Pakistan has taken the opposite view.

Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar said the ruling “decisively rejects” India’s attempt to place the treaty in abeyance and reaffirmed that it remains “fully in force and binding on both parties.”
“The Award vindicates Pakistan’s consistent position that a binding international treaty cannot be unilaterally suspended or set aside,” Dar said in a post on X.

Pakistan welcomes the unanimous Award of the Court of Arbitration today, which decisively rejects India’s unlawful attempt to place the Indus Waters Treaty “in abeyance” and reaffirms that the Treaty remains fully in force and binding on both parties. The Award vindicates… — Ishaq Dar (@MIshaqDar50) August 31, 2026
He added that India must comply with its obligations under the treaty and with binding decisions arising from its dispute settlement mechanisms.
Ayesha Siddiqa, a Pakistani political scientist and defense analyst, said the ruling may be difficult to implement if India refuses to accept it.
“The arbitration court’s ruling may not be implementable because the court doesn’t have the force to do so,” Siddiqa told DW.
But she said the decision gave Pakistan an advantage as a lower riparian state.
“It does give Pakistan a moral edge,” said Siddiqa, a senior fellow in the Department of War Studies at King’s College London.
She also questioned what India’s rejection of the ruling could mean for its international position, particularly given that India has accepted international legal decisions in other disputes.
“This is not just an issue of pure military power but an international standing where India will not be able to justify its position to the world any longer,” she said.
Shanthie Mariet D’Souza, a South Asia analyst and founder of the Mantraya think tank, said the ruling did not materially change India’s position.
“The Permanent Court of Arbitration is an administrative body, not a conventional sovereign court with enforcement capabilities,” D’Souza told DW.

“In this particular case, India chose not to participate in the proceedings. This allows it not to recognize the tribunal’s rulings. Therefore, it has no enforceable constraint on India and nothing changes materially for New Delhi,” she said.
A dispute over the rules
India and Pakistan have disagreed for years over the interpretation of the treaty, particularly over Indian hydropower projects on rivers allocated primarily to Pakistan.

Uttam Kumar Sinha, a senior fellow at the Manohar Parrikar Institute for Defence Studies in New Delhi and author of “Trial by Water,” said India is now no longer merely contesting the interpretation of the treaty, but rather “contesting the authority of the treaty’s dispute-settlement mechanism itself.”
New Delhi maintains that the tribunal was improperly constituted and that its decisions have no legal effect on India.
Sinha described the emerging contest as “lawfare,” with Pakistan likely to use the ruling in international forums and frame the dispute around treaty obligations and international law.
The limits of India’s leverage
The practical implications will also depend on what India does with its infrastructure on the western rivers.
D’Souza said the treaty’s abeyance gave India more political and psychological leverage than an immediate ability to alter the flow of the rivers.

“To effectively stop or significantly alter the flows of the Indus, Jhelum and Chenab rivers, substantial infrastructure like dams, canals and large storage systems would be required, and such structures do not currently exist,” said D’Souza.
“Furthermore, geographical and technical constraints limit India’s capacity to block these rivers.”
Sinha echoed this view.
“India cannot simply ‘turn off’ the western rivers,” he said.

Large storage and diversion projects would take years or decades, require substantial investment and involve difficult construction in the mountainous Himalayan region, as well as environmental and domestic approvals.
“There is a significant gap between India’s potential strategic freedom on the western rivers and its actual physical capacity to change water flows,” Sinha said. /dl

articles.title: Unicef: 1 in 5 youths targeted by online sexual abuse
articles.summary: The internet is not a safe place for unsupervised children and young people — by now, that’s common knowledge. Social media platforms are adept at tweaking their algorithms to ensure users of…

blocks.text: The internet is not a safe place for unsupervised children and young people — by now, that’s common knowledge.

Social media platforms are adept at tweaking their algorithms to ensure users of any age remain on their sites. To do that, they often disseminate content that can be dangerous and upsetting for young people.

Studies regularly find a connection between what’s known as doomscrolling and a higher risk of psychological problems in the young, including suicidal thoughts. And some of the latest trends in video creation on platforms like TikTok directly endanger the safety of users.
In the United States, Meta, which owns both Instagram and Facebook, recently opted to settle a case against it out of court. A number of US states had claimed that the two platforms harmed children.

Meta agreed to pay up to $17.1 billion (€14.7 billion) to the states involved and to limit teenagers’ access to its platforms to just two hours a day. During the night, access will be completely blocked.

A new survey by UNICEF, the UN agency for children, puts the spotlight on another danger that young people constantly face in the digital world: sexual assault, a threat experienced by one in five people between the ages of 12 and 17 over the past year.
What are the key findings?
The UNICEF report, which DW saw in advance of publication, explains how such attacks often happen.
“It often begins without warning,” the authors of the study wrote. “Conversation becomes coercion, and coercion becomes entrapment.”

The survey found that more than 15 million children had been exposed to unwanted sexual content. An estimated 9 million were pressured into sexual conversations or asked to share sexual images, while some 4 million had sexual images shared without their consent. The report’s authors, however, warn that the true scale is likely far higher.

“The report reveals a painful reality,” said UNICEF Executive Director Catherine Russell. “These experiences cause profound emotional and mental distress. Many children suffer in silence, unsure where to turn for help.”

Often, the perpetrator of the assault puts pressure on a victim. The victims then feel ashamed and this makes it difficult to tell anybody about what has happened. Of those surveyed, 41% had never told anybody about their assault. Others said they had first confided in friends, siblings or their mothers. Fewer than 1% were reported to authorities.

blocks.caption: UNICEF: 1 in 5 youths targeted by online sexual abuse

blocks.text: The stereotype many have of a complete stranger harassing young people online actually only applies in 16% of cases. Most perpetrators — 57% — are already known to their victims. They may be friends, family members or even romantic partners.

In addition, 27% of respondents were not able to identify the people behind the profiles. When perpetrators are known, they include adults but also minors. In many cases, attacks take place in real life as well as online.

The major social media platforms are also the main gateways for this kind of behavior. The UNICEF report says 60% of assaults come primarily from Facebook, WhatsApp and Instagram (all of which are owned by Meta), followed by Snapchat, TikTok and YouTube. And 14% of respondents cited online gaming platforms as the location of an assault — gaming platforms usually have direct messaging channels.
How was the data collected?

The report polled around 21,000 young people in 21 countries, aged between 12 and 17, who regularly use the internet. Data from 12 countries — Ethiopia, Indonesia, Cambodia, Kenya, Malaysia, Mozambique, Namibia, the Philippines, Tanzania, Thailand, Uganda and Vietnam — had already been collected in 2020 and 2021 and analyzed in an earlier report.

For this new report, additional data was collected in Armenia, Brazil, Colombia, the Dominican Republic, Mexico, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Pakistan and Serbia. The surveys were also supplemented by longer interviews with 100 young people who had experienced abuse.

blocks.caption: Children and young people also come into contact with inappropriate content in the form of fakes created by generative AI, such as these images generated by Grok of the platform XImage: Leon Neal/Getty Images

blocks.text: Europe, US surveys find similar results
Researchers familiar with this issue would not be surprised by the scale of the problem.
The 2020 EU Kids Online Survey, based on a poll conducted in 19 European countries, indicated that 22% of all participants had received sexually explicit messages online.

In a Spanish study conducted in seven secondary schools in 2021 and 2022, 21% of female respondents said they were sexually harassed online “occasionally,” while 5% said this happened “frequently.” For male respondents in the Spanish study, the percentages were a few points lower.

A similar survey conducted by the Pew Research Center in 2022 found that 17% of 13- to 17-year-olds in the US said they had been sent explicit images without their consent. The survey did not differentiate between sexually explicit content and other material that showed things like violence.

blocks.caption: UNICEF: 1 in 5 youths targeted by online sexual abuse

blocks.text: The UNICEF report calls on governments, tech companies and other stakeholders to better protect children and young people in the digital world.
Among the requests:

items: Design more secure digital platforms, with stronger protection for the privacy of minors.
Strengthen national regulations and criminal law, and close loopholes.
Establish trustworthy reporting and support systems for young people.

blocks.text: Coming just after Meta’s out-of-court settlement in the US, the new UNICEF report will likely add fuel to the fire for those seeking to ban social media for young people, an ongoing debate in many countries.

In December 2025, Australia became the first country in the world to introduce an age limit for social media in order to protect minors. There, anyone under 16 is prohibited from having an account on platforms like YouTube, X, Facebook, Instagram, TikTok and Snapchat, a rule the platforms themselves are required to monitor.

A similar age limit will come into effect in the UK in 2027, while France is the first EU country to have passed a law adopting an age limit — 15 years old — for social media users. However, it has since been blocked by France’s top court, the Constitutional Council, which ruled it might infringe on freedom of expression and privacy.
In June, a German commission proposed a tiered model. This would come with age limits, requirements for proof of age and strict rules requiring the cooperation of social media platforms. /dl

articles.title: Human fat, blood dumped into sinks, toilets at Seoul clinics
articles.summary: Twenty-five plastic surgery and dermatology clinics in Seoul violated medical-waste rules, including two cases in which human fat and blood from cosmetic procedures were dumped into sinks and…

blocks.text: Twenty-five plastic surgery and dermatology clinics in Seoul violated medical-waste rules, including two cases in which human fat and blood from cosmetic procedures were dumped into sinks and toilets, the Seoul Metropolitan Government said Thursday.

The city’s special judicial police investigated 120 sites — 112 medical clinics and eight waste collection and transport companies — from January 2025 through July this year. Investigators uncovered 36 violations at 25 clinics.

In the two cases of illegal disposal, human fat and blood from liposuction and other cosmetic procedures were poured into sinks or toilets. Medical waste was also discarded in ordinary trash bins alongside household waste.

Other violations involved improper storage. Some clinics mixed human tissue waste with general medical waste and kept it at room temperature before handing it over for disposal. Others stored medical waste for three to six months beyond the permitted period.

Blood, bodily fluids, used needles and other medical waste must be handled separately because of the risk of infection. Human tissue waste, including fat, must be kept in designated containers at 4 degrees Celsius or below.

“Human tissue waste can rapidly decompose at room temperature, increasing odors and the risk of infection,” said an official from the city’s special judicial police bureau. “Medical institutions must strictly comply with storage and disposal standards from the moment the waste is generated.”

Investigators booked 25 people in connection with the violations and referred them to prosecutors in August with recommendations for indictment. Violating medical waste disposal standards is punishable by up to two years in prison or a fine of up to 20 million won ($14,700), according to the city.
The investigation also found that some doctors, nurses and waste-handling workers lacked sufficient knowledge of disposal requirements.

The city plans to improve training and inspection procedures and revise penalties to reflect the seriousness of each violation. It will share the cases with district offices and continue investigating related waste collection and transport companies.

The findings come amid a surge in medical tourism to Seoul, driven largely by demand for dermatological and cosmetic procedures. A record 1.76 million foreign patients received treatment in the city in 2025, up 75.6 percent from a year earlier. /dl

articles.title: Nepal flood survivors lack space even to mourn their dead
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — Families of people who went missing in the Bhotekoshi floods have begun performing the funeral rites of their loved ones using effigies made of kusha grass, as they did not receive…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — Families of people who went missing in the Bhotekoshi floods have begun performing the funeral rites of their loved ones using effigies made of kusha grass, as they did not receive any clues of their whereabouts even after eight days of the disaster.
Most flood victims have been left without a place to observe the mourning rituals, as the floodwaters not only swept away family members but also their houses.
Those who lost everything in the floods and came to the capital city seeking shelter have also been unable to find space at public facilities for the rituals.

Nirajan Poudel of Nuwakot reached the Kiriyaputri Bhawan at Rudramati Mahadev Temple in Tarakeshwar-5 after losing family members in the devastating floods. “After we could not find any space to stay during the mourning period, we came here,” he said. “We managed to get a room here.”

Poudel, a resident of Bidur Municipality-7, lost his father, mother, uncle, aunt and sister (his uncle’s daughter) in the devastating August 26 disaster. On Wednesday, he and his cousin performed the funeral rites of all five using effigies made of kusha, the grass holy for Hindus with the scientific name Desmostachya bipinnata, and began the mourning rituals.

The Rudramati Mahadev Temple and Kiriyaputri Bhawan are still under construction. However, after flood victims requested a place to observe mourning rituals for relatives lost in the Bhotekoshi floods, the temple management committee decided to open the facility in whatever condition it was, said Raj Kumar Phuyal, treasurer of the temple management committee.

“The entire country is currently in mourning. To help the relatives of the victims, we opened this Kiriyaputri Bhawan after the floods,” he said. “As construction isn’t over yet, mourners may face some difficulties.”
There are currently eight groups staying at the Kiriyaputri Bhawan, and each group has lost three to five members of the family in the Rasuwa flood.

“There is no space to accommodate even one more mourner family,” said Sudarshan Chapagain, a social activist. “So many people have come asking for a place to observe the mourning ritual but we have not been able to accommodate them all.”

He said construction of the Kiriyaputri Bhawan was still underway and that a lack of funds had delayed its completion for years. The Tarakeshwar Municipality had provided only Rs1 million for its construction while local residents also collected donations to build the three-storey building.

Like in Rudramati Mahadev Temple and Kiriyaputri Bhawan, all eight rooms at the nearby Gupteshwar Mahadev Temple’s Kiriyaputri Bhawan are occupied by families who lost relatives in the Bhotekoshi floods. After more and more people began coming to request a place to observe the rituals, the building management committee put up tents and created six additional rooms.

“Now we do not have any room available until the current groups complete their mourning,” said Rishi Prasad Nepal, a member of the Gupteshwar Temple Kiriyaputri Bhawan management committee. “We keep receiving phone calls from flood victims for a place to mourn but we simply do not have one to offer.”
The committee has decided to charge only Rs1,000 for each family for using its room to mourn and complete rituals.
“Mourners’ families themselves have to bring gas, as we are unable to manage gas for them,” said Nepal. “LP gas is no longer available for purchase.”

Rajan Raila of Bidur Municipality-7, who lost his mother, younger brother and sister-in-law in the floods, performed the funeral rites of the deceased using kusha effigies at Pashupati Aryaghat on Wednesday and then came to Gupteshwar Temple to observe the mourning rituals. He said he and his brothers, who are observing the rituals together, were given only one room.

“We got only one room for the mourning rituals of three deceased family members,” he said. “Even that room has not yet become available. We will get it only after those whose 13th-day ritual is completed today leave. Until then, we have to wait outside.”

Relatives of victims said they had begun performing the rituals using kusha effigies because there was little possibility of finding their missing family members, and even if bodies were recovered, identifying them had become difficult. They also complain that bodies were being buried rapidly in mass graves, leaving families with no option but to perform symbolic funerals.
Victims said around 100 people were missing in Sole of Bidur Municipality-7 alone in the floods.

“There could be many more, as we do not know how many people who were staying indoors, walking along the roads or working at construction sites were swept away,” said Ram Chandra Dhakal, a flood victim displaced from Bidur-7, Sole.

Dhakal and his brother Uttam are also observing the mourning ritual for their mother at the Kiriyaputri Bhawan in Gupteshwar. She was found dead after being caught in the flood. Although the body was cremated in their village, they had to come to Kathmandu, as there was no house in the village where they could observe the mourning rituals, he said.

Victims said all the rooms at the Kiriyaputri Bhawan at a place known as Gumba in Balaju-16 have also been occupied by people who lost relatives in the floods. Even those displaced by the floods who came to Kathmandu to stay with relatives or in rented rooms have struggled to observe mourning rituals, as it is not possible to conduct such rituals in their relatives’ homes or their own rented rooms.
The lack of space at public kiriyaputri buildings has compounded their difficulties in observing the mourning rituals.

More than 1,200 bodies of people who died in the August 26 floods have been recovered while thousands are still missing. Pilgrims, tourists, engineers and others are among those who disappeared in the floods.

The floods swept away more than 7,000 houses, while many of the houses that are still standing have become uninhabitable. Dozens of concrete and suspension bridges and roads have been washed away. Dozens of settlements along the Trishuli riverbanks have been completely destroyed in the floods. /dl

articles.title: DFA: ‘Geopolitical forces’ led to failed PH’s UN Security Council bid
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Foreign Affairs Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro cited “forces in geopolitical issues” as factors behind the Philippines’ failed bid for a nonpermanent seat on the United Nations…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Foreign Affairs Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro cited “forces in geopolitical issues” as factors behind the Philippines’ failed bid for a nonpermanent seat on the United Nations (UN) Security Council.

Lazaro told lawmakers that securing the seat had required a “herculean” campaign, as she faced questions about the Philippines’ loss during a House of Representatives appropriations committee hearing on the Department of Foreign Affairs’ proposed 2027 budget.
“Unfortunately, there are many other forces in geopolitical issues,” she maintained.

“If a reason is being asked why we failed in our bid, the only answer to that is the geopolitical issues. I can spell it, but I would prefer in writing so I can tell you. But, it is geopolitical issues,” she added without further expounding.
The Philippines lost to Kyrgyzstan in its bid last June for a nonpermanent seat on the UN Security Council for the 2026–2027 term.
For its part, Malacañang blamed “political noise from obstructionists” for the country’s loss.
At the hearing, DFA Financial Management Services chief Assistant Secretary Emilio Fernandez noted that their department had been allotted a total of P70 million through its 2025 and 2026 budgets.
Fernandez added that, of the P70 million allotted, only P52.5 million had been utilized.
The Philippines previously served on the council in 1957, 1963, 1980–1981 and 2004–2005, while Kyrgyzstan had never served on the council before. /dl

articles.title: Indonesian haze blankets Bukidnon skies
articles.summary: VALENCIA CITY, Bukidnon — Residents across Bukidnon have observed a thin haze blanketing the skies since September 1, particularly during sunrise, with authorities confirming Thursday that it was due…

blocks.text: VALENCIA CITY, Bukidnon — Residents across Bukidnon have observed a thin haze blanketing the skies since September 1, particularly during sunrise, with authorities confirming Thursday that it was due to forest and land fires in Kalimantan, Indonesia.

Ejay Zuniga, weather specialist at the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) Mindanao Regional Services Division, confirmed on Thursday morning that cross-equatorial winds from the Southern Hemisphere brought the haze.Zuniga explained that winds originating from Indonesia—where massive forest and peatland fires have been burning for weeks—are drifting toward Visayas and Mindanao.

EMB is an agency under the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR).The DENR-10 station in Cagayan de Oro recorded an AQI of 133, which is classified as “Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups.”

EMB-10 officially attributed the deteriorating air quality to transboundary smoke from forest and land fires in Kalimantan, Indonesia.In response, the Department of Health (DOH) urged the public to take precautionary measures, including wearing masks and limiting strenuous outdoor activities.The DOH advised vulnerable groups—such as children, older adults, pregnant women, and individuals with pre-existing heart or lung conditions—to exercise heightened caution and keep their prescribed medications readily available.Outdoor workers were also advised to take regular indoor breaks.Residents are encouraged to continuously monitor official air quality updates from the DENR-EMB and their respective local government units./coa

articles.title: Nepal sent alert 38 minutes after glacier collapse. It wasn’t enough
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — Nima Dorje Tamang was in Hakubesi, a hamlet south of Syafrubesi in Rasuwa, when the flood struck. Before Tamang could prepare, he heard a thunderous roar and saw the flood gushing…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — Nima Dorje Tamang was in Hakubesi, a hamlet south of Syafrubesi in Rasuwa, when the flood struck. Before Tamang could prepare, he heard a thunderous roar and saw the flood gushing toward him, its waves taller than him.

Tamang and his family ran uphill for their lives but the waves caught him and a rock struck his leg, fracturing it. Swept into the river, he managed to grab a tree near the bank and clung to it for what felt like two hours until his father and his brother came to rescue him. For the next 24 hours, he said he slipped in and out of consciousness before a helicopter brought him to Kathmandu.

At the orthopedic inpatient ward of Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital, Tamang told the doctors, “Even the air makes it hurt,” when they pressed his left foot. It was still swollen after the surgery. But from his hospital bed, Tamang worried about his family back home. “We lost our uncle, aunt, sister, and brother-in-law,” he said. “And everyone says there will be a massive flood again.”

Like Tamang, communities and authorities were caught off guard when the glacier collapsed at 8:37 AM on August 26. Scientists say the likelihood of predicting this particular type of disaster was minimal, and the resulting flash flood surged so rapidly through the steep mountain terrain that there was little time to warn communities downstream. But the disaster exposed a deeper problem: Nepal’s warning systems remain largely designed around individual hazards, while disasters in the Hindu Kush Himalaya are becoming increasingly complex, cascading and transboundary.

“There is no such thing as an early warning system in Nepal. Simply having sensors does not mean it’s a system; it has to be much more comprehensive,” said Anil Pokhrel, former chief executive of National Disaster Risk Reduction & Management Authority (NDRRMA), stressing the word “system.” For it to be a system, it needed to have a proper assessment of who and what is at risk, he said, then an observation system to anticipate hazards in real time, a comprehensive communications plan for timely alerts, and preparedness for emergencies.
“If the Chinese sensors detect something upstream, a series of sirens should automatically go off all at once. Text messages should go off with a loud buzzer even if it is on silent mode,” he added.

Over the last decade, Pokhrel said Nepal had invested a lot on the observation side, installing sensors. Without multiple sets of sensors monitoring different hazards across different locations, as we saw with Rasuwa floods, it is inadequate to save lives.

When the massive glacial collapse hit the Lhende valley, near the Nepal-Tibet border, Nepal’s Department of Mines and Geology recorded seismic activity. “Our records showed a 4.4 magnitude. But the frequency of the seismic activity did not match that of an earthquake, which is the department’s monitoring mandate, so we did not alert the public like we usually do,” said Lok Vijay Adhikari, chief of National Earthquake Monitoring and Research Center in the Department of Mines and Geology. The US Geological Survey also initially recorded the event at magnitude 4.4, but later revised its assessment, attributing the seismic activity to the glacial collapse.

In the minutes that followed, rising water levels in Bhotekoshi in Rasuwa could potentially have provided another opportunity to alert the public. It was the same Lhende Khola, a transboundary high-altitude river that originates in Gyirong County in Tibet and flows toward the Nepal border, feeding into Bhotekoshi as well as Trishuli downstream. But at 8:50 AM, the flash flood swept away the gauge in the Bhotekoshi river in Rasuwa, at the Syabrubesi hydrological station. Designed to detect gradual rises in the rivers, the gauges were ill-equipped to detect the high-speed flood.
Who knows what to do with the warnings

Twenty-three minutes later, the District Administrative Officer in Rasuwa informed the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology (DHM) about the flash flood. “We informed DHM at nine. We could not do much in Rasuwa because the flood had destroyed the [communications] towers, yet local authorities informed communities, and people went from door to door warning each other,” said Shanti Mahat, spokesperson of NDRRMA.
“But for people downstream we used every means to inform them—through text alerts, caller tune, media broadcasts, and police miking,” she added.

Within 15 minutes of receiving the information, at 9:15 AM — 38 minutes after the ice-rock avalanche — people in Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, and Chitwan got text alerts that advised them to immediately move to safe, higher ground as water levels in the Bhotekoshi river in Rasuwa had crossed the danger threshold. It also listed hotlines for rescue assistance.

blocks.caption: Nima Dorje Tamang’s mobile phone showing the warning text message he received.

blocks.text: Such alerts are critical in a crisis. Over 95 percent of Nepali adults have mobile phones with data, and it is an effective method even if language and literacy levels may hinder access.
Early warning mechanisms can also be basic, where people are vigilant, spot a danger, inform on time, and those at risk know how to act.

Himanshu Thakkar, coordinator of the South Asia Network on Dams, Rivers & People recalled an incident from the 2021 glacier collapse in Chamoli of Uttarakhand in India, part of the Hindu Kush Himalayan region. “A woman who was on top of a hill saw the flood [in Rishi Ganga] ravaging from a distance and immediately informed her husband, who was working at the hydropower project downstream,” Thakkar said. Her husband initially did not believe her because he could not see the flood. When he finally caught sight of it, he alerted his colleagues, and a group of them ran uphill and survived.

He juxtaposed that with having information about a risk and not knowing how to act on it, referring to the tour guide Ziha Yitie and other mountaineers in Tibet who videographed the slab of glacier falling off of Langtang Lirung Peak. But they did not immediately understand what they were seeing and realized the magnitude of the disaster only after descending down.
Where does accountability lie?

Ultimately, the responsibility for timely warning lies with the state. Nepal already has a bilateral flood-forecasting mechanism with India where the two countries exchange rainfall and river level data. But Nepal is mainly the provider of information, as most of the monitoring stations are in Nepal’s upstream rivers. On the other hand, despite agreements between the two presidents—Xi Jinping and Bidya Devi Bhandari—in 2019, committing to promote cooperation in different fields, including addressing climate change and protecting the environment, seven years on, the countries still do not have even a rudimentary early warning plan.

“There is no protocol. The practice that we have right now is that we cooperate with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs to share information,” said Prakash Pokhrel, Geologist at NDRRMA. “Whenever a foreign country is involved, we have to go through the ministry.”

The danger of not having a mandatory protocol, former NDRRMA chief executive Anil Pokhrel warned, is that, “It comes down to the subjective judgement of individuals in authority who may or may not choose to inform.”

After last year’s catastrophic supraglacial flood in the same Bhotekoshi river in Rasuwa, Nepal’s monitoring of that area remained limited. The northern side of Nepal’s mountain range, however, happened to be in a “blind spot” that no one, including Nepal, China, and international geologists, was monitoring.
Asked if the area was a low priority for Nepal, government officials suggested it was easier said than done.

“The terrain above the settlement in Timure is extremely remote and difficult to access,” said Mahat. “While we have monitoring stations at the Bhotekoshi river, setting up stations that provide real-time data farther out has been very challenging. Even now we’re struggling to get images using drones.”
Dinkar Kayastha, information officer at the DHM, says that looking at the resources at their disposal, it is impossible to monitor everything, especially when 20 to 25 percent of Nepal is mountains.
Pointing to the Thame flood of 2024 in the Everest region, Kayastha said, “We saw that even such small glacier lakes, that were not considered threatening, can become devastating.”
As of now, according to him, Nepal has monitored major “high-risk” glacial lakes including Imja Tsho in the Khumbu, Everest region, and Tsho Rolpa in Rolwaling valley of Dolakha.

After last year’s flood in Bhotekoshi, Pokhrel, the geologist at NDRRMA, said they were monitoring potentially dangerous glacial lakes every day using satellite images to identify the risk of glacial lake outburst floods. International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) has identified 21 potentially dangerous glacier lakes in Nepal across Gandaki, Koshi, and Karnali river basins and mapped 2070 lakes. Their numbers and their size are not absolute; ICIMOD’s research found that as temperatures rise, both the number and size of the lakes are increasing in Nepal.

blocks.caption: Nepal sent its disaster alert 38 minutes after the glacier collapse. It wasn’t enough

blocks.text: Earlier this year in March 2026, ICIMOD also warned that glaciers in the Hindu Kush Himalaya were melting at double the rate since 2000. They warned that catastrophic floods and water uncertainty were testament to the fact that it was a critical decade for the cryosphere, where retreats in certain parts could be irreversible. Yet, out of the 38 glaciers ICIMOD monitored, only seven met the global benchmark, and many in the region remained largely unmonitored.

But Prakash Pokhrel said the same satellite images are far less useful for anticipating a glacier collapse. “Many places look stable. We can’t know from the images how fractures have developed or if weathering has occurred,” he said.
When “Clean & Green” development deepens risks

For Thakkar, the responsibility is also on the investors of the 13 hydropower plants in Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts that were damaged by the floods, disconnecting roughly 431MW, a tenth of its total power, from the national grid.

The Asian Development Bank, the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, and International Finance Corporation were among the major financiers of the Upper Trishuli-1 hydropower project, while China’s state-owned Exim Bank funded the Upper Trishuli 3A project. The projects also included financing from British International Investment, Korea Development Bank, and Exim Bank of Korea, as well as the Netherlands FMO, OPEC Fund and Canadian Climate Fund.

The Asian Development Bank’s panel of independent experts overseeing the Upper Trishuli-1 project had recommended strengthening the warning system and emergency plan, coordinating alerts with hydropower projects upstream and downstream, and putting evacuation protocols in place for dangerous floods.

blocks.caption: Nima Dorje Tamang receiving treatment at Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital.

blocks.text: “But they don’t do it. It’s complete callousness. There is no accountability in South Asian countries,” said Thakkar. “They [funders] know nobody is going to be held accountable so they just get away with it.”

Thakkar said that hydropower projects can aggravate disaster risks by creating additional vulnerabilities in already fragile Himalayan landscapes through deforestation, tunnelling, blasting, excavation and muck dumping. Dams can also worsen downstream flooding, while reservoirs accumulate silt that can create additional risks. When multiple hydropower projects are built in a cascade, he said, these impacts accumulate and multiply.
Climate change is adding another layer of risk through more intense rainfall, warmer winters, melting glaciers and thawing permafrost.

“Our dishonest EIAs, lack of accountability in governance and non-implementation of basic monitoring, forecasting and implementable disaster management plans is worsening the disaster impacts in river valleys with multiple hydropower projects,” said Thakkar. “By not doing independent post-disaster impact assessments, we have shut the doors for learning any lessons for the future.”

Nepal’s Trishuli river basin alone, which originates in Rasuwa, has 36 hydropower projects in various stages of construction and planning. In Tamang’s village in Hakubesi, he said about eighty percent of the population worked at the Upper Trishuli-1 hydropower plant, and the rest of them were children or the elderly.

“We have no choice but to go to Kathmandu or to the Dhunche [headquarters of Rasuwa] for work. But with the hydropower people stayed back. Now all of them are trapped in it, the hydropower is gone, we have nothing,” he said. The government’s latest data shows 639 people remained trapped in Upper Trishuli-1 and Trishuli 3A.
What next?

For Dr. Saswata Sanyal, who is a disaster risk reduction specialist at ICIMOD, people need to understand the changing realities of living in the Hindu Kush region, where the risks we were familiar with yesterday are no longer the same today.

The Rasuwa flood was a testament to the complex interactions of hazards. “Something triggered an ice avalanche that led to flash floods, debris, sediments and boulders,” he said. Relief efforts since the disaster have also been affected by monsoon rains and flood alerts.
“The risks can be further exacerbated by earthquakes or climate change, so we need to understand the complex nature of hazards in the mountains,” he added.

Flood sensors, even if some of them were washed away in the flash floods in the Trishuli river in Galchchi, continued to be critical in monitoring the drastic increase in water levels and warning people. Sanyal suggested that it’s imperative for Nepal to increase those sensors upstream, not just in its own territory, but other countries in the Hindu Kush region should collaborate to do the same.

Pokhrel, the former chief executive of NDRRMA, added that Nepal needs to set up multiple sensors in diverse locations. Even for floods, he suggested, it’s not enough to install sensors in the bridges, and recommended setting them up on top of hills that can detect seismic waves or the rumble of boulders and floods to alert people using sirens.
Sanyal says people need to comprehend the scale of the Hindu Kush region.

“It has around 54,000 glaciers and more than 2000 glacier lakes, and permafrost covering an even larger area,” he said. While it is not possible to track every inch of the region, he suggested prioritizing the monitoring of areas with settlements downstream, with the countries not only sharing data but also working closely with each other.

Similarly, to identify risks in remote mountain areas that are difficult for scientists and government officials to routinely access, Anoop Nautiyal, climate advocate based in Dehradun, Uttarakhand, recommended training local communities on basic glaciology and hazard monitoring. “They are on the frontline dealing with the climate crisis and need to play a central role in prevention and disaster risk reduction.”

But monitoring cannot stop at national borders when the hazards themselves do not. Many disasters across the Hindu Kush Himalaya are transboundary, making regional cooperation critical. Climate activists, scientists, as well as researchers emphasised the importance of tripartite agreements between Nepal, China, and India, as well as bilateral agreements that go beyond non-binding commitments and include mandatory protocols and action plans for timely communication and response. “Every sensor, siren, drill is ultimately to ensure next time more people get a chance to reach safety,” said Sanyal.

Meanwhile, Tamang is worried about his grandparents back at home in Hakubesi. He said they are staying on higher grounds right now, but is concerned that they will soon run out of the limited food they have.

“Rescue, relief, everything reaches very late in our village. I don’t know why. There are still 100 to 200 people waiting with no rescue,” he said, showing his mobile phone, which showed that he received the warning text message at 9:42 AM. “I wish they would take them to Dhunche, because I hear there will be another massive flood; perhaps the water won’t reach as high.” /dl

articles.title: El Niño to be ‘very strong,’ last until February, UN warns
articles.summary: GENEVA — El Niño is set to become “very strong” in the months ahead, with the weather phenomenon near certain to persist through to February, the United Nations’ climate agency warned Thursday.…
