blocks.text: GENEVA — El Niño is set to become “very strong” in the months ahead, with the weather phenomenon near certain to persist through to February, the United Nations’ climate agency warned Thursday.
The World Meteorological Organization said El Niño would peak toward the end of this year, though its knock-on impacts on the climate will continue well into 2027.

“El Niño is firmly established and will intensify into a very strong event in the coming months, with big impacts on rainfall and temperature patterns and associated risks of floods, drought and extreme heat,” the WMO said.
El Niño is a natural climate phenomenon and is not caused by climate change.
But scientists expect it will exacerbate the heat of a planet already warming from burning fossil fuels, while amping up weather extremes.
“El Niño is being supersized before our eyes,” said UN chief Antonio Guterres.

“The science leaves no room for doubt: the planet is in uncharted waters, and those waters are heating up. Sea surface temperatures are rising, temperatures keep climbing, and the world is in the danger zone of extreme weather.
“The race now is between rising risks and our commitment to take climate action and protect people. We must win that race.”
‘Massive blow’ to economies
El Niño tends to peak late in the year, but heat in the oceans releases more slowly into the atmosphere, pushing up global temperatures the following year.
The hottest year on record is 2024, following the last El Niño.
“This exceptional El Niño… has the potential to deliver a massive blow to communities and economies across the world,” said WMO chief Celeste Saulo.
“We are already seeing disruption and devastation from droughts and floods, and we expect these impacts to increase as El Niño intensifies.”
She put disaster management authorities and climate-sensitive sectors like agriculture, health, energy and water on notice, saying there was “no time to lose” in getting ready.
El Niño warms surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, bringing worldwide changes in winds, pressure and rainfall patterns.
It typically takes place every two to seven years and lasts around nine to 12 months.
Conditions oscillate between El Niño and its opposite, La Niña, with neutral conditions in between.
“Fuelled by exceptionally warm ocean conditions across the tropical Pacific, El Niño is expected to strengthen further during the coming months to a very strong intensity,” the WMO said.
The UN agency classifies El Niño events as weak, moderate, strong or very strong, meaning it is set to reach the highest level out of four.
The WMO said there was an “exceptionally high likelihood of nearly 100 percent” that El Niño will continue through to February.
Pacific Ocean heating up
El Niño can reshape weather and climate patterns thousands of kilometres away from the tropical Pacific.

Every El Niño is different, but major events often follow familiar patterns. This includes drought across parts of the Amazon, Indonesia and Australia, disrupted monsoons in India, and shifting rainfall throughout the tropics.

For September-November, WMO forecasts indicate an increased likelihood of above-normal temperatures “across almost all land areas,” alongside rainfall patterns showing a “pronounced and classic atmospheric response to the strong Pacific El Niño,” the UN’s weather and climate agency said.
The index which measures sea surface temperature anomalies in the central eastern equatorial Pacific has strengthened from an average 1.5C above normal between May and July.
Weekly values between late July and mid-August ranged from around 2.2C to 2.6C above average, indicating continued El Niño intensification.
In some areas, subsurface ocean temperatures were more than 8C above average during July and early August. /dl

articles.title: Korea sees surge in suicide-encouraging content, most posts not deleted
articles.summary: SEOUL — More than 600,000 reports of online content that could encourage or facilitate suicide were filed in South Korea last year, but 7 in 10 remained online at the end of the year,…

blocks.text: SEOUL — More than 600,000 reports of online content that could encourage or facilitate suicide were filed in South Korea last year, but 7 in 10 remained online at the end of the year, government data showed Wednesday.

The Health Ministry received 602,781 reports of what Korean law defines as “suicide-inducing information” in 2025, according to data provided to Rep. Seo Mi-hwa of the ruling Democratic Party of Korea and first reported by Seoul Shinmun.
The category includes posts seeking suicide partners, content encouraging suicide and information on obtaining or using potentially lethal materials.
The number of reports has more than quadrupled from 142,725 in 2021. In 2025, only 176,163 of the reported items, or 29.2 percent, had been removed by year-end.
Social media accounted for 525,643 reports, with X responsible for 99.9 percent of them.
Online communities had the lowest removal rate. Of the 73,036 reports involving community posts, only 4,132, or 5.7 percent, resulted in removal.

The government had only one official dedicated to monitoring such content through 2024. Staffing was increased to four in September 2025, while the annual budget rose from 30 million won ($21,900) in 2024 to 207 million won this year.
The removal rate improved to 45.1 percent in the first half of this year, but more than half of reported content remained online.

Beginning Nov. 12, online platforms will be required to immediately remove or block suicide-inducing information they identify and restrict its search and transmission. The government also plans to introduce round-the-clock monitoring using artificial intelligence. /dl

articles.title: Nepal floods: Four hours under the rubble, 97 years above it
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — Guna Maya Bohara sometimes sings at night. It is the same bhajan—Hare Ram, Hare Krishna—that she used to sing during her stay at the elderly care home and during temple visits.…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — Guna Maya Bohara sometimes sings at night. It is the same bhajan—Hare Ram, Hare Krishna—that she used to sing during her stay at the elderly care home and during temple visits. Sometimes after singing, she asks a question: “Why did the water hit me?” The 97-year-old has asked the question more than once.

Apart from that, however, Bohara has mostly stopped speaking. Bohara is currently receiving treatment at Bir Hospital in Kathmandu. Her arms and legs have turned black and blue. She sometimes moves suddenly, almost involuntarily. She lies still for a while. Then another movement breaks the stillness. Doctors have diagnosed her with acute stress disorder.

On the morning of August 26, Bohara was in her room on the ground floor of the elderly care home at Devighat, a riverside town in Nuwakot. She was unaware that a glacier had collapsed high in the Himalayas. The collapse triggered a landslide, sending water and debris thundering down into the Trishuli River. The furious waters reached the ground floor, where Bohara was. It pushed her to the edge of the ground floor and left her there. The current was less intense on this side of the floor, witnesses say. Some of those caught in the current did not survive.

Nepal Police and Nepali Army personnel worked for about four hours to reach her, carefully clearing rubble carefully so as not to injure anyone still buried beneath it. Bohara’s relatives also rushed to the site. They brought a JCB excavator. With it, they worked together to move the debris away, inch by inch — moving, moving, moving, Dipak, Bohara’s great nephew, remembers, until there was space to lift her clear in its bucket.
Last Wednesday’s floods, however, were only the latest of Bohara’s ordeals in her long life.

At 97, Bohara has outlived her husband by 81 years. She was eight when she married him in Nuwakot’s Suryagadhi, at a time when child marriage was common practice. At 83, she chose on her own to move into a nursing home—Senior Citizens Welfare Foundation—in Devighat, close enough that her nieces could visit daily. She liked it there, among people her own age and looked forward to birthdays—her own and other residents—celebrated together.

By her twenties, she had already outlived nearly everyone who shared her blood: her husband, eight years into their marriage; both her parents, four years after that; her only brother, sometime later.
She never had children of her own.

What she had instead was her husband’s family, his three brothers, their wives, and in time their children. She raised thirteen nephews, twelve nieces as her own, sending every one of them to school, packing roasted maize for their lunch. Dipak says her family regards women of her generation as having quietly carried entire households through decades few now remember.
Bohara is the last of her generation left in the family.

Physically, she has proved more resilient than her age might lead one to expect. She has a pre-existing disability in her legs and an injury to her hand, caused by the torrents of water, is still being assessed, a CT scan and an X-ray pending. She survived on fruit juice for the first two days and has since moved to milk and full meals, Dipak said.

Of the people who share Guna Maya Bohara’s blood, none remain. Of the people who call her family, the nephews and nieces she once packed lunches for, there are twenty-five now, and they take turns at her bedside, waiting.

Dipak said that Bohara has not stopped asking, “Why did the water hit me?” He has tried to explain to her—more simply than what actually happened—that a lake, Gosaikunda, had burst far above them. She seems to understand, for a while. But hours later, she asks again: “Why did the water hit me?” /dl

articles.title: Filipinos’ visa-free stay in Thailand back to 30 days
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines – Thailand’s 60-day visa exemption will be replaced with 30-day visa free stays for tourists from 60 countries, including the Philippines, starting September 15, according to the…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – Thailand’s 60-day visa exemption will be replaced with 30-day visa free stays for tourists from 60 countries, including the Philippines, starting September 15, according to the Tourism Authority of Thailand (TAT).

“From 15 September 2026, travelers previously covered by the 60-day visa exemption will instead be subject to the applicable 30-day visa exemption, 15-day visa exemption, Visa on Arrival, or other relevant entry arrangements, depending on nationality,” the TAT said, citing the measure published in Thailand’s Royal Gazette on August 31.
The change effectively halves the visa-free period that Filipinos have enjoyed since Thailand expanded its visa-exemption policy in July 2024.
For most Filipino tourists, however, the change is unlikely to affect typical short trips, as stays of up to 30 days will remain visa-free.
From September 15, passport holders from the following 60 countries and territories may enter Thailand visa-free for tourism and stay up to 30 days:

Australia, Austria, Bahrain, Belgium, Bhutan, Brunei, Bulgaria, Canada, Croatia, Cyprus, Czech Republic, Denmark, Estonia, Fiji, Finland, France, Georgia, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Iceland, India, Indonesia, Ireland, Israel, Italy, Japan, Jordan, Kuwait, Kyrgyzstan, Latvia, Liechtenstein, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malaysia, Maldives, Malta, Netherlands, New Zealand, Norway, Oman, Philippines, Poland, Portugal, Qatar, Romania, Saudi Arabia, Singapore, Slovakia, Slovenia, South Africa, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, Taiwan, Turkey, Ukraine, United Arab Emirates, United Kingdom, and the United States.
TAT also explained that those using 30-day visa exemptions may enter through land-border immigration checkpoints no more than twice per calendar year. /dl

articles.title: China’s falling emissions amid Iran war spark hope of decarbonisation watershed
articles.summary:
Oil consumption plummets and EV sales soar as analysts say demand may not fully return even if crude price falls

China’s carbon dioxide emissions fell by 1% after the outbreak of the…

blocks.text: China’s carbon dioxide emissions fell by 1% after the outbreak of the US-Israeli war on Iran, thanks to a sharp reduction in oil consumption and a steady rise in the use of electric vehicles and public transport, analysis shows.

The report reveals the role of clean energy in cushioning the price shocks caused by the strait of Hormuz crisis to the world’s biggest oil importer. It also reinforces hopes that China, which is the world’s biggest greenhouse gas emitter, may be nearing a turning point in decarbonising its economy.

China was able to increase overall transportation use, despite cutting oil imports by 32%, according to second-quarter energy data reported by the country’s National Bureau of Statistics and analysed for Carbon Brief by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air.

The reduction – equivalent to about a million barrels a day – from the world’s biggest petro-customer helped to stabilise global oil prices, which nevertheless surged by about 60% in the weeks and months after the first US airstrikes in late February.

How that was achieved has been the subject of considerable speculation. The analysis indicates that about two-thirds of the fall in imports came from running down, rather than building up, strategic oil stockpiles. The remaining third was largely covered by a reduction in demand.

blocks.caption: Wind turbines on the Yellow Sea coast of Yancheng, China. Photograph: Alex Plavevski/EPA

blocks.text: The country’s use of oil fell by 9% overall and by 16% for transport. While large numbers of petrol and diesel vehicles stayed off the roads, there was a surge in journeys by electric cars, buses, trains and trucks.

This electrifying trend had begun long before the strait of Hormuz crisis. China is by far the world’s biggest manufacturer, user and exporter of batteries, e-vehicles, wind turbines and solar panels. The disruption of oil supplies from the Gulf has strengthened the economic and strategic imperative of reducing petro-dependence.
In the first half of 2026, China’s shift towards electric vehicles displaced the equivalent of the UK’s entire oil consumption over a six-month period.
after newsletter promotion

Analysts predict much of this demand will not return even if global oil prices fall. “In a qualitative sense, there’s no question that the transport sector decarbonisation has been accelerated,” said Lauri Myllyvirta, the lead analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air. “It’s a validation of the energy security strategy that China has in place … It’s very clear that electrification is the winning strategy to insure against these kinds of shocks.”
Myllyvirta noted this was the first time China’s overall emissions had fallen due to a reduction in oil use rather than in coal consumption.

In fact, coal generation rose during the quarter due to shifting economic incentives and delays in adapting the country’s grid, which caused considerable wastage of wind and solar power. Despite this, observers believe the longer-term trend in China is away from fossil fuels.

Dr Muyi Yang, a senior analyst at Ember, which will next week publish a separate overview of China’s energy trends, said a fossil fuel peak was coming into view at the provincial and sectoral level. “The Iran crisis reinforces the case. The way China has been able to absorb its impact strengthens the confidence to go deeper and further.

“The risk of oil-import dependence increasingly comes from the geopolitical domain. This is a risk no country can effectively manage. So the more effective strategy is to reduce that exposure altogether. And China’s experience is demonstrating that this works.”

articles.title: Barclays faces complaint over backing for power plant near world’s largest mangrove forest
articles.summary:
Bangladeshi complainants allege Rampal power station’s pollution and climate risks threaten the Sunderbans, a world heritage site

Barclays Bank is facing a formal complaint over its…

blocks.text: Barclays Bank is facing a formal complaint over its financial links to a coal-fired power station near the Sundarbans, the world’s largest mangrove forest and home to millions of people in Bangladesh and India.

Three complainants from the region have submitted a case to the UK government’s Office for Responsible Business Conduct, alleging that the British bank breached international guidelines by underwriting companies involved in the emission-heavy Maitree super thermal power project, also known as the Rampal power plant.

The coal-fired power station is situated near the Sundarbans, a Unesco world heritage site made up of more than 100 tiny islands across a river delta that supports hundreds of plant and animal species, including the Bengal tiger.

Sharif Jamil, an environmental campaigner based in the Bangladeshi capital, Dhaka, who is one of the complainants, said heavy-metal pollution from the plant and the industrial development surrounding it was entering the Sundarbans through its interconnected rivers and canals.
“The Rampal power plant is right on the bank of the Pasur River, which is the lifeline of the Sundarbans,” he said. “The health of the forest is in trouble.”
Last November, a study found elevated levels of mercury and arsenic in water samples taken from the Sundarbans, with the highest concentrations recorded in the Pasur River.

Researchers identified industrial discharge and port-related activities among the sources of heavy-metal contamination and said the Rampal power station posed “a significant environmental threat due to emissions from coal combustion and increased navigation traffic”.

blocks.caption: The Sundarbans, the world’s largest mangrove forest and one of the last habitats of Bengal tigers, supports the livelihoods of millions of people.  Photograph: Bengal Picture Library/Alamy

blocks.text: Millions of people live in the Sundarbans, and many depend on the river and forests for food and other resources.

The claimants allege that Barclays failed to conduct sufficient due diligence on the environmental and human rights risks before providing financial services to organisations connected to the project.

Barclays underwrote debt of India’s state-owned NTPC Ltd (formerly the National Thermal Power Corporation), one of the joint-venture partners behind the plant, according to King’s Legal Clinic, which is assisting the complainants. It also says Barclays underwrote bond issues for the Export-Import Bank of India between 2016 and 2019, which provided a loan for the Rampal project.

The complainants argue that emissions from the plant will contribute to global heating, rising sea levels and extreme weather in a region already highly vulnerable to the climate crisis. Mangroves act as a natural barrier against cyclones and other extreme weather.

The power station faced sustained opposition during its planning and construction, including concerns raised by Unesco in a report in 2016, which concluded that “air and water pollution have a high likelihood to irreversibly damage the … World Heritage property”. Some financial institutions, including banks in France, refused to support the project because of its potential environmental and social effects, the complaint says.

Jamil said Barclays’ international standing obliged it to consider the consequences of financing. “The greater your reputation, the greater your responsibility to behave responsibly towards the planet and its people,” he said. “Barclays is a reputed global organisation, and that is why it also has a responsibility.

“Other banks and financial institutions were divesting from, or declining to finance, this project,” he added. “Barclays and other financial organisations should change their policies and examine how their operations can protect the planet from climate catastrophe.”

Jamil also called on banks to direct more funding towards renewable energy rather than imported fossil fuels. “Bangladesh has sunlight throughout the year,” he said. “Why should we expand fossil fuels when there is enormous potential to produce electricity from renewable energy?”
The other complainants include Animesh Mandal, a farmer and politician, and the Dakshinbanga Matsyajibi Forum, a trade union representing fish workers in West Bengal.
They are being assisted by students and lawyers at King’s Human Rights and Environment Clinic, part of King’s College London’s law school.

Sue Willman, a solicitor at the clinic, said: “Rural communities in the Sundarbans are on the frontline of the climate and nature crisis. We hope to persuade banks and financial institutions to think again before financing oil and coal developments that are contributing to that crisis.”
The Office for Responsible Business Conduct, part of the Department for Business and Trade, will assess whether to consider the complaint.
Barclays Bank and BIFPCL (Bangladesh India Friendship Power Company Ltd), the holding company for the Maitree super thermal power project, declined to comment.

articles.title: Guinea-Bissau voters approve new constitution expanding presidential powers
articles.summary:
Changes include fewer seats in parliament and new rules on presidential candidates ahead of December elections

Guinea-Bissau voters have approved a new constitution significantly expanding…

blocks.text: Guinea-Bissau voters have approved a new constitution significantly expanding presidential powers ahead of elections due in December.

According to provisional results, 70% of voters approved sweeping changes in the tiny west African state’s first constitutional amendment since revisions that ended the one-party socialist state more than three decades ago.
The turnout for Sunday’s referendum was reportedly over 55%, amounting to an estimated 544,060 people.

The new constitution will reduce the number of seats in parliament from 102 to 65 and cut electoral constituencies from 29 to 12. New provisions will require presidential candidates to have lived continuously in the country for at least five years before the vote, which is believed to target diaspora-based politicians with significant followings.

The referendum’s outcome is expected to pave the way for December’s elections, which many hope will steady the political landscape in Guinea-Bissau, which has been through a series of politically turbulent periods since its declaration of independence from Portugal was globally recognised in 1974. Since then it has had at least 10 coup attempts, half of which have been successful.

The most recent came after last November’s disputed presidential elections. Both candidates declared themselves winners, citing electoral malpractice by the other’s camp. The military forcefully intervened, setting up a transitional ruling council headed by Gen Horta Inta-A Na Man, a former military chief of general staff.
Na Man said: “What we want after this referendum is to allow whoever wins the elections to see out their mandate without hindrance.”
Nelson Moreira, the second vice-president of the transitional council, said the outgoing constitution, which came into effect in 1993, had often been cited as “the cause of instability in Guinea”.

The leading opposition party, the African Party for the Independence of Guinea and Cape Verde (PAIGC), which was barred from fielding a presidential candidate in the 2025 election, had asked its supporters to boycott the referendum, which it called a democratic farce.
“What will happen on 30 August is the continuation of the coup d’état carried out on 26 November,” its leader, Domingos Simões Pereira, had said.

articles.title: Japan halves speed limit to 30km/h on all narrow city streets
articles.summary:
Speed limit dropped from 60km/h for around 70% of general roads in the hope of making narrow streets of crowded cities safer

Drivers on residential roads in

blocks.text: Drivers on residential roads in Japan have been forced to take their foot off the accelerator, after the speed limit was slashed from 60km/h (37mph) to 30km/h in an attempt to reduce deaths and injuries among pedestrians on narrow urban streets.
The new limit, which went into effect on Tuesday, applies to residential roads with no centre line or maximum speed signs, media reports said.

Narrow roads with no centre lines or pavements are a common sight in crowded Japanese cities, with data indicating that children and older people are at particular risk of being involved in a fatal or serious accident.

The measures apply to about 870,000km of roads that are less than 5.5 metres wide and do not have centre lines or median strips, according to the Mainichi Shimbun. They account for about 70% of the country’s general roads, the newspaper said.
Authorities hopes the restrictions will address concerns that residential areas are not experiencing the same improvements in safety seen on larger roads.

While the overall number of deaths in traffic accidents is in decline – falling to a record low of 2,457 last year – those involving children and older people on residential roads has remained steady at about 300 a year since 2021, and rose for the first time in three years in 2025, according to the national police agency.
The introduction in 2011 of “zone 30” areas on a limited number of residential streets and along school routes resulted in a 30% reduction in fatalities and serious injuries, the Mainichi said.

Police agency data show that the mortality rate among pedestrians is less than 1% in accidents involving vehicles traveling at or below 30km/h, with the rate rising to 2.7% at speeds of 30-40km/h, and to 17.4% at 50-60km/h.

“We ask drivers to recognise that they need to take particular care on roads shared by vehicles, pedestrians and cyclists,” the police agency’s commissioner general, Yoshinobu Kusunoki, told reporters this week.

articles.title: Relief as five Australians missing in Nepal-Tibet flood disaster found alive
articles.summary: Several missing Australians have been found since Tuesday morning, bringing the total citizens unaccounted for to 38

blocks.text: A total of five Australians missing after devastating floods ravaged the Nepal-Tibet border last week have been found.
Of the five Australians confirmed safe, one was found in Nepal, one in Tibet, and three outside the crisis-hit area. The total number still missing is 38.
These Australians had not spoken to families and next of kin since the disaster struck seven days ago.
There were “grave concerns” for the dozens of citizens still missing in the disaster, the minister for multicultural affairs, Anne Aly, told the ABC on Wednesday morning.
“There are real logistic issues, including communications to find out where people are,” she said.

“For those families that are still waiting, those 38 individuals unaccounted for, we understand that it’s a really concerning time, and we’ll continue to do what we can to try and locate those people.”
Earlier, the minister for the Pacific, Pat Conroy, told Radio National the government was “focused on establishing their whereabouts and supporting their families”.
The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (Dfat) has received nearly 800 calls in relation to the floods, with 18 Australian personnel having travelled to Nepal to join staff on the ground.
More humanitarian and disaster relief from Australia was due to arrive in Nepal on Wednesday afternoon.
Another Australian, 25-year-old Cara Severino, was safely located last week.
After an Australian in Tibet made contact with family and Dfat yesterday, the foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, said the government was “incredibly thankful”.
“It’s hard to imagine the sense of relief their loved ones must be feeling after what will have been an incredibly harrowing few days.”
The death toll from the ⁠unprecedented deluge of ice, rock, mud ​and debris on Wednesday last week has risen to 939 people, with 16 more dead reported in Tibet.
More than 4,400 people are missing.
Wong said the government needed to “remain realistic” about the days ahead.
“Communications remain difficult, infrastructure has been destroyed and many areas are still difficult to reach,” she said.
“As each day passes, our grave concerns for those still unaccounted for inevitably grow.
“Our thoughts remain firmly with all those waiting for news of family and friends, and with the search and rescue teams working in extraordinarily difficult circumstances.”
Australia has sent a $8m assistance package for affected communities on the border between Nepal and the Chinese region of Tibet.
Nepal has deployed nearly 20,000 security personnel to support search and rescue, and Chinese state media has reported that 2,141 emergency personnel have been deployed.

articles.title: British aid worker mistakenly identified as a survivor of Nepal-Tibet disaster
articles.summary:
More than 1,000 people confirmed dead and more than 4,000, including 36 British nationals, remain missing

A British aid worker was mistakenly identified by Nepalese authorities as a rescued…

blocks.text: A British aid worker was mistakenly identified by Nepalese authorities as a rescued survivor after returning to Kathmandu on a humanitarian aid flight.
Alastair Chambers, a 45-year-old former Gloucester councillor, said he flew to Nepal last week to distribute sleeping bags, food and essentials to communities cut off by collapsed bridges.
After spending several days in a village near the Trishuli river in central Nepal, Chambers returned by helicopter to the capital, where he was greeted by police officers asking for his details.
“I gave them my details, just abiding by the rules, and they obviously thought that I’d been rescued,” Chambers told the Press Association.
Chambers appeared on a list of 119 names released by local authorities on Tuesday. An army spokesperson then told reporters at a press conference that a British national was among those rescued.

“I was contacted by about 15 different journalists in the last few hours, just asking how I was and how I’m feeling after being rescued, and I had to say: ‘Well sorry, I haven’t been rescued,’” Chambers told PA.
Those rescued included 118 Nepali nationals – 44 women and 74 men.
Thirty-six British nationals are missing, the Foreign Office minister, Stewart Wood, told the House of Lords on Tuesday. The figure had previously been put at 33.

Chambers was fined £49,000 after pleading guilty in June 2022 to breeding and selling dogs without a licence. The 45-year-old, who was the leader of a group of community independents on Gloucester city council until 2024, is due to face trial in November after denying he used homophobic slurs against a bar owner and former council worker.
At least 1,050 people have been confirmed dead in Nepal since Wednesday’s flash floods, while Chinese state media said 66 people had been killed in Tibet. More than 4,000 people are still missing.
Nepal’s prime minister, Balendra Shah, said 11,000 people had been rescued across the affected region. This included 330 foreign nationals, the Nepalese tourist board said in an update on Tuesday.
Preliminary analysis of satellite imagery suggests the collapse of a glacier high in the Himalayas was the primary cause of the disaster.

The collapse – so large it was initially recorded as a magnitude-4.4 earthquake – triggered a deadly torrent of water, mud and ice that tore along the Lhende Khola, Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers on Wednesday.
Crews have faced dangerous and difficult conditions while searching unstable terrain and flood debris.
Search efforts are now focused on attempts to reach about 600 workers believed to be trapped inside tunnels at several hydropower stations in the region.
“Massive work has been going on in the tunnel, all the tunnels,” the army spokesperson said on Tuesday.

A rapid deployment rescue team from the UK arrived in Nepal on Saturday to provide support for Britons and their families as part of the government’s £5m commitment to support relief and recovery efforts.
The Red Cross estimates that 93,000 people have been directly affected by the disaster.

articles.title: 'Tapusin na yan!': Prosecution to finish confidential funds article next week, says Chua
articles.summary: Saying they don't want an overly lengthy impeachment trial, members of the House prosecution panel intend to conclude its presentation on the confidential funds misuse article against Vice President…

blocks.text: Saying they don't want an overly lengthy impeachment trial, members of the House prosecution panel intend to conclude its presentation on the confidential funds misuse article against Vice President Sara Duterte next week.
According to solon-prosecutor Manila 3rd district Rep. Joel Chua, the team is already looking to shift to the two remaining articles of impeachment.

“Masasabi natin, baka by next week ay matapos na, hopefully, ang confidential funds, and we will move on to the next article,” Chua said Tuesday afternoon, Sept. 1 during the prosecution's post-hearing press conference.
(We can say that, hopefully, we could finish the confidential funds article by next week, and we will move on to the next article.)

On Tuesday, Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) Colonels Manaros Boransing II and Magtanggol Panopio testified about Army certifications that were used in the Department of Education’s (DepEd) response to state auditors.

In an effort to shorten its witness list, Chua said two other military officers would no longer be presented since their expected testimony would largely repeat the points already placed on the record.
“Iisa lang naman iyong sasabihin nila. To shorten—ayaw naman natin ng protracted hearing. Gusto natin matapos na rin ito.”
(They would only be saying the same thing. To shorten [the proceedings]—we don’t want a protracted hearing. We also want this to be finished.)
Chua said prosecutors already covered the central points involving the Youth Leadership Summits (YLS) and the military certifications.

Respondent Duterte is being accused--among other things--of misuing a total of P612.5 million worth of confidential funds released to the Office of the Vice President (OVP) and Department of Education (DepEd).
On Wednesday, Sept. 2, the prosecution expects to present former DepEd undersecretary and chief-of-staff Michael Wesley Poa, as well as a representative of the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA)

Poa, currently Duterte’s defense lawyer, is expected to address the chain behind the military certifications, while the PSA witness will cover its checks of names appearing in confidential-fund records.

After those witnesses, the Manila solon said the remaining article I lineup would be short. “Ang natitira na lamang si Mr. Edward Fajarda, and probably isa—or at most, dalawa,” he said, referring to DepEd’s former special disbursing officer (SDO).
“The only one remaining is Mr. Edward Fajarda, and probably one—or at most, two [more witnesses].”
He said the prosecution will make its final lineup decision after Wednesday’s hearing. The panel previously finished its presentation of evidence on article IV, or the death threats article.
Defense's turn next
Chua reminded impeachment trial watchers that once the prosecution finishes all four articles of impeachment, the defense must present its own case.
“May target kasi tayo. We have to understand, after us mayroon pang defense; sila naman ang magpe-present. Siyempre ayaw naman natin na umabot pa ito by next year,” he said.
(We have a target. We have to understand that after us, there is still the defense; they will be the ones to present [their case]. Of course, we don’t want this to extend into next year.)

"Sana, hopefully, by November tapos na lahat (Hopefully, everything will be finished by November), so by December we can have the decision of the impeachment court whether or not to convict the Vice President," Chua said.

articles.title: Will impeachment trial prosecutors resign? Not anymore, says Chua
articles.summary: The House prosecution team's core of 11 solon-prosecutors will remain intact in Vice President Sara Duterte's impeachment trial. Thus, said prosecutor Manila 3rd district Rep. Joel Chua, with the…

blocks.text: The House prosecution team's core of 11 solon-prosecutors will remain intact in Vice President Sara Duterte's impeachment trial.
Thus, said prosecutor Manila 3rd district Rep. Joel Chua, with the revelation shelving a proposal for some of them to resign from the panel so they could speak publicly about the merits of the case.
“We have decided, wala na lang munang mag-resign,” Chua said Tuesday, Sept. 1 following day 20 of the high-stakes proceedings.
The panel considered a reshuffle after the Senate impeachment court reiterated the sub judice rule, or the limits on public comments about matters being tried.

One option was for selected House prosecutors to leave the panel and serve only as spokespersons. “Noong una, isa iyon sa mga naging discussion kung ganoon ang mangyayari. Kasi iyon ang talagang unang option,” Chua said.
(At first, that was one of the discussions, if that was what would happen. Because that was really the first option.)
The idea drew support from lawyers working with the team. “May mga suggestion ang ibang private prosecutor at public prosecutor na may ilan mag-resign para maging spokesperson."
(Some private prosecutors and public prosecutors suggested that some members resign so they could serve as spokespersons.)
But Chua said the prosecution members ultimately chose continuity. He noted that changing the structure of the team at this stage would require finding replacements.
“After considering everything, total isang buwan na lang kung masusunod iyong ating target...Too late na kung magbabawas tayo at magdadagdag pa,” Chua said.
(After considering everything, there’s only about a month left if we follow our target...It’s too late if we start removing and adding members.)
As such, the team will keep public briefings focused on schedules, witness sequencing, and other procedural updates.
More importantly, Chua said the prosectors "will just try to explain things in a way that does not touch on the merits [of the case]".

That was also why Chua, a public prosecutor, appeared at Tuesday’s briefing. He said reporters could still ask about what comes next without forcing prosecutors into a public discussion of the evidence.
“Baka may magtanong tungkol sa procedural aspect outside the merits of the case, so I can answer that,” said the veteran lawmaker from Manila.
(Someone might ask about the procedural aspects outside the merits of the case, so I can answer that.)
The approach allows the public to receive practical updates while the same prosecutors continue their work inside the impeachment court, Chua said.
It also preserves the team’s current assignments as the prosecution tries to finish article I on confidential funds and move to the remaining articles of impeachment against Duterte.
Fifteen private prosecutors are helping the solon-prosecutors gain a conviction from the respondent, free of charge.

articles.title: Philippines prepares for unprecedented 5-million tons rice imports
articles.summary: The Philippines will import a record-high five million metric tons (MT) this year, as it turns to foreign supplies to offset a projected shortfall in domestic production caused by El Niño, according…

blocks.text: The Philippines will import a record-high five million metric tons (MT) this year, as it turns to foreign supplies to offset a projected shortfall in domestic production caused by El Niño, according to the Department of Agriculture (DA).

“As we are facing El Niño, we are projecting that we might need to import up to five million MT for this year,” said Agriculture Secretary Francisco Tiu Laurel during his agency’s budget hearing on Tuesday, Sept. 1.
The projected import volume this year is nearly four percent higher than the current record of 4.81 million MT set in 2024.
Total rice imports as of Aug. 13 reached 3.46 million MT, already higher than the 3.39 million MT recorded last year, according to the Bureau of Plant Industry (BPI).
Tiu Laurel said the additional rice supply will serve as a buffer as the country’s rice production losses are estimated to reach 900,000 MT within the year.
He said the decline represents the “worst-case scenario” of a strong El Niño in the fourth quarter of the year, which is projected to damage several hectares of rice farms.
“What we are all doing this year is precautionary. It is better to be prepared and have enough supply rather than risk having a shortage,” said Tiu Laurel.
Tiu Laurel noted that increased rice imports for the year will also serve as a supply cushion for the first quarter of next year in order to get ahead of a potentially weaker harvest season.
Considering this, the import volume for 2027 may go down to the normal range of between 3.8 million MT and four million MT.
While the country relies on foreign supplies to meet domestic demand, Tiu Laurel said the main objective of the government continues to be increasing local output.
He told lawmakers that the DA is focused on rolling out mechanization measures, expanding irrigation, and developing new rice seeds to further boost productivity.
The agency is also preparing to implement a program requiring traders to first invest in rice mills and processing facilities before they allowed to purchase rice from abroad.
It is estimated that around 80 percent of rice importers in the country are engaged solely in importing and have yet to commit investments in the local rice sector.
“That is one of the plans to make the industry self-sustaining and competitive in the international market,” said Tiu Laurel.
Based on BPI data, Vietnam has maintained its position as the country’s top rice supplier with imports reaching 2.56 million MT, or 74 percent of the total volume, as of Aug. 13.
Other top sources of rice include Thailand with 378,404 MT, Myanmar with 286,052 MT, Pakistan with 107,485 MT, and Cambodia with 87,802 MT.
The DA’s proposed budget for next year is ₱198.45 billion, down eight percent from the allocation of ₱215.69 billion for this year.

Under this budget, the agency wants to prioritize programs that raise farm and fishery productivity, improve infrastructure, reduce post-harvest losses, strengthen logistics and market access, and expand the use of technology.

articles.title: Creamline stays unscathed; EST Cola sweeps Farm Fresh
articles.summary: Creamline routed Ho Chih Minh City, 25-18, 25-16, 25-6, to remain unscathed, while EST Cola swept Farm Fresh, 25-21, 25-16, 25-22, to barge into the win column in the PVL Invitational at the Smart…

blocks.text: Creamline routed Ho Chih Minh City, 25-18, 25-16, 25-6, to remain unscathed, while EST Cola swept Farm Fresh, 25-21, 25-16, 25-22, to barge into the win column in the PVL Invitational at the Smart Araneta Coliseumon Tuesday, Sept. 1.
The Cool Smashers exposed the Vietnamese’s lethargic plays, needing 61 minutes to dominate the guest team for their second straight win in as many outings.
Tots Carlos, Jema Galanza and Jaja Santiago-Minowa paced Creamline with 12 points apiece, including combined 21 kills from Carlos and Galanza, and three blocks from Santiago-Minowa.
So dominant were the Cool Smashers that they overpowered the Vietnamese spikers on attacks, 49-19; blocks, 11-4; and aces, 5-3.
None from Ho Chi Minh City scored in twin figures with skipper Dang Thi Kim Thanh and Le Thi My Xuyen pacing only eight and six points, respectively, as they absorbed their second straight loss.
Earlier, EST Cola made its title bid to improve its record to 1-1 behind the efforts of Papatchaya Phontham.
Phontham blasted 17 points built on 13 kills, three aces and one block to shackle Farm Fresh, which struggled despite the 15-point effort of Trisha Tubu.

articles.title: Yamsuan bent on helping CHEd once travel tax windfall stops
articles.summary: A solon who holds a key position in the House 2027 national budget process has vowed to help find alternative funding for the Commission on Higher Education (CHEd) should the measure abolishing the…

blocks.text: A solon who holds a key position in the House 2027 national budget process has vowed to help find alternative funding for the Commission on Higher Education (CHEd) should the measure abolishing the travel tax becomes a law this year.

Parañaque City 2nd district Rep. Brian Raymund Yamsuan has noted that CHEd, which regulates higher education and administers the government’s financial aid programs for tertiary-level students, gets part of its funding from 40 percent of the total gross collections from the travel tax.

Yamsuan, a member of the House Budget Amendments and Review Subcommittee (BARSc) pointed out that under Malacañang’s National Expenditure Program for Fiscal Year 2027, a portion of the allocation for the CHEd’s Higher Education Development Fund (HEDF) would still be sourced from the travel tax collections of the Tourism Infrastructure and Enterprise Zone Authority (TIEZA).

“Kami po ay magtatrabaho sa Kongreso para hanapan kayo ng alternative sources of funding once mangyari po ang pagsasabatas ng abolition ng travel tax,” Yamsuan told CHEd Chairperson Shirley Agrupis during the House Committee on Appropriations’ recent budget deliberations on the agency’s proposed 2027 budget.
(We will work in Congress to look for alternative sources of funding once the travel tax measure is enacted into law.)

Formed during last year's budget cycle as a pro-transparency measure, the BARSc effectively replaced the so-called "small committee", which incorporates individual ammendments to the General Appropriations Bill (GAB) or proposed national budget.

If the bill abolishing the travel tax is passed into law, Agrupis told the House Committee on Tourism last March that without a substitute funding source, the CHEd would lose 85.6 percent of the funding for the HEDF.
She calls this prospect “a structural loss that directly affects scholarships, research and institutional upgrading, and tourism education programs".

The House of Representatives approved on March 16 the measure seeking to abolish the travel tax. Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian earlier said the Senate version of the measure is included in the chamber’s priority list of bills and will be passed this year.

“Kami bilang member ng BARSc, sisiguraduhin ko po na sa susunod na pagpupulong with (Committee on Appropriations) Chair Mika (Suansing) ay gagawa po kami ng paraan upang maibalik ang pondo para hindi maantala ang magagandang programa ng CHEd,” Yamsuan added.

(As member of the BARSc, I would make sure that in the next meeting with Committee on Appropriations Chairperson Mikaela Angela Suansing, we would find ways to restore CHEd’s funding so as not to delay the implementation of CHEd’s good programs)

During the hearing, the Parañaque solon also thanked the CHEd for its efficient implementation of the government’s higher education initiatives and financial assistance to tertiary-level students, particularly the Tulong Dunong Program (TDP).
The TDP provides a financial grant of up to P7,500 per semester or a total of P15,000 per school year to help cover the tuition and other daily expenses of qualified college students.
Yamsuan urged the CHEd to conduct more consultations with Local Universities and Colleges (LUC) to help them institute reforms that would allow them to take part in the TDP.
Out of 170 LUCs, only 116 are CHEd-recognized institutions qualified to accept TDP grants from its enrollees.

articles.title: On the borderline
articles.summary: With these three novels, we use borderline in both a physical sense and in a metaphorical manner, as the trio of books explores what ‘the other side’ can mean. "Sublimation" by Isabel J. Kim Think of…

blocks.text: With these three novels, we use borderline in both a physical sense and in a metaphorical manner, as the trio of books explores what ‘the other side’ can mean.
"Sublimation" by Isabel J. Kim

Think of the immigrant experience, but now seen through a SciFi lens, and you have an idea of what this novel bravely explores. Kim has written short stories that have won Nebula, Locus, and Shirley Jackson Awards, and this is her debut novel. Soyoung Rose Kang is the protagonist here, and at the age of 10, she left Korea with her mother to emigrate to the USA. She left an ‘instance’ in Korea, who would continue to interact with her family and grandfather. And now, with the death of the grandfather, Soyoung (the instance in Korea) gets in touch with Rose (the instance in the USA), to let her know it was their grandfather’s wish that she come to Seoul for the funeral. What Rose isn’t aware of is that Soyoung harbors the desire to reintegrate. This gets complicated by the fact that the grandfather has left his house to Rose - who never tried to establish a relationship with Soyoung, or her ‘lolo’.

Structured initially so that the chapters alternate between Soyoung and Rose’s POVs, Kim pulls off this delicate balancing act with a lot of skill and charm. She endeavors to make both Soyoung and Rose distinct, while also having such similarities so we appreciate how they are, in fact, two versions of the same person. They’re not twins or doppelgangers, but two ‘instances’-and before the grandfather’s death and meeting in Seoul, have not really been in contact with each other. To make our reading more intense, there’s a Yujin in Korea, and his instance, YJ, in New York. Childhood friend of Soyoung, the Yujin pair have their own set of issues, but have been friends since the moment of ‘instance’, communicating regularly. Their story and how it intersects with that of Soyoung Rose take up the last half of this novel, which takes us to some hard decision-making and the facing of consequences. Bold, imaginative writing that speaks of borders and identity.
"The Pinnacle" by Abir Mukhergee

Set in the penthouse of a luxury condominium called The Pinnacle in Mumbai, this new novel from the author of Hunted, which was named 2025 Thriller of the Year, is both a locked-room mystery thriller and a penetrating study of class dynamics in India today. George Abercrombie is an over-the-hill Hollywood actor who’s married to Sweety Sahota, the current queen of Bollywood. Gemma is Sweety’s PA who joined them in India all the way from the US. The premise has to do with George waking up after a quarrel with Sweety and a drinking binge, and finding her murdered on their king-size bed. With no recollection of what he did the night before, one narrative strand has to do with George having to prove he’s innocent. Then there’s Gemma, who’s receiving cryptic text messages. And finally, there’s Amit, George’s shadow and PA, who seems to know too much and goes on the run.

The seedy underbelly of luxury living is exposed in this gripping adventure. We may be on the 68th floor of an upscale skyscraper, but the hypocrisy, filth, and societal evil still reach these heights. The novel revolves around three plots, and the borders of society and social standing are constantly placed as reminders of what our protagonists have to face on a Daily basis. As in Hunted, Mukhergee is excellent at piling on the action and turning the screws tighter as the novel enters the home stretch. If you’re the type who reads late at night before getting a good night’s sleep, be forewarned that this is a biting thriller, and you’ll be reluctant to put it down, as you’ll be wanting to know what happens next. It’s that well-paced. I would not be surprised if both Hollywood and Bollywood will go bidding for the movie rights to this book; and I know I’ll be looking forward to its film adaptation, and the casting.
"The Lighthouse At the End of the World" by Philip A. Suggars

Think Oliver Twist, but updated for today’s London; then add a spice of portal-esque fantasy - and you’ll have an idea of just how original an adventure this debut novel of Suggars is. It's Charles Dickens meets SciFi, and Oyster McCellan is our scrappy 15-year-old guide to this nifty piece of world-building - two distinct worlds, to be exact. First time we meet Oyster, he’s a member of the Urbans, a small-time gang of grifters who operate around Westminster, hoping to fleece unsuspecting tourists. His father, Lucas, was formerly the head of the gang, but he disappeared without any explanation. So now Oyster has to earn a keep, to help his sister Cecile continue her studies, and their mother Paris, who is still in something of a daze. It’s when a money drop goes terribly wrong that Oyster finds himself in an alternate Greater London.

The novel is familial trauma mixed with immersive world-building. Greater London is a version where leviathans roam the seas, and strangely sympathetic and communicating ink beetles nestle beneath the skin of Oyster’s armpit. Plus there looms the nagging question of whether his father Lucas escaped here, and what his role is in the scheme of things. Meanwhile, as we join Oyster, our tourist guide to Greater London, we encounter the enigma Nonesuch, a female practitioner of rappelling and scavenging skills, the escapist Marya Petrovna who seems to take Oyster under her protective wing but for what deeper purpose, and the terrifying Mr. Primrose, who seems to have his finger on all of Oyster’s movements between worlds, and seems to have confederates from within Oyster’s own gang of Urbans. There’s so much to relish and enjoy as we suspend disbelief and surrender to Suggars' vision and world-building.

articles.title: Philippines, Nigeria can develop, explore many opportunities — Marcos
articles.summary: The Philippines and Nigeria can explore and develop many opportunities, President Marcos said as he welcomed Nigeria’s new ambassador to the country. Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of…

blocks.text: The Philippines and Nigeria can explore and develop many opportunities, President Marcos said as he welcomed Nigeria’s new ambassador to the country.

Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of the Federal Republic of Nigeria to the Republic of the Philippines Ibok-Ete Ekwe Ibas presented his Letter of Credence to Marcos at Malacañan Palace on Tuesday, Sept. 1.
During the presentation of credentials, Marcos told the Nigerian envoy that their countries can potentially expand their partnership in energy security, trade, and investment.

"The Philippines and Nigeria have significant potential to expand cooperation especially in energy security, trade and investment, and pursue initiatives that would mutually benefit our peoples and our countries," Marcos said.
"There are many things that, in my view, we can explore and develop. There are so many opportunities that will be of mutual benefit to both our countries," the President added.
"During your tenure as Ambassador, I look forward to further strengthening bilateral relations between our two countries," Marcos also said.
Marcos further said he looks forward to working with the Nigerian ambassador to promote and deepen the Philippines' and Nigeria's collaboration and cooperation, which has spanned 64 years.
Ambassador Ibas, for his part, assured the President that he would work hard to strengthen the friendly, strong bilateral relations between the two countries.
Ibas was joined by his wife and other Embassy officials during the ceremony.
Also present during the event were Foreign Affairs Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro, DFA Assistant Secretary Germinia Aguilar-Usudan, and Deputy Chief of Presidential Protocol Dennis Briones.
The Philippines and Nigeria established diplomatic relations on August 1, 1962, and will mark 65 years of diplomatic relations in 2027.

articles.title: Severe offenders face exclusion: DepEd tightens penalties for bullying, violence, threats in schools
articles.summary: Learners who commit severe acts of bullying, physical assault, or threats may face immediate exclusion, non-readmission, and mandatory referral to law enforcement or social welfare authorities under…

blocks.text: (PHOTO: PIXABAY)

Learners who commit severe acts of bullying, physical assault, or threats may face immediate exclusion, non-readmission, and mandatory referral to law enforcement or social welfare authorities under stricter Department of Education (DepEd) rules.

This was the agency’s warning as it formalized consolidated learner protection protocols under DepEd Order No. 006, s. 2026, or the Guidelines on Ensuring a Safe and Motivating Learning Environment (ESMLE).

According to DepEd, its campaign against violence and classroom disruptions is being implemented in coordination with partner agencies, local government units (LGUs), law enforcement authorities, and local communities.
While learners deserve an opportunity to change, Angara said DepEd would never put the safety of the majority at risk.
“Ang paaralan ay dapat maging ligtas at tahimik na lugar para sa lahat (Schools should be safe and peaceful places for everyone),” he said in a statement.
The education department said severe offenses will prompt immediate inter-agency action under the policy.

“Grounded in a whole-of-society framework, the guidelines mandate direct coordination between school administrations, the Philippine National Police (PNP), the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD), LGUs, and communities to address safety threats both on-site and online,” it said.

Per DepEd, a school’s Child Protection Committee must immediately investigate any reported bullying incident or safety threat, secure the victim’s safety, and provide affected learners with mental health and psychosocial support.
“The policy enforces a progressive disciplinary framework depending on the severity of the offense,” the agency stated.
DepEd said first-level or minor infractions will result in a written reprimand, parental notification, and guidance counseling.

“Second-level or serious offenses such as repeated bullying and online harassment result in an immediate suspension of up to five days and mandatory DSWD referral, escalating to non-readmission on the second offense, and full exclusion on the third,” it added.

Meanwhile, the agency said third-level or high-risk acts, including those involving severe physical harm, bomb threats, or dangerous hoaxes, will result in non-readmission for the first offense and permanent exclusion for the second, as well as immediate turnover to law enforcement authorities.
“School heads are also authorized to issue a 30-day preventive suspension during ongoing investigations if a learner poses a continuing risk to campus safety,” it stated.
As such, DepEd said it has streamlined the response to bullying incidents, with teachers tasked to directly handle and resolve conduct considered a precursor to bullying.

“For Second-level offenses that cause harm to other learners and stakeholders, the Learner Formation Officer intervenes and provides recommendations to the school head, as the case may be,” the agency said.
“A Third-level offense is resolved by the School Head who also imposes the appropriate sanction. At all levels, the parents of the learner-offender are informed.”
DepEd stressed that aside from administrative sanctions, offenders referred to external authorities may face criminal liability or custodial intervention, depending on the offense.
Angara warned that DepEd would strictly enforce the measures to uphold its zero-tolerance policy against violence and disruption.

"Kung ang isang estudyante ay gagamit ng dahas, mananakit, magdadala ng patalim o baril, mag-aaksaya ng oras sa paggawa ng bomb threat jokes o pranks, o patuloy na mambubully ng kaklase, hindi natin ito papalampasin (If a student resorts to violence, harms others, brings a knife or firearm, makes bomb threats as jokes or pranks, or repeatedly bullies a classmate, we will not let it pass),” he said.

“Ipatutupad natin ang pinakamabigat na parusa kabilang ang pagpapatalsik sa paaralan at direktang pag-turnover sa mga awtoridad (We will impose the most severe penalties, including expulsion from school and direct turnover to the authorities),” he added.
Under non-readmission, an offender may finish the current academic year but cannot re-enroll the following year, DepEd said.
Exclusion, meanwhile, immediately removes the learner from the school’s active rolls, with education continuing only through alternative interventions.

articles.title: Marcos: We are prepared for Bangsamoro first parliamentary elections
articles.summary: Despite several postponements, the first parliamentary elections in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) will push through, President Marcos affirmed. The government, Marcos…

blocks.text: Despite several postponements, the first parliamentary elections in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) will push through, President Marcos affirmed.
The government, Marcos said, is prepared to finally make it happen.

"We are prepared for the first parliamentary elections in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao on September 14th," Marcos said during the opening ceremony of the 2026 National Peace Consciousness Month on Tuesday, Sept. 1.
"Despite several postponements, the government never lost hope and remains fully committed to supporting this democratic exercise," he added.
The Chief Executive assured the Bangsamoro region that the administration will ensure the upcoming polls will be held peacefully.
"Be assured that this administration will do everything within our mandate to ensure that the elections are safe, peaceful, and credible," Marcos said.

"We will protect the right of every Bangsamoro voter to cast a ballot freely and without fear. Let this election show that the future of the Bangsamoro is shaped by the people themselves, through your voices, your choices, and your hopes for your respective communities," he added.
Marcos also said that the election in Bangsamoro is "another opportunity to show that the gains of peace can be strengthened through democratic institutions."
Peace must be chosen, lived, strengthened
In his speech, the President underscored that "peace entails responsibility," urging the citizenry to always choose to be at peace with fellow Filipinos.
"It must be chosen. It must be lived, protected, and strengthened every single day," he said.
Marcos stressed that every Filipino has a role to play in strengthening peace in the country, emphasizing that "peace is the seed of progress."

"Let us always choose to be at peace with our fellow Filipinos. Just like any family, we may have different and disagreeing views. However, we remain bound by something much stronger than our differences," he said.
"We share one home. We share one future. We share one Filipino identity," he added.

articles.title: Duped on confidential funds? Prosecution spoxes say DepEd under VP Sara pulled a fast one on AFP
articles.summary: The Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) was allegedly "duped" into issuing certifications that were later used by the Department of Education (DepEd) under then-secretary, Vice President Sara…

blocks.text: The Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) was allegedly "duped" into issuing certifications that were later used by the Department of Education (DepEd) under then-secretary, Vice President Sara Duterte to help justify the liquidation of P15.54 million in confidential funds, House prosecutors said Tuesday.

House prosecution panel layman spokespersons Lanao del Sur 1st district Rep. Zia Alonto Adiong and Robert Ace Barbers had this to say during day 20 of Duterte’s Senate impeachment trial, which featured the testimony of Col. Manaros Boransing II.
“Isa lang po ang puwedeng ma-draw as a conclusion from the testimony of Colonel Boransing: nabudol po ang AFP,” Adiong said in no uncertain terms.
(Only one conclusion can be drawn from Colonel Boransing’s testimony: the AFP was duped.)

Boransing testified that his Jan. 1, 2024 certification to DepEd--as presented before senator-judges Tuesday--covered eight Youth Leadership Summits (YLS) and 53 Information Education Campaign (IEC) activities conducted by the 1st Infantry “Tabak” Division with other stakeholders in 2023.

He also testified that no DepEd money was released or downloaded to his division for the activities. He said he understood the document as a routine certification of participation, and only learned during an October 2024 House probe that DepEd had used it in responding to the Commission on Audit's (COA) findings on the agency’s confidential funds.
“Nabudol ang AFP dahil hiningan sila ng certification na ang paggamit noon ay i-justify nila sa COA,” Adiong said.
(The AFP was duped because they were asked for a certification that was later used to justify [the expenditure] before the COA.)

DepEd attached the Army certifications to its April 17, 2024 response to COA Audit Observation Memorandum No. 2024-015, which sought records supporting rewards totaling P15.54 million for the reported success of information-gathering or surveillance activities.
Adiong said the certifications could only establish that the activities took place, not that confidential funds were spent on them.

“The certificate only proves that there was a summit that was conducted. There was such an event that happened on that particular date. It did not prove anything as to the utilization of confidential funds. It did not prove anything that the reward was made during that event."
Likewise, Barbers underscored that the AFP certifications were obtained without the issuing officers knowing how they would eventually be used.

“The AFP was duped. Its certifications were obtained, but the officers who issued them did not even know that their documents would later be used to support the liquidation of P15 million in confidential funds,” Barbers said.

Former DepEd Undersecretary Michael Poa had acknowledged requesting then-undersecretary Nolasco Mempin to secure military certifications in connection with the liquidation of the confidential-fund expenditure.

“You cannot use an AFP certification to prove that money was spent when the AFP did not receive the money, did not spend the money, and did not know its certification would be used as proof of the expenditure,” stressed the former three-term Surigao del Norte representative.
Up to court to decide

Barbers said the impeachment court would ultimately determine whether or not the episode resulted from gross negligence or was part of a deliberate scheme to create a paper trail for the P15.54-million expenditure.
“If the AFP itself says it did not fund these activities and did not know why its certifications were being secured, then what exactly were those certifications supposed to clear?” Barbers asked.
“The documents may carry official seals and signatures, but those signatures do not magically turn an unsupported expenditure into a legitimate one,” he further said.

articles.title: ‘Survivor Philippines,’ ‘StarStruck’ director Monti Parungao dies at 58
articles.summary: Film and television director Monti Puno Parungao, known for his work on GMA Network programs “Survivor Philippines,” “StarStruck,” and “Dear Uge,” died Tuesday, September 1. He was 58. Parungao died…

blocks.text: Film and television director Monti Puno Parungao, known for his work on GMA Network programs “Survivor Philippines,” “StarStruck,” and “Dear Uge,” died Tuesday, September 1. He was 58.
Parungao died at his home in Quezon City after battling Stage 4 colon cancer, according to his brother Hardy Parungao.
The Parungao family announced his passing on social media.
“It is with great sadness that the Parungao family announces the passing of Edgardo Puno Parungao III (Direk Monti) on September 1, 2026,” the family said.
“Details of a service to celebrate and honor his life will follow. The family is grateful for your prayers, love and support,” it added.
Parungao began working at GMA in 1987 and went on to build a career spanning television, film, advertising, theater, and events.
He was among the directors of “Survivor Philippines,” the local version of the international reality competition franchise, and also worked on “StarStruck,” GMA’s long-running talent search.
He also directed episodes of “Dear Uge,” the comedy anthology series hosted by Eugene Domingo.
Beyond television, Parungao worked as a screenwriter, producer, editor, and director. He was also known for LGBTQ-themed films, including “Sagwan” and "Bayaw".
Parungao underwent several surgeries in recent months as he battled cancer.

articles.title: Philippines in running for full MCC compact after securing $60-million energy grant
articles.summary: Fresh from securing approval for a $60-million United States (US) grant for energy-sector reforms, the Philippines is now among 91 countries in the running for a full-fledged Millennium Challenge…

blocks.text: Fresh from securing approval for a $60-million United States (US) grant for energy-sector reforms, the Philippines is now among 91 countries in the running for a full-fledged Millennium Challenge Corp. (MCC) compact, potentially opening the door to a much larger development grant similar to the $434-million package it received more than a decade ago.

In its Candidate Country Report for Fiscal Year (FY) 2027 published last Monday, Aug. 31, MCC included the Philippines among countries that may be considered for its flagship compact assistance program.

The Philippines’ inclusion as a candidate, however, does not yet guarantee another compact, as MCC will still assess which countries will qualify and ultimately be selected for negotiations with the US before year-end.

In choosing eligible countries, MCC considers their commitment to just and democratic governance, economic freedom, and investments in their people, as well as their potential to reduce poverty and generate economic growth.
Candidate countries must also have gross national income (GNI) per capita of no more than $8,105 for FY 2027 and remain eligible to receive US economic assistance.

The development comes just over two months after MCC’s board approved the Philippines’ second threshold program, providing about $60 million in grant financing to address policy and institutional constraints in the energy sector.
Unlike loans, MCC grants do not have to be repaid by recipient governments.
Threshold programs are smaller grants focused on policy, regulatory, and institutional reforms, while compacts are MCC’s larger, five-year grants aimed at reducing poverty through economic growth.

Department of Finance (DOF) Secretary Frederick D. Go earlier told Manila Bulletin that the latest threshold program “serves as a critical stepping stone toward qualifying for a future MCC compact program.”

The $60-million threshold grant will finance the Energy Development Governance Efficiency Project, aimed at removing bottlenecks that delay power projects and strengthening the reliability of the country’s electricity supply.

The program will support reforms to streamline energy planning, programming, and permitting, alongside targeted investments aimed at improving energy-sector operations as well as encouraging greater private investment.
The Philippines was first selected to develop the latest threshold program in December 2023 and was reselected in December 2024 before receiving final approval from MCC’s board last June 24.

The latest grant is the Philippines’ second threshold program. Its first, implemented from 2006 to 2009 during the Arroyo administration through the now-defunct US Agency for International Development (USAID), focused on improving fiscal policy and strengthening the government’s fight against corruption.

That program provided training, technical support, as well as information technology (IT) systems to investigators, prosecutors, revenue officials, and anti-corruption agencies. More than 3,000 government personnel received specialized training, while all nine performance targets were exceeded, including those covering corruption convictions, tax administration, and anti-smuggling enforcement.
The Philippines subsequently graduated to a full-scale MCC compact worth $434 million, implemented from 2011 to 2016 during the Benigno Aquino III administration.
The five-year compact financed projects to modernize government business processes, rehabilitate roads, and support community-driven development initiatives.

During the administration of former President Rodrigo R. Duterte, however, the Philippines did not secure a second MCC compact after the US aid agency deferred its reselection in 2016 due to “significant concerns around rule of law and civil liberties,” amid human rights concerns surrounding the deadly war on drugs.

articles.title: Palace: Marcos spent time with wife, but not during peak of flooding
articles.summary: Malacañang has set the record straight about a video of President Marcos singing during First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos’ birthday celebration on Aug. 26, saying the event took place before heavy rains…

blocks.text: Malacañang has set the record straight about a video of President Marcos singing during First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos’ birthday celebration on Aug. 26, saying the event took place before heavy rains hit Luzon, causing severe flooding.

Palace Press Officer and Communications Undersecretary Claire Castro clarified that the event, which surfaced over the weekend, did not occur during the peak of flooding in Metro Manila and Central Luzon provinces.
Castro said there is no truth to the narrative detractors allegedly want to spread.

"Naganap po ang pagharana ng Pangulo, kay First Lady, hindi po ito iyong kasagsagan noong malakas na ulan, hindi po ito kasagsagan ng pagbaha (The President’s serenade for the First Lady did not take place at the height of the heavy rains. It was not during the height of the flooding)," Castro said in a Palace briefing on Tuesday, Sept. 1.
The Palace spokesperson alleged that it was the message circulated by those who spread the video, whom she called "detractors and obstructionists."

"So, kumalat at ang dumating na mensahe sa iba nating mga kababayan ay nangharana ang Pangulo kay First Lady noong gabing malakas ang ulan at noong gabing bumabaha ng todo-todo dito sa Central Luzon at sa Metro Manila. Hindi po iyan ang katotohanan (The message that reached some of our fellow Filipinos was that the President serenaded the First Lady on the night when heavy rains were falling and when severe flooding was occurring here in Central Luzon and Metro Manila. That is not the truth," Castro stressed.
Castro said she cannot blame the public for calling the video insensitive as they only reacted to what the detractors wanted them to see.
"So, naiintintihan po namin kayo, kasi iba po iyong kwentong naipalabas ( We understand you because a different story was being portrayed)," she said.

"Pero, sana makita rin po natin na sa buong linggo, hanggang kahapon kahit walang pasok at holiday, ang Pangulo po ay tutok hindi po nagpapabaya ang Pangulo para maibigay lahat ang pangangailangan ng ating mga kababayan, lalong-lalo na iyong mga naapektuhan (But I hope we can also see that throughout the entire week, up until yesterday, even though there were no classes and it was a holiday, the President remained focused and did not neglect his duties to provide everything our fellow Filipinos needed, especially those who were affected)," she added.
'The President gave only a little of his time'
Castro also clarified that the President serenaded the First Lady after finishing his work.
She pointed out that the President dedicated only a small portion of his time to the celebration.

"Kung nagharana man ang Pangulo, para sa kanyang asawa at mga kasama ang ilang malalapit na kamag-anak, kaunting oras lang po ang ibinigay ng Pangulo, para sa kanyang pamilya, para sa kanyang asawa para i-celebrate ang buhay (If the President did serenade his wife, in the presence of a few close relatives and companions, the President gave only a little of his time to his family and to his wife to celebrate her life)," Castro said.

"At hindi po nagpabaya ang Pangulo sa kaunting oras na ito na ibinigay para sa kanyang asawa (During that brief time he set aside for his wife, the President did not neglect his responsibilities)," Castro added.
The Palace mouthpiece further clarified that even though the President attended the event, "he continued to monitor the situation and what the weather conditions might be."
"Pero at that time, wala pong masamang panahon, iyon po ang dapat nating linawin (At that time, however, there was no bad weather. That is what we need to clarify)," Castro said.

articles.title: Cop killed while trying to arrest robbery suspect in Batangas
articles.summary: BALAYAN, Batangas - A police officer was killed by a robbery suspect in a follow-up operation in Barangay Sampaga here on Saturday afternoon, Aug. 30. The report identified the fatality as Police…

blocks.text: BALAYAN, Batangas - A police officer was killed by a robbery suspect in a follow-up operation in Barangay Sampaga here on Saturday afternoon, Aug. 30.
The report identified the fatality as Police Staff Sergeant Von Rico Macuha, a member of Sta. Teresita, Batangas Municipal Police Station (MPS).
He was shot in the head by the suspect who was allegedly involved in robbery incident and was identified as Carlo Arcilla Sape, a resident of Sta. Rita town.

According to the report police team went to the temporary residence of the suspect in the said village but he sensed the presence of the police and fled, prompting the police team to pursue him at about 4 p.m.
During the pursuit, the suspect proceeded to an elevated area and allegedly fired at the pursuing police operatives, hitting Macuha in the head.
Macuha was immediately taken to a medical facility in Calaca City and was transferred to the Intensive Care Unit (ICU) in s hospital in Balayan town where he died.

The Provincial Police Intelligence Unit, Batangas Police Provincial Office (PIU-BPPO), and Provincial Mobile Force Company (PMFC) were immediately deployed to augment Sta. Teresita MPS in the ongoing hot-pursuit operation against the fleeing suspect.
